note: QBank/GT layer for Trace: bank chips, top-up lines, Crossfire and checked fixes per card, plus Top-up cards per deck. Card text is never changed.

lines: DocT: Read BS-13 by its bullets, not its table: the table's column headers are swapped. p <0.05 = outside the 95% zone = significant = H0 rejected; p >0.05 = inside the zone = not significant = H0 not rejected.

DocT: p = 0.09 is not significant at alpha 0.05, so H0 is 'not rejected' (not 'accepted'); it is weak evidence against H0 (a trend), not proof of no effect. 'Insufficient power' cannot be concluded from the p-value alone; that needs the sample-size calculation or a wide CI.
DocT GT: Grade the p-value: <0.05 significant, <0.01 highly significant, <0.001 very highly significant. So p = 0.008 is 'highly significant' and H0 is rejected.

fix.t: Swap headers: **p-value > 0.05** | **p-value < 0.05** (or swap the row cells). Also "H0 accepted" → "fail to reject H0".
fix.why: Table column headers swapped: p < 0.05 sits under "non-significant / H0 accepted". Bullets below are correct.

lines: DocT + DocT GT: The p-value is NOT 'the probability the result occurred by chance' (the card's wording, a common misdefinition). It is the probability of data this extreme or more extreme IF the null hypothesis were true, so a small p = strong evidence AGAINST H0; it gives no effect size, causation or strength of relationship.

DocT (×2): A 95% CI estimates the POPULATION parameter, not the sample mean (that is known exactly). Strictly, 95% of intervals from repeated samples would contain the true value; 'a 95% probability the true value lies in this interval' is the accepted exam shorthand. Narrower CI = more precision (larger n).

fix.t: p-value = probability of getting a result at least this extreme IF the null hypothesis is true
fix.why: Defines p-value as "probability the result occurred by chance" — the classic misdefinition.

lines: DocT (×2): A parallel control arm (placebo, standard care or no intervention) separates the drug's effect from natural course, regression to the mean, repeated-testing and placebo effects, which a single-group pre/post design cannot. Placebo also allows blinding; when an effective treatment exists the control must be the active standard (Declaration of Helsinki).

DocT (×2) + DocT GT: When no option says 'each patient is their own control', DocT keys 'minimise carry-over effects in a repeated-measures study'. Strictly, washout is what minimises carry-over, but the other options (groups with different baselines, long-term effects, blinding) are plainly wrong for a crossover.
cross: DocT and DocT GT key 'to minimise carry-over effects' as the purpose of a crossover design. Truth: the purpose is that each subject is their own control (less between-subject variability, smaller sample); carry-over is its main drawback, handled by a washout. If 'own control' is offered pick it; otherwise pick carry-over.

lines: DocT: Using both qualitative and quantitative data in one study = MIXED-METHODS research. 'Qualitative first' is only one design (exploratory sequential); explanatory sequential is quantitative first then interviews, and convergent runs both together then merges.

DocT: Content analysis = systematic coding of text, speech or images into categories and themes, a qualitative method (codes can be counted). Do not confuse it with content VALIDITY (whether a questionnaire covers all domains of a construct).

DocT: SIMPLE randomisation = each patient allocated independently by a pure random process (computer, random-number table, coin); BLOCK randomisation keeps arm sizes equal within blocks of 4–6. Alternate patients or odd/even dates is systematic allocation, NOT randomisation, because the next assignment is predictable.

DocT (×2): The purpose of probability sampling is a REPRESENTATIVE sample (every unit has a known, non-zero chance), so results generalise and sampling error can be calculated. It MINIMISES selection bias but does not 'eliminate' it (non-response, poor sampling frame), the option two thirds of the cohort chose.

DocT: Sampling bias = SYSTEMATIC error in who gets selected (convenience, volunteers, poor frame, non-response), so the sample differs from the target population. Unlike random sampling error it does NOT shrink with a bigger sample; only proper probability sampling and a good response rate reduce it.

DocT: Prevalence = all existing cases (old + new) ÷ population at a point or period; incidence = only NEW cases over time among those at risk. Prevalence ≈ incidence × mean duration, so longer disease or better survival without cure raises prevalence without changing incidence.

cross: Wilcoxon signed-rank as 'the non-parametric test'. Truth: chi-square is also distribution-free, so two options are technically correct; Wilcoxon is the rank-based alternative to the paired t-test for non-normal numerical data. If both appear, pick Wilcoxon (chi-square is filed as the test for categorical data).

lines: DocT: For a DIFFERENCE measure (mean difference, ARR, regression coefficient) the no-effect value is 0, not 1: a 95% CI that includes 0 = not significant (p >0.05). The null value is 1 only for ratios (RR, OR, HR).

DocT GT: Low power only threatens a NEGATIVE result (type II error = missing a real effect). If an underpowered trial still finds P <0.001, the effect was big enough to detect, so accept it; the type I error risk is fixed by alpha, not by sample size.

DocT: Mann-Whitney U IS the Wilcoxon rank-SUM test (two names, one test): the non-parametric partner of the UNPAIRED t-test. It compares rank distributions (often summarised as medians), not means, so 'compares the means' is the trap (cohort 0% correct).

fix.t: BS-16: Kappa = (Observed agreement − Expected agreement) / (1 − Expected agreement). BS-23: n = 4PQ/L²; P = prevalence; Q = 100 − P (%) or 1 − P (decimal); L = allowable (absolute) error; "4" ≈ (1.96)² = Z² for 95% confidence.
fix.why: Kappa formula and 4PQ/L² terms garbled from the scan.

lines: DocT: Internal validity = how far the observed effect is truly due to the exposure and not bias, confounding or chance; it is NOT 'precision' (the card's wording). Precision (reliability) reflects random error and shows as a narrow CI; a study can be precise yet internally invalid if biased.

fix.t: Internal validity = freedom from bias and confounding (accuracy/systematic error), judged by design, randomisation, blinding. Repeat-and-agree = reliability/precision (random error). External validity = generalisability, depends on representativeness of the sample.
fix.why: Calls internal validity "precision". That is reliability; internal validity is freedom from bias and confounding.

lines: DocT: Power analysis is done at the PLANNING stage to find the minimum sample size, using alpha (0.05), power 1-beta (80-90%), expected effect size and variability. Smaller effect, more variability or higher power → bigger sample. 'Post-hoc power' of a finished study is discouraged because it only restates the p-value.

DocT: After prevalence, SPECIFICITY moves PPV more than sensitivity, because most people screened are disease-free and a small loss of specificity floods the few true positives (prevalence 1%: Sp 99% → 95% cuts PPV from ~50% to ~15%; Sn 90% → 99% barely moves it).

DocT: A massive unilateral pleural effusion (tension hydrothorax) causes OBSTRUCTIVE shock with a HIGH CVP (15–18), the tamponade pattern: raised pleural pressure compresses the heart and cuts venous return. Clue = white-out hemithorax with mediastinal shift away; fix = urgent drainage, not pressors. LV failure (B) gives bilateral effusions with a high PAWP; PE (A) gives a near-clear film.

Marrow: NEUROGENIC shock is distributive: lost sympathetic tone gives low SVR with venous pooling, so low CVP/PAWP and low CO — with BRADYCARDIA and warm skin, unlike other shock. Warm high-output states: sepsis, cirrhosis/liver failure, pancreatitis, burns, anaphylaxis, thyrotoxicosis, AV fistula, beriberi, severe anaemia; MI shock is cold.
cross: DocT keys PE for CVP 18 + acute respiratory failure + tachycardia with BP 140/90 (and its explanation calls the patient hypotensive). Truth: a normal BP makes this at most intermediate-risk PE, and a smoker's COPD exacerbation with cor pulmonale fits equally. If the stem gives SBP <90 or a clear chest with RV strain, pick PE; if a smoker with wheeze and chronic hypercapnia, pick COPD with cor pulmonale.

DocT GT keys 'cirrhosis with portal hypertension' as the cause of a CVP of 22 in a cirrhotic. Truth: portal hypertension sits upstream of the IVC and cirrhosis is hyperdynamic with a normal-low CVP; a CVP of 22 means right-heart failure or volume overload (AKI fluid overload, cirrhotic cardiomyopathy, tense ascites). If AKI with fluid overload is offered, it is the physiological answer; DocT's cohort followed the key.

lines: DocT: Portal hypertension does not raise the CVP: portal pressure sits upstream of the liver, and the hyperdynamic cirrhotic circulation leaves CVP low-normal. A CVP of 22 in a cirrhotic points to the right heart or chest: portopulmonary hypertension, cirrhotic cardiomyopathy, tense ascites/hydrothorax raising intrathoracic pressure, or volume overload from AKI.
cross: DocT 4 key: portal hypertension raises the CVP. Truth: physiologically wrong; a high CVP in cirrhosis means a cardiac, pulmonary-vascular or volume cause. If 'AKI with fluid overload' or a cardiac cause is offered, pick it.

DocT keys septic shock for cold peripheries, oliguria and a LOW ScvO2 with no fever or source. Truth: low ScvO2 = low delivery/low cardiac output, i.e. cardiogenic shock; sepsis gives a normal/high ScvO2 except when early and unresuscitated. If there is no infective clue, pick cardiogenic.

lines: DocT: Dilated RV + CVP 20 + abdominal distension (ascites) = CHRONIC RV failure from pulmonary hypertension, not massive PE: PE dilates the RV abruptly (McConnell, 60/60 sign) with no time for ascites to build or the wall to thicken; tamponade gives small, collapsed right chambers.

DocT GT: Kerley lines are oedematous (thickened) interlobular septa, not swollen lymphatics. B lines: short (~1 cm) horizontal lines at the peripheral bases, perpendicular to the pleura; A lines: longer (2–6 cm) lines deep in the lung radiating toward the hila.

DocT GT: Cardiogenic pulmonary oedema on CXR: cardiomegaly, upper-lobe diversion, perihilar 'bat-wing' opacities, Kerley B lines, peribronchial cuffing, widened vascular pedicle (>70 mm) and effusions. ARDS gives patchy peripheral opacities with a normal heart and pedicle, air bronchograms and few effusions or septal lines.

DocT Recall25: BNP rises with any myocardial stretch or poor clearance, not only heart failure: PE (RV strain), AF, renal failure, sepsis, ACS and older age. Obesity LOWERS BNP, and hypothyroidism has no stretch mechanism, so it is the odd one out in 'all raise BNP except'.

DocT GT: The old SSC 6-hour bundle required reassessment of volume status and tissue perfusion after the initial fluid: a repeat focused examination, or two of CVP, ScvO2, bedside cardiovascular ultrasound and passive leg raise/fluid challenge. Pulmonary function tests have no place in it.
cross: DocT keys fluids/vasopressors (A) over antibiotics (D) as the first action for hypotension with lactate 5. Truth: the Hour-1 bundle STARTS both within the hour, and antibiotics within 1 h for shock is a strong recommendation. If the stem stresses hypotension and high lactate, pick resuscitation; if asked what must not be delayed, antibiotics.

DocT GT keys norepinephrine as the initial intervention for warm septic shock with MAP 58 and CVP 5 before any fluid. Truth: SSC starts a crystalloid bolus (30 mL/kg within 3 h) with norepinephrine early, even peripherally, if MAP stays <65. If no fluid has been given and a bolus is offered, pick fluid; once fluids are in, pick norepinephrine.

lines: DocT: A cirrhotic with ascites who suddenly becomes hypotensive and confused has SBP until proved otherwise: infection drives both the encephalopathy and the vasodilatory shock, whereas HE alone does not cause shock. Tap the ascites before antibiotics.

DocT: SSC suggests against dopamine except in highly selected patients (low tachyarrhythmia risk, absolute or relative bradycardia); the add-on for persistent hypoperfusion with cardiac dysfunction is DOBUTAMINE, so 'avoid dobutamine' is the false statement.

DocT: SOAP II (NEJM 2010, 1,679 shock patients): dopamine vs norepinephrine gave the same 28-day mortality but twice the arrhythmias on dopamine (24% vs 12%) and more deaths in the cardiogenic-shock subgroup — norepinephrine wins on safety, not overall survival.

DocT: Once MAP holds and perfusion recovers (lactate falling, urine back), wean pressors; on norepinephrine + vasopressin taper NOREPINEPHRINE first, because stopping vasopressin first causes more hypotension (~50% vs ~15%, retrospective). Antibiotics are de-escalated by culture, not run a fixed 14 days.
Marrow: Septic shock is the commonest shock type in ICU; mortality is highest in septic (and cardiogenic) shock and lowest in hypovolaemic shock.

Marrow: Neurogenic shock = vasodilation ± bradycardia; target MAP 85–90 mmHg for 7 days with fluid then vasopressor: noradrenaline (alpha + beta, supports HR) preferred; pure alpha phenylephrine can worsen bradycardia.

DocT GT: Cut the induction dose to about 1/4–1/2 in ANY shock, septic as well as haemorrhagic: slow circulation and a small central volume deliver a high concentration to brain and heart → peri-intubation collapse. Etomidate is not 'strictly avoided' (single-dose mortality effect unproven), and ketamine can still drop BP in catecholamine-depleted patients.
cross: Marrow keys phenylephrine (pure alpha-1) for neurogenic shock. Truth: most guidelines prefer noradrenaline because phenylephrine causes reflex bradycardia. Pick phenylephrine only if the stem says no bradycardia and noradrenaline is not offered.

lines: DocT: Hypotension that appears AFTER diuresis in a patient who was 120/80 is over-diuresis (preload removed): hold the diuretic and reassess volume before any vasoactive drug. Milrinone (C) would vasodilate further.

Marrow: Recurrent flash pulmonary oedema with resistant hypertension and rising creatinine = bilateral renal artery stenosis (Pickering syndrome): renal angiography and stenting prevents recurrence; renal denervation does not.
cross: DocT keys dopamine for post-diuresis hypotension. Truth: dopamine is outdated (SOAP II: more arrhythmias, higher mortality in cardiogenic shock); first stop the diuretic, then norepinephrine for MAP or dobutamine for output if a drug is needed. If norepinephrine is offered, pick it.

Crossfire · ESC HF 2021 profile algorithm: wet-cold SBP <90 → inotrope, vasopressor if refractory; AHA/ACC 2022 HF, SCAI & ACC/AHA ACS 2025: hypotensive cardiogenic shock → noradrenaline first, then add dobutamine. In exam: SBP <90 = noradrenaline first; SBP ≥90 low output = dobutamine.

lines: DocT: Dopamine is no longer preferred in low-output HF or cardiogenic shock: in SOAP II's cardiogenic subgroup it caused more arrhythmias AND higher mortality than norepinephrine; current practice is norepinephrine for MAP + dobutamine for output. Dopamine now survives mainly in the bradycardia algorithm.

Marrow: In calcium-channel-blocker poisoning, after IV calcium and high-dose insulin euglycaemia, choose the vasoactive drug by phenotype: low cardiac index → inotrope (dobutamine/adrenaline); low SVR (vasoplegia) → norepinephrine.
cross: DocT keys 'decrease dobutamine' for a patient still hypotensive on dobutamine. Truth: dobutamine's β2 effect vasodilates, so the BP fix is to add norepinephrine (MAP <65 → norepinephrine, as this card says); cutting dobutamine slows HR but does not raise BP. If the stem stresses tachyarrhythmia on dobutamine, pick reduce dobutamine; if hypotension, pick add norepinephrine.

DocT keys dopamine for low output at BP 80/50. Truth: outdated (SOAP II); norepinephrine for the BP, dobutamine or milrinone for output. If norepinephrine is offered with hypotension, pick it; pick dopamine only if it is the sole vasoactive option.

lines: DocT GT + Marrow: Omecamtiv mecarbil is a cardiac myosin activator — longer systolic ejection and more SV WITHOUT raising cAMP, intracellular Ca2+ or MVO2 (GALACTIC-HF: modest fall in HF events), its edge over dobutamine/milrinone; serelaxin is a relaxin-2 VASODILATOR, not an inotrope.
Marrow: Milrinone is renally excreted, so it accumulates in AKI/ESRD (hypotension, arrhythmias): reduce the infusion rate by creatinine clearance and skip the loading dose.

DocT GT: Dobutamine (β1) → Gs → adenylate cyclase → cAMP → protein kinase A. PKA phosphorylates L-type Ca channels and ryanodine receptors (more systolic Ca release: inotropy), phospholamban (releases SERCA2a: faster Ca reuptake, lusitropy) and troponin I (faster Ca release from troponin C).
Marrow: Dobutamine speeds AV-nodal conduction and can worsen AF with RVR; in low-EF AF digoxin is a first rate-control option because it slows the node without negative inotropy.
cross: DocT keys an IV β-blocker for AF with RVR in HFrEF admitted with worsening dyspnoea. Truth: that is decompensated HF — avoid IV β-blockers; use amiodarone or digoxin for rate and IV diuretics for congestion. If the patient is decompensated, pick amiodarone/digoxin; β-blocker only once compensated.

lines: DocT GT: Levosimendan also keeps working under β-blockade: it sensitises troponin C to calcium (and opens K-ATP channels), bypassing the β-receptor/cAMP pathway, so ESC prefers it (or milrinone) over dobutamine in β-blocked patients. Dopamine, adrenaline and dopexamine all act through β-receptors and lose effect.
cross: DocT keys dobutamine for HFrEF with low output at SBP 85 (ESC: wet-cold SBP <90 → inotrope first, vasopressor if refractory). Truth: AHA/SCAI, as this card says, start norepinephrine below SBP 90. If the stem says 'low output' with a borderline SBP, pick dobutamine; if 'shock' with MAP <65 or SBP clearly <90, pick norepinephrine first.

lines: DocT: S3 gallop + bibasal crackles without ST change = congestive (left, systolic) heart failure. The S3 is rapid early-diastolic filling into a stiff, overfilled ventricle with raised LVEDP — specific (~90%) but insensitive for low EF or high filling pressure.

DocT GT: A survivor of VF/VT arrest with no reversible cause (no acute MI, electrolyte or drug cause) gets a secondary-prevention ICD regardless of EF (class I; AVID, CIDS, CASH: ICD beats amiodarone on mortality). Coronary assessment is part of the work-up but must not delay the ICD decision.

DocT: Chest pain + no ST elevation + troponin above the 99th centile with a rise/fall = NSTEMI even with a normal ECG. With BP 180/110 and no prior CAD think type 2 MI from a hypertensive surge, and exclude aortic dissection (D) — BP in both arms, pain character — before antithrombotics.

Marrow: High ACS likelihood: prior documented angina or known CAD, transient MR murmur or hypotension during pain, new ST deviation ≥1 mm or T inversion in multiple precordial leads; low likelihood: T flattening or inversion <1 mm in leads with a dominant R.

DocT: Regular wide-complex tachycardia in an older patient with heart disease is VT until proved otherwise (~80%; >90% with prior MI). VT clinchers: AV dissociation, fusion and capture beats, QRS >160 ms, northwest axis, precordial concordance.

DocT GT + Marrow: Carotid sinus massage: supine, on continuous ECG, one side only (right first) at the level of C3 for 5–10 s, never bilateral; contraindicated with a carotid bruit or prior TIA/stroke (plaque embolism). Modified Valsalva (strain at 40 mmHg for 15 s, then supine with legs raised; REVERT 43% vs 17% conversion) is the safer first manoeuvre.

DocT GT: SA exit block — Type I (Wenckebach): PP intervals progressively shorten, then a pause shorter than two PP; Type II: constant PP with a sudden pause that is an exact multiple (usually 2×) of the basic PP. A sinus pause/arrest bears no fixed relation to the PP cycle.

Marrow + DocT GT: Nodal (Mobitz I) vs infranodal (Mobitz II) block: atropine and exercise speed AV-nodal conduction, so they IMPROVE Mobitz I but WORSEN Mobitz II; carotid massage does the opposite. Mobitz I usually has a narrow QRS, Mobitz II a wide one, so in 2:1 block a narrow QRS in a vagal setting (sleeping athlete) favours benign nodal block, a wide QRS infranodal block needing pacing.

DocT: Inferior STEMI: ST elevation III > II with reciprocal depression in aVL/I = RCA; II ≥ III with ST elevation in I/aVL or V5–V6 = LCx. The RCA supplies the AV node in ~90%, hence the bradycardia and AV block of inferior MI.

DocT: Pathological Q waves (≥40 ms or ≥25% of the following R, in ≥2 contiguous leads) WITHOUT ST elevation mean an OLD healed infarct — Q in I, aVL, V5 = prior lateral MI. Q waves are permanent scar; ST elevation marks acute injury.
Marrow: ST elevation in V1 with a NEW RBBB = PROXIMAL LAD occlusion (the septal perforators supply the right bundle); distal LAD gives V3–V4 elevation without RBBB.

DocT GT: New AF in septic shock or with labile BP: correct triggers first (K, Mg, volume, catecholamine dose); for rate control a short-acting β1-blocker (esmolol: onset 2–3 min, t½ ~9 min via red-cell esterases, so it can be switched off within minutes; or landiolol) beats diltiazem, whose negative inotropy and vasodilation worsen hypotension. IV amiodarone if BP is marginal; DC cardioversion only if unstable, and AF often recurs while sepsis persists.
Marrow: Never give IV verapamil or diltiazem soon after an oral or IV β-blocker: additive AV-nodal block and negative inotropy can cause profound bradycardia, hypotension or asystole.

Marrow + DocT GT: Pharmacological cardioversion of recent-onset (<48 h) AF or flutter: ibutilide 1 mg IV over 10 min, repeat once; it converts typical flutter (~60–75%) better than AF (~30–50%); torsades risk, so correct K/Mg and monitor ≥4 h. Flecainide only without structural heart disease (give an AV-nodal blocker first in flutter to avoid 1:1 conduction); amiodarone when there is structural disease.
cross: Marrow keys ibutilide for stable recent-onset AF. Truth: the AHA stable irregular narrow-complex pathway is rate control (β-blocker or non-DHP CCB); ibutilide is a rhythm-control drug for AF <48 h. If rate control is offered, pick it; if the stem asks to restore sinus rhythm in AF <48 h, pick ibutilide.

lines: Marrow: Flecainide toxicity: blurred vision (commonest dose-related non-cardiac effect), dizziness, QRS widening and proarrhythmia; contraindicated in structural or ischaemic heart disease (CAST: excess deaths after MI).
cross: DocT GT (AIM1 Q36, GT4 Q56) keys verapamil as THE drug contraindicated in pre-excited AF. Truth: adenosine, β-blockers (esmolol) and IV amiodarone are also harmful (AHA 2023 class 3), so several options are correct. Pick verapamil as the classic answer; treatment is cardioversion if unstable, procainamide/ibutilide if stable.

lines: DocT: Paediatric SVT that converts with adenosine but recurs within seconds and leaves the child unstable → synchronised cardioversion 0.5–1 J/kg, then 2 J/kg; repeating adenosine buys only another 30 s. Avoid verapamil and diltiazem (C) in infants — cardiovascular collapse.
cross: Marrow keys securing the airway first for an unstable tachyarrhythmia when cardioversion is not among the options. Truth: unstable tachycardia → synchronised cardioversion; intubating first delays electrical therapy. If cardioversion is offered, pick it; if not, the airway option is the keyed least-wrong.

lines: DocT: CVP 4 is normal (RA mean 1–5) and with stable vitals excludes shock, but a CVP cannot show adequate oxygen delivery (needs ScvO2/lactate). In COPD, gas trapping raises intrathoracic pressure and can falsely RAISE the CVP.

DocT GT: Cardiac myosin-binding protein C (cMyC) is cardiac-restricted, more abundant than troponin and released faster, so with hs-troponin it improves early rule-in/rule-out; copeptin is the other early add-on. IMA, BNP and microRNA-208b are not used for MI diagnosis.

Marrow: Reinfarction is diagnosed with TROPONIN, not CK-MB (ESC/ACC): a >20% rise from an already raised baseline (sampled at symptom onset and 3–6 h later). CK-MB is used only where troponin is unavailable.

fix.t: CK-MB: less specific; only if troponin unavailable. Re-infarction: repeat hs-cTn — >20% rise from a stable/falling raised baseline.
fix.why: Uses CK-MB for re-infarction. ESC/ACC use troponin (>20% rise from a raised baseline).
fix.src: Fourth Universal Definition of MI 2018; ESC ACS 2023

cross: DocT keys 'ibuprofen and reassure' for chest pain with chest-wall tenderness. Truth: tenderness does not exclude ACS, and exertional pain relieved by rest with a family history of MI is anginal — ECG + troponin (and aspirin) first. If an ECG/troponin option is offered, pick it.

lines: Marrow: Active diabetic haemorrhagic retinopathy is a relative contraindication to fibrinolysis; a previous MI is not a contraindication; CPR counts only if prolonged (>10 min) or traumatic.
Marrow: Riociguat (soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator) is a nitrate contraindication alongside PDE-5 inhibitors: both amplify the NO–cGMP pathway, so a nitrate causes profound hypotension.
cross: DocT keys oesophageal spasm as 'most likely' for acute chest pain relieved by nitroglycerin with a normal ECG and negative troponin. Truth: nitrate relief proves nothing, and with a single negative troponin unstable angina is still the classic answer; oesophageal spasm is a diagnosis of exclusion after serial hs-troponin. If serial troponins are negative and ACS is ruled out, pick spasm; otherwise pick unstable angina.

lines: DocT GT: Hypotension with warm peripheries, bounding pulses and a WIDE pulse pressure (low diastolic) = low SVR, i.e. distributive shock (sepsis, adrenal crisis, liver failure, vasoplegia). Hypovolaemic and cardiogenic shock give a NARROW pulse pressure (low stroke volume) with cold peripheries.

DocT Recall25: Stent thrombosis presenting with ST elevation is a STEMI: load DAPT (aspirin + P2Y12) with anticoagulation and send for immediate primary PCI. Lysis works poorly on platelet-rich stent thrombus; heparin alone or beta-blockers are not reperfusion.

Marrow: TEE signs of dissection: an undulating intimal flap separating true and false lumens, colour-flow in both lumens, entry/exit tears, false-lumen stasis or thrombus, and intramural haematoma (crescentic wall thickening without a flap).
cross: DocT keys TEE as first imaging for a stable patient (BP 205/110). Truth: 2024 ESC first-line is ECG-gated contrast CT neck to pelvis (I, C); TEE is for patients too unstable to move, CT contraindication, or intra-operative guidance. If the patient is stable and CT is offered, pick CT; if unstable in theatre/ED, pick TEE.

lines: DocT GT: In ventilated ICU patients CTPA is still the reference test, though motion and ventilation-related bolus interruption lower sensitivity. A D-dimer cannot rule out PE in ICU (almost always raised), a negative leg ultrasound does not exclude PE, and Wells/Geneva are not validated in the critically ill.

DocT GT: In DKA, hypotension persisting after adequate fluid (e.g. 4 L) with a HIGH CVP and ST changes is cardiogenic - think MI as precipitant or complication, often silent in diabetics; hypovolaemia or GI bleeding gives a low CVP. Acidosis and hyperkalaemia also distort the ECG and raise troponin, so confirm with echo.

DocT GT: Corrected Na = measured Na + 1.6 x (glucose mg/dL - 100)/100 (Katz; Hillier's 2.4 is better above 400 mg/dL): Na 130 with glucose 600 corrects to 138. The measured low sodium is dilutional, and the corrected value - not the measured one - chooses 0.45% vs 0.9% saline after the first litre.

DocT GT: The counter-regulatory hormones - glucagon, catecholamines, cortisol and growth hormone - drive both DKA and HHS, raising gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis and, with insulin lack, lipolysis and ketogenesis; stress (infection, MI) pushes them higher. Insulin deficiency is the other half - never insulin excess.

DocT + DocT GT: Alcoholic ketoacidosis (binge, then starvation and vomiting; glucose normal or low, anion gap high, beta-hydroxybutyrate dominant so urine ketones read only trace) is treated with thiamine BEFORE dextrose-saline (D5NS or D5-half-NS), with K, Mg and PO4 replacement. Dextrose triggers endogenous insulin and switches off ketogenesis, so insulin and bicarbonate are not used; plain saline lacks the carbohydrate and D5W lacks the volume.

DocT GT: A fasting binge drinker becomes hypoglycaemic 6-36 h after drinking because ethanol oxidation floods the liver with NADH, diverting pyruvate to lactate and oxaloacetate to malate, so gluconeogenesis stops while glycogen is already exhausted. Treat with thiamine and IV dextrose; glucagon fails because there is no glycogen to release.

DocT GT: Headache, irritability and a falling GCS during DKA treatment in a child mean cerebral oedema (0.5-1% of paediatric DKA, mortality up to 25%): treat on clinical grounds BEFORE imaging with mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg over 10-15 min or 3% saline 2.5-5 mL/kg, head up, and slow (not stop) the fluids. CT comes afterwards, to exclude a bleed or thrombosis.

DocT GT: Treat hypoglycaemia by consciousness and access: awake and able to swallow gets 15-20 g oral glucose with a recheck at 15 min; obtunded or unsafe swallow with IV access gets 25 g dextrose (50 mL of D50 or 250 mL of D10); no IV access gets glucagon 1 mg IM or SC.
cross: DocT keys oral glucose tablets for a confused-but-arousable ICU patient on an insulin infusion. Truth: glucose 48 mg/dL is level 2 hypoglycaemia, and with altered sensorium plus existing IV access most ICU protocols give IV dextrose. Pick oral glucose only when the stem makes the swallow clearly safe; otherwise IV dextrose.

lines: DocT GT: Beta-hydroxybutyrate is the most abundant ketone in DKA: the high NADH:NAD ratio pushes acetoacetate to beta-OHB, taking the ratio from about 1:1 up to 10:1. Measure beta-OHB directly (diagnostic at >=3 mmol/L); acetone is exhaled as the fruity breath and lactate is not a ketone.

Marrow: The same trap runs the other way at presentation - a pump patient with an anion gap of 23 and vomiting can have NEGATIVE urine ketones, because the nitroprusside dipstick misses beta-OHB. A negative urine ketone test never excludes DKA.

DocT: Thyroid storm has no confirmatory test, so its ICU mimics matter: sepsis (fever, tachycardia, delirium, shock) and adrenal crisis (shock, vomiting, confusion) first, then phaeochromocytoma crisis, sympathomimetic toxicity, NMS and serotonin syndrome. Send TSH, free T4 and a cortisol, take cultures, and give hydrocortisone, which covers both storm and adrenal insufficiency.

DocT: Infection is the commonest trigger of thyroid storm in a patient whose hyperthyroidism was never diagnosed, while stopping antithyroid drugs leads in known treated patients (Japanese national survey). Work up and treat infection alongside the storm, because fever alone cannot separate the two.

DocT: Storm up-regulates beta-1 receptors, so coexisting infection, beta-agonists or high-dose pressors readily trigger AF, ischaemia or high-output failure. Give propranolol early, but switch to short-acting esmolol if storm cardiomyopathy has lowered the ejection fraction.

DocT: T3 is the riskier hormone in myxoedema coma - 3-4 times as potent as T4 and acting within hours, it raises myocardial oxygen demand fast and can cause angina, arrhythmia or MI in the elderly or coronary patient. IV T4 is the backbone; T3 is a cautious add-on at the low end (5-10 microgram, then 2.5-10 microgram 8-hourly) or avoided in cardiac patients.

DocT: Aspiration pneumonitis is the typical pulmonary complication: depressed consciousness, blunted airway reflexes, hypoventilation, ileus and macroglossia all favour it. Protect the airway early (intubate if obtunded or hypercapnic) and decompress the stomach.

DocT: In overt primary hyperthyroidism TSH is undetectable (<0.01-0.05 mIU/L on third-generation assays); a low but detectable TSH of 0.1-0.4 suggests subclinical disease, non-thyroidal illness or dopamine/steroids. Pick undetectable over low when both are offered; the exception is a TSH-secreting adenoma, where TSH is normal or high.

DocT: Lithium belongs on the drug list twice over - it blocks hormone release (hypothyroidism, goitre) and causes painless silent thyroiditis with transient thyrotoxicosis. Checkpoint inhibitors and interferon-alpha give the same thyroiditis-then-hypothyroidism sequence.

DocT GT: In the first trimester TSH FALLS (often <0.1) because hCG shares the alpha subunit and weakly stimulates the TSH receptor, raising free T4; this is physiological and peaks at 10-12 weeks. Prolactin, cortisol and ACTH rise through pregnancy, while vasopressin is unchanged despite faster clearance by placental vasopressinase.

DocT: Myxoedema also flattens or inverts T waves (diffuse repolarisation change, worse with a pericardial effusion), and T-wave inversion is the keyed ECG finding. Distractors map elsewhere: ST elevation to MI or pericarditis, AF to thyrotoxicosis, short QT to hypercalcaemia.

DocT: Hypothyroid hyponatraemia comes mainly from a low cardiac output and GFR, so less filtrate reaches the diluting segments and free water cannot be excreted, with non-osmotic ADH release adding to it. Glucocorticoid deficiency works the same way, since cortisol is needed for water excretion and CRH is co-secreted with ADH.

DocT GT: Thyroid storm with AF and decompensated heart failure: full-dose propranolol can precipitate cardiogenic collapse, so rate control uses a short-acting titratable beta-1 blocker (esmolol or landiolol, stoppable at once) or digoxin with a cautious beta-blocker - digoxin needs higher doses in thyrotoxicosis, and diltiazem is negatively inotropic.
cross: GT5 Q90 keys digoxin plus a cautious beta-blocker for storm with AF and severe heart failure. Truth: the Japan Thyroid Association 2016 prefers landiolol or esmolol when Killip >=III, so an esmolol infusion is equally supported. If both appear, pick digoxin plus cautious beta-blocker as DocT does; never full-dose propranolol or diltiazem.

lines: DocT: Autoimmune adrenalitis causes 80-90% of primary adrenal insufficiency (tuberculosis still matters in India). The trap: chronic steroid use is the commonest cause of adrenal insufficiency overall, but it is secondary through HPA suppression, so aldosterone and potassium stay normal.

DocT: The same doses are the surgical steroid cover for Addison's or a chronic steroid user (prednisolone >=5 mg/day for over 4 weeks): hydrocortisone 100 mg IV at induction, then 200 mg/24 h while nil by mouth, then double the usual oral dose for 48 h (Association of Anaesthetists 2020). Minor procedures need only the usual dose plus a single 25-50 mg; 200 mg is the daily total, never the induction bolus.
Marrow: A single dose of etomidate inhibits 11-beta-hydroxylase for 6-48 h and can produce pressor-refractory shock; the treatment is hydrocortisone 100 mg IV, not more catecholamine.

DocT GT: CIRCI means cortisol activity inadequate for the severity of illness - a dysregulated HPA axis, tissue glucocorticoid resistance and low CBG, with NO structural adrenal or pituitary lesion, so a normal-looking cortisol can still be too low in septic shock. Autoimmune destruction, pituitary tumour and adrenal haemorrhage are absolute, structural causes.
cross: GrandT1 Q49 keys autoimmune adrenal destruction as the basis of CIRCI, and DocT Q18 keys the high-baseline, low-increment pattern as the only CIRCI response. Truth: CIRCI is functional and has no structural cause (the GT2 repeat keys this correctly), and the 2017 SCCM/ESICM criterion is a cortisol increment <9 microgram/dL, which a normal baseline with no rise also meets. If asked for the mechanism, pick the functional/dysregulated axis; if asked which Synacthen response is CIRCI, any delta <9 qualifies.

lines: DocT: IL-6 acts beyond the anterior pituitary - it also stimulates the adrenal cortex directly, releasing cortisol independently of ACTH, which partly explains high cortisol with low ACTH in prolonged critical illness. IL-1 and TNF-alpha act mainly on the hypothalamus, and TNF-alpha actually blunts the adrenal response to ACTH.

DocT GT: Drugs that precipitate CIRCI: etomidate (one dose blocks 11-beta-hydroxylase for 24-72 h), azoles such as ketoconazole (block steroidogenesis) and enzyme inducers - phenytoin, rifampicin, phenobarbital - that speed cortisol metabolism. A patient on all three needs hydrocortisone.
cross: DocT keys CIRCI for a flat cosyntropin response (delta <9 microgram/dL) in a long-term steroid user. Truth: in that patient the same flat response is adrenal atrophy from HPA suppression (secondary/tertiary insufficiency), and the test cannot separate the two. If the stem names chronic steroid use, secondary insufficiency is at least as correct; either way the treatment is hydrocortisone 200 mg/day.

lines: DocT: A high potassium with low aldosterone but NORMAL cortisol is isolated hypoaldosteronism, usually hyporeninaemic (diabetic CKD, NSAIDs, calcineurin inhibitors) or heparin-induced. Primary adrenal insufficiency also gives low aldosterone and high potassium, but adds a low cortisol, high ACTH, hyponatraemia and pigmentation.

DocT: Cortisol-based selection comes from Annane 2002 (hydrocortisone 50 mg 6-hourly + fludrocortisone 50 µg × 7 days), where mortality fell only in ACTH non-responders (Δ ≤9 µg/dL); CORTICUS (2008) found no mortality benefit in responders or non-responders, so cortisol testing no longer selects patients.
Marrow: Refeeding hypophosphataemia weakens the diaphragm and causes failure to wean; check and replace phosphate before blaming ICU-acquired weakness.

DocT GT: LaSRS (persistent ARDS day 7–28, methylprednisolone) improved oxygenation, compliance and BP and gave more ventilator-free and shock-free days at day 28, but no survival benefit and more neuromuscular weakness; so 'more ventilator- and shock-free days' is the correct outcome.

Marrow: HYPRESS (2016): hydrocortisone in severe sepsis WITHOUT shock did not prevent progression to shock or lower mortality — steroids are for an ongoing vasopressor need only. (PROWESS activated protein C, ARR 6%, was withdrawn after PROWESS-SHOCK was negative.)

DocT: In lithium nephrogenic DI, lithium enters principal cells through ENaC and inhibits GSK-3beta, down-regulating aquaporin-2 (main mechanism); loss of the urea transporter UT-A1 lowers medullary tonicity as well. Lithium never stimulates V2 or ADH release, so urine osmolality stays ~180-200 at a normal plasma osmolality.

DocT: After pituitary stalk injury (transsphenoidal surgery, TBI) sodium can run triphasic: DI from axonal shock on days 1-5, then SIADH as degenerating neurons leak stored ADH on days 5-10 (stop desmopressin, restrict water), then permanent DI if >80-90% of neurons are lost. Many patients show only phase 1 or an isolated day-7 hyponatraemia.

DocT: Adipsic DI (hypothalamic lesion, anterior communicating aneurysm clipping) destroys the osmoreceptors, so thirst and osmotic ADH release are both lost while baroreceptor-driven release persists; hypertonic saline produces no ADH rise. Treat with fixed-dose desmopressin plus a prescribed daily water intake guided by weight and sodium.
cross: DocT keys sarcoidosis as NOT a cause of nephrogenic DI. Truth: sarcoid causes central DI directly by granulomatous infiltration of the hypothalamus and stalk, and nephrogenic DI indirectly through hypercalcaemia and nephrocalcinosis. If the question asks for sarcoid's primary mechanism, pick central DI; the ENDO-20 table listing sarcoid under nephrogenic should be read as the indirect route.

fix.t: Central: add "granulomatous — sarcoidosis, histiocytosis (LCH)". Nephrogenic: keep sarcoid but tag "(via hypercalcaemia / interstitial nephritis)".
fix.why: Lists sarcoid under nephrogenic DI. Sarcoid mainly causes central DI; nephrogenic only via hypercalcaemia.

lines: DocT: Hyponatraemia is the commonest complication of desmopressin: continuous antidiuresis means any water drunk or infused is retained (usually mild, Na 131-134). Check sodium daily, restrict free water, and allow a daily escape by delaying a dose so a water diuresis can break through.

DocT: For early lithium-induced nephrogenic DI, amiloride is the first drug - it blocks ENaC, the channel lithium uses to enter collecting-duct cells, reducing polyuria and further injury without raising lithium levels as thiazides do. Desmopressin fails (the receptor is resistant) and fluid restriction risks hypernatraemia.
Marrow: Desmopressin's adverse effects are hyponatraemia (main) and, rarely, thrombocytopenia or purpura, especially in type 2B von Willebrand disease.
cross: Marrow keys desmopressin as the cause of new thrombocytopenic purpura. Truth: desmopressin-related thrombocytopenia is rare and essentially confined to type 2B vWD, while co-trimoxazole is a far commoner drug cause of immune thrombocytopenia. Pick desmopressin only when the stem says the lesions appeared before, or names type 2B vWD.

fix.t: Nephrogenic: stop the drug, correct K/Ca; thiazide ± NSAID. Lithium NDI: AMILORIDE first (blocks ENaC, the channel lithium enters the collecting-duct cell through). [Card already lists amiloride — only the lithium-specific line is missing.]
fix.why: Thiazide given as the drug for lithium nephrogenic DI. Amiloride is first-line: it blocks the ENaC channel lithium uses to enter the cell.
fix.src: Endotext DI 2022; KDIGO-era reviews (Christensen, Kidney Int)

lines: DocT: Check cortisol in central DI (pituitary surgery, TBI, apoplexy): the same lesion often removes ACTH, and cortisol lack masks DI because cortisol is needed to excrete free water. Polyuria may appear only once hydrocortisone is started, so give steroid cover first.

DocT + DocT GT: Read the water-deprivation-then-desmopressin test by urine osmolality: complete central DI stays <300 and then rises >50% after DDAVP; partial central DI rises submaximally to 300-800 and then another 10-50%; nephrogenic DI stays <300 with <10% rise; primary polydipsia concentrates to >600-800 with no further rise.

DocT: Vasopressin does not cause thirst - thirst is driven by hypothalamic osmoreceptors and angiotensin II. Its other actions are V1a vasoconstriction and platelet aggregation, V1b pituitary ACTH release with CRH, and V2 endothelial release of von Willebrand factor and factor VIII (the basis of desmopressin in bleeding).
cross: GT6 Q74 keys 'oxytocin and ADH are secreted from the anterior pituitary' as true. Truth: both are made in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei and released from the POSTERIOR pituitary - DocT's own explanation says so, and all four options are false. If this stem recurs, pick the keyed option only knowing it is an error; learn posterior pituitary.

lines: DocT: Vasopressin antagonists are the only treatment aimed at the core defect of SIAD: they block the V2 receptor and give aquaresis (free water out, no sodium), whereas fluid restriction, urea, loop diuretic with salt and hypertonic saline all work around ADH. Addressing the mechanism does not make them first-line - Europe still prefers restriction, then urea.

cross: DocT keys NSAIDs as the SIADH drug in a depressed patient. Truth: the commonest causes in that patient are SSRIs (classically in the elderly within 2-4 weeks), then venlafaxine, TCAs and mirtazapine - but no antidepressant was offered, and PPIs, also on DocT's own list, are as defensible as NSAIDs. If an antidepressant appears, pick it; NSAIDs are keyed because they potentiate ADH by blocking renal prostaglandins.

DocT keys increased ADH as the least likely mechanism only after the urine data; the card already places urine osmolality around 100 with primary polydipsia and low solute intake. Truth: a dilute urine argues hardest AGAINST increased ADH secretion, so when the urine osmolality is <=100 that option is the one to exclude.

lines: DocT: Reset osmostat accounts for about a third of SIAD (pregnancy, malnutrition, tuberculosis, chronic illness): the ADH threshold is lowered but still responsive, so sodium sits stable at 125-135 whatever the intake and the patient can still dilute a water load. It needs no treatment, and fluid restriction is futile.

DocT + DocT GT: Plasma NGAL has usable cut-offs: >150 ng/mL predicts AKI that persists at least 48 h and >300 ng/mL predicts severe AKI needing RRT, rising 24-48 h before creatinine. So 200 ng/mL means early persistent AKI, not recovery.

DocT GT: Urinary IL-18 belongs beside NGAL and KIM-1 as a proximal tubular injury marker: it rises 24-48 h before creatinine and tracks AKI severity and mortality (cardiac surgery, ARDS, sepsis). Serum IL-6 is systemic inflammation, not kidney-specific.
Marrow: Hold the classic index table alongside the FENa: prerenal urine Na <20 vs ATN >40 mEq/L; urine osmolality >500 vs <350; BUN:creatinine >20 vs <10; urine:plasma creatinine >40 vs <20.

Marrow: Established postrenal obstruction looks tubular, not prerenal: urine osmolality <350, urine Na >40, FENa >2-4%, with a bland sediment. Only early obstruction (first hours) can show a low FENa, which is why obstruction sits in both columns.

DocT + DocT GT: Plasma IL-6 is not kidney-specific, but a high early level in septic shock independently predicts later AKI and death even after adjusting for APACHE III, and it rises before creatinine. [TIMP-2]x[IGFBP7] is the FDA-cleared ICU marker; IL-18 and KIM-1 are tubular damage markers with less consistent ICU performance.

DocT: Urinary IL-18 is a proximal tubular damage marker: it rises about 6 h after cardiopulmonary bypass and 24-48 h before creatinine, predicts severity and mortality, and is not raised in prerenal azotaemia or CKD.

DocT + DocT GT: Among the add-on drugs only high-dose statin before coronary angiography has RCT support (PRATO-ACS: rosuvastatin 40 mg, CI-AKI 6.7% vs 15.1%; atorvastatin 80 mg; ESC 2018 class IIa in statin-naive ACS or PCI), while KDIGO and ACR still do not recommend it. NAC was null in PRESERVE and furosemide is harmful without matched hydration; the backbone remains isotonic saline 1-1.5 mL/kg/h before and after.

DocT: Respiratory compensation for a metabolic acidosis starts within minutes through peripheral then central chemoreceptors, is largely established by 30-120 min and reaches its full Winter's value over 12-24 h, whereas renal compensation for a respiratory disorder takes 3-5 days. So a gas drawn minutes after an acute acid load can look under-compensated without a second disorder.

DocT GT: For HIT on RRT in an ANURIC patient, argatroban is the choice: hepatic clearance, not removed by the filter, monitored by aPTT 1.5-3x. Bivalirudin is about 20% renally cleared and accumulates in anuria, fondaparinux is renally cleared and unlicensed for HIT, and LMWH cross-reacts with HIT antibodies. Reverse the logic in liver failure, where bivalirudin or citrate is preferred.

DocT + DocT GT: PRIS = failure of mitochondrial fatty-acid oxidation: lactic acidosis, hyperkalaemia, rhabdomyolysis, high triglycerides, AKI, Brugada-like ECG, bradycardia → asystole. Risk: propofol >4 mg/kg/h for >48 h, catecholamines, steroids, sepsis, TBI, youth and LOW carbohydrate intake ('excess carbohydrate' is the trap). Stop propofol; support (RRT, VA-ECMO).

DocT + DocT GT: In CKD/AKI fentanyl (or remifentanil) is the safest IV opioid: hepatic CYP3A4 → inactive norfentanyl. Renal traps: morphine (M6G sedation/respiratory depression, M3G neuroexcitation), hydromorphone (H3G myoclonus, seizures) and tramadol (seizures, serotonin toxicity).

DocT GT (×3): Lorazepam is glucuronidated (phase II, preserved in cirrhosis: 'OLT' = Oxazepam, Lorazepam, Temazepam), unlike diazepam, clonazepam and chlordiazepoxide. Its propylene glycol diluent (also in IV diazepam, phenobarbital and some IV nitroglycerin preparations) is metabolised to lactate: prolonged high-dose infusion → high-anion-gap lactic acidosis with osmolal gap >10–12, delirium, hypotension, AKI and haemolysis; stop or switch (cyanide and coronary steal belong to nitroprusside).

DocT (×4): CURRENT (amperage = V/R) sets electrical injury severity: ~1 mA felt, 10–20 mA AC = 'let-go' threshold, 50–100 mA across the chest → VF, several amperes → asystole and deep burns; then pathway, duration, contact area. AC is ~3× more dangerous than DC because tetany clamps the hand on; DC throws the victim (blunt trauma). Age changes prognosis, not the injury.

DocT (×2): Tissue resistance rises nerve < vessel < muscle < skin < tendon < fat < bone. Nerves conduct easily, so neural injury (and delayed cord syndrome days–months later) can occur without skin burns; bone resists most, heats most and cooks peri-osseous muscle, which is why skin burns underestimate deep necrosis.

DocT (×2) + DocT GT: Lightning = brief massive DC → asystole + apnoea; the heart often restarts but apnoea persists, so reverse triage (treat the apparently dead first, ventilate). Most energy flashes over the skin (Lichtenberg figures), so deep damage is usually LESS than high-voltage AC. Myocardium is stunned directly (ECG + serial troponins); look for tympanic rupture, transient keraunoparalysis and cataracts months later (refer to ophthalmology).
cross: DocT keys PATHWAY as the main determinant of electrical injury in one item and AMPERAGE in another (Q24). Truth: amperage is the single most important determinant (Rosen/Tintinalli); pathway decides which organs. If amperage is offered, pick it; if not, pick pathway.

DocT keys escharotomy for a high-voltage forearm with tense compartments. Truth: fasciotomy opens the deep compartments; escharotomy only releases a constricting eschar. Pick fasciotomy unless the picture shows a circumferential full-thickness eschar.

lines: DocT + Marrow: Rewarm below the ECLS tier by stage: mild 32–35 °C passive external (dry, insulate; shivering adds ~1–2 °C/h; room-temperature fluid cools); moderate 28–32 °C active external (forced air) + IV fluid warmed to 38–42 °C; severe <28 °C or unstable = active internal (ECLS first, thoracic/peritoneal lavage if unavailable), which also counters afterdrop.

DocT: Hypothermic arrest <30 °C (ERC 2021): up to 3 shocks, then withhold further shocks, adrenaline and antiarrhythmics until core >30 °C (cold myocardium does not respond, drugs accumulate); at 30–35 °C double the drug interval (adrenaline every 6–10 min). Handle gently and keep horizontal — the cold heart is irritable and lidocaine does not work. AHA is more permissive; DocT keys ERC.

Marrow: In hypothermic arrest a serum K >12 mmol/L means massive cell lysis (asphyxia or death before cooling) — non-survivable, so stop CPR and do not start ECLS; fixed pupils and Osborn waves are unreliable for prognosis in the cold.

DocT GT + Marrow: Classic (non-exertional) heat stroke in the elderly: cool fast by evaporation + convection (lukewarm mist and fan, ice packs to neck, axillae, groin) or ice-water immersion, aiming below 39 °C within 30 min. With no rectal probe, cool immediately until shivering (tympanic/axillary readings are unreliable). Dantrolene and paracetamol do not work: the set point is normal.

DocT: Box jellyfish (Chironex): douse with VINEGAR for 30 s to inactivate undischarged nematocysts before removing tentacles; no rubbing, no fresh water. Death comes in minutes from cardiotoxicity and apnoea. Contrast stingray/venomous fish: hot-water immersion (heat-labile venom).

DocT + DocT GT: Descent and O2 are definitive for all altitude illness (descend until symptoms resolve, usually 300–1000 m; 'at least 100 m' is false). Acetazolamide 250 mg 12-hourly treats AMS (125 mg prevents); HAPE treatment if descent/O2 unavailable = nifedipine SR 30 mg 12-hourly (PDE-5 inhibitors mainly prevent); dexamethasone is for HACE, not HAPE; a Gamow bag simulates descent.
cross: DocT keys 'cool to 36 °C' in exertional heat stroke. Truth: stop cold-water immersion at about 38.6–39 °C (ACSM 2023, WMS 2019) because the core keeps falling after removal and 36 °C risks iatrogenic hypothermia. If '38.5–39 °C' is offered, pick it.

lines: DocT: No trial supports dantrolene in stimulant hyperthermia (cocaine, amphetamine, MDMA): the heat comes from agitation, muscle activity and central drive, not an RyR1 calcium leak. Cool actively and, above 41 C, add paralysis and ventilation. Malignant hyperthermia is the only one that gets dantrolene, 2.5 mg/kg IV repeated to 10 mg/kg.

DocT GT: Malignant hyperthermia is triggered only by volatile anaesthetics and suxamethonium in RYR1/CACNA1S carriers; propofol, midazolam, opioids, ketamine and non-depolarising relaxants such as rocuronium are safe. Rising ETCO2 with tachycardia and rigidity comes before the temperature.

Marrow: Physostigmine is contraindicated in asthma, cardiac conduction defects, ventricular arrhythmia and in hypotension not caused by an anticholinergic agent, since it can precipitate bradyasystole and bronchospasm.

DocT: First stop the burning: remove clothing, rings, watches and jewellery at once (metal holds heat and becomes a tourniquet as the limb swells), then cool with running tap water for 20 min (useful up to 3 h after the burn). Steroids have no role.

Marrow: Causes of rhabdomyolysis beyond crush: electrical injury, malignant hyperthermia, heat stroke, myxoedema, sea-snake (myotoxic) envenomation; neurotoxic cobra venom paralyses without rhabdomyolysis. Labs: CK >5× normal, high K and PO4, low Ca; target urine pH >6.5 if alkalinising.

DocT: No RCT shows that earlier cooling helps: prehospital cold-saline cooling (Kim, JAMA 2014, n=1,359; RINSE) gave no survival or neurological benefit and caused more re-arrest and pulmonary oedema.
cross: DocT keys 32–34 °C for 12–24 h (the 2002–2010 AHA answer). Truth: after TTM (33 vs 36) and TTM2 (≤33 vs ≤37.5) showed no difference, AHA 2025 recommends temperature control 32–37.5 °C for ≥36 h in any comatose survivor, any rhythm; ERC/ESICM 2021 prevent fever (≤37.7 °C) for 72 h. If a 32–37.5 °C / fever-prevention option exists, pick it.

DocT keys 'cooling as early as possible (time to target)'. Truth: no RCT shows time-to-target matters and prehospital cooling trials are negative; every option is flawed by 2025 standards. If forced, pick DocT's 'early' option as least-wrong.

Marrow keys 34 °C. Truth: 34 °C sits inside AHA's 32–36/32–37.5 range, but TTM2 and ERC 2021 favour fever prevention ≤37.5 °C. If the question follows AHA, 34 °C is acceptable; if ERC, pick normothermia/fever prevention.

lines: DocT: Skin counter-warming plus magnesium is the first answer for shivering during temperature control because neither sedates nor drops BP; opioid boluses (D) are a later sedating tier, cold saline (A) worsens shivering, and paralysis (B) is the last resort, with EEG.
cross: DocT GT keys dexmedetomidine for controlling shivering while minimising hypotension and sedation. Truth: the Columbia ladder puts magnesium (with buspirone, paracetamol and counter-warming) BEFORE dexmedetomidine, and magnesium has the least hypotension and sedation. If magnesium is offered for 'least hypotension/sedation', pick magnesium; dexmedetomidine is the next tier.

lines: DocT: Rewarm after temperature control at ≤0.25–0.5 °C/h: fast rewarming raises cerebral metabolic demand in a brain with fragile O2 delivery, causes vasodilatory hypotension and REBOUND HYPERkalaemia as K+ moves back out of cells (option C has the direction wrong). Afterdrop (D) is an accidental-hypothermia phenomenon.

DocT GT: Temperature control is for comatose survivors after ROSC (not every arrest); hypothermia is held for 24 h (not 48), shivering must be suppressed, and earlier initiation is linked to better outcome. Current ERC-ESICM practice is active fever prevention (≤37.5–37.7 °C) for at least 72 h.

DocT GT: Temperature control slows CYP450 metabolism by roughly 7–22% per °C below 37: midazolam (CYP3A4) and fentanyl accumulate, prolonging sedation and confounding neuroprognostication. Atracurium and cisatracurium (Hofmann elimination/ester hydrolysis) are not CYP-dependent; hydromorphone is glucuronidated.

Marrow: Bedside Shivering Assessment Scale 0–3: 0–1 → counter-warming (skin surface warming); 2 → add sedation/analgesia; 3 (trunk + limbs shaking) → escalate to neuromuscular blockade under deep sedation.

DocT: A krait-bitten patient with PaCO2 60 is in ventilatory failure: intubate and ventilate now, because oxygen alone masks the rising CO2. Intubate early for bulbar palsy with pooled secretions, neck-flexor weakness, paradoxical breathing or a falling single-breath count; presynaptic block may need days to weeks of ventilation.

Marrow: The 10-vial Indian polyvalent rule is not universal: CroFab for North American pit vipers starts at 4-6 vials, with the same dose in children. The constant across both is that children get the adult dose, because the snake injects the same venom.

DocT Recall25: DocT describes the Indian SAKTI trial as comparing low-dose with high-dose ASV in haemotoxic (viper) bites, with low dose non-inferior for restoring clotting and outcomes - supporting the low-dose regimen (trial details as given by DocT, not independently verified).

DocT: Russell's viper with oliguric AKI and persistently incoagulable blood needs both a repeat antivenom dose (an abnormal clotting test means venom is still active) AND early renal replacement therapy, because ATN from haemoglobin and myoglobin, DIC and direct nephrotoxicity rarely reverses on fluid alone. Steroids have no role, and FFP only after antivenom.

DocT: Antivenom has no absolute contraindication: give it whenever there is systemic envenoming, because untreated envenoming is deadlier than the reaction. A previous equine-serum reaction or atopy means having resuscitation drugs ready, not withholding antivenom, and egg allergy is irrelevant (that belongs to vaccines).

DocT Recall25: A krait bite presenting at 48 h and already intubated still gets ASV if envenomed: circulating venom may remain and ASV stops further binding, though it cannot reverse toxin already bound - krait toxin is presynaptic, so neostigmine does not help either.

DocT: In antivenom anaphylaxis (hypotension, wheeze, rash) stop the infusion and give IM adrenaline 0.5 mg (0.01 mg/kg in a child) FIRST, not only if severe (WHO SEARO 2016); chlorphenamine and hydrocortisone are slow adjuncts, so any option that omits adrenaline is wrong. The card's 'IM adrenaline if severe' should read 'adrenaline first'.

fix.t: Stop; IM adrenaline 0.5 mg (child 0.01 mg/kg) at the FIRST sign, even mild urticaria; then chlorphenamine 10 mg + hydrocortisone 100 mg IV; restart slowly
fix.why: Antivenom anaphylaxis: WHO gives IM adrenaline 0.5 mg first, not "if severe".
fix.src: WHO SEARO Snakebite Guidelines 2016 (Warrell); India NSBP 2017

cross: DocT keys a pressure-immobilisation bandage for any suspected snakebite. Truth: that is Australian elapid practice. The Indian National Snakebite Protocol (Do it R.I.G.H.T.) and WHO SEARO 2016 say immobilise the limb without a tight bandage, because most Indian bites are viper bites where pressure worsens local necrosis. In an Indian stem pick immobilisation and transport; reserve pressure immobilisation for a purely neurotoxic elapid bite.

lines: DocT: Indian polyvalent antivenom is standardised so that each mL neutralises 0.6 mg of Russell's viper venom (and 0.6 mg cobra, 0.45 mg krait, 0.45 mg saw-scaled viper), making one 10 mL vial worth 6 mg. A Russell's viper injects about 63 mg on average and up to ~150 mg, which is why the starting dose is 10 vials (~60 mg) and children get the same dose.

DocT GT: A raised or rising BUN at 24 h (prerenal azotaemia from third-space loss) is the lab marker of intravascular depletion in acute pancreatitis and predicts mortality, which is why BUN sits in BISAP. Amylase level has no prognostic value, and hypocalcaemia reflects saponification and low albumin, not volume.

DocT: Plain X-ray signs of acute pancreatitis are the sentinel loop (a single dilated jejunal loop in the left upper quadrant = localised ileus) and the colon cut-off sign (gas-filled transverse colon stopping at the splenic flexure). Both are non-specific; the film's real job in an acute abdomen is to exclude free gas.

DocT: Idiopathic (recurrent) pancreatitis with a normal ultrasound needs EUS and/or MRCP: secretin-MRCP for duct anatomy (divisum, strictures), EUS for microlithiasis, sludge and small tumours, mandatory to exclude a neoplasm if age >40. ERCP is not a diagnostic test: it causes pancreatitis in 3–15%.
cross: DocT 8 key: MRCP as the sole first-line test for idiopathic pancreatitis. Truth: ACG/AGA place EUS at least level with MRCP (higher yield for microlithiasis and small tumours) and ahead of it after 40. If both are offered and the patient is >40, pick EUS; if only MRCP is offered, it is acceptable.

lines: DocT: TENSION (Lancet 2018; 98 infected-necrosis patients): endoscopic step-up vs surgical step-up gave the same major complications or death (43% vs 45%), but fewer pancreatic fistulas (5% vs 32%) and a shorter stay. So PANTER = step-up beats open necrosectomy; TENSION = endoscopic step-up equals surgical step-up, with fewer fistulas.

DocT: Disconnected duct syndrome (viable tail cut off from the head → persistent high-output external fistula or recurrent collections) cannot be bridged by a transpapillary stent. First line now is EUS-guided transmural drainage with long-term indwelling plastic stents; distal pancreatectomy is the definitive surgery when that fails, and octreotide only lowers output.

DocT: A PARTIAL duct leak (duct still in continuity: high-amylase drain fluid, pancreatic ascites or effusion) is treated by ERCP with a transpapillary pancreatic stent that bridges the leak and turns an external fistula into internal drainage.

DocT + DocT GT: Post-ERCP pancreatitis is the commonest ERCP complication (3–15%): new epigastric pain within hours with lipase/amylase >3× normal, from papillary trauma plus hydrostatic and chemical injury of contrast injected into the pancreatic duct. Highest risk with difficult cannulation, pancreatic-duct injection and young women; prevent it with rectal indomethacin or diclofenac 100 mg, a pancreatic-duct stent in high-risk cases and generous Ringer's lactate.
Marrow: ALT >150 IU/L (~3× normal) with raised ALP/bilirubin early in acute pancreatitis predicts a gallstone cause; AST > ALT points to alcohol. Confirm with ultrasound.

cross: DocT 19 key: CTSI 6 for a peripancreatic collection plus 30–50% necrosis. Truth: Balthazar scores a single fluid collection 3 (peripancreatic inflammation alone 2), so collection + 30–50% necrosis (4) = 7. If the CT shows a discrete collection, pick 7; if only peripancreatic inflammation, 6.

lines: DocT + DocT GT: A diverticular bleed found at colonoscopy is treated there and then (clips or band ligation ± adrenaline injection), so a stable patient needs neither embolisation nor surgery. Polyethylene glycol is bowel preparation, not treatment.

DocT + DocT GT: An unstable lower GI bleeder after failed endoscopic therapy goes to catheter mesenteric angiography + embolisation, which both localises and treats (ACG 2023 puts CTA first only if it causes no delay). A tagged-RBC scan is slow and non-therapeutic, and total colectomy is the last resort.

DocT GT: Upper GI blood is digested and absorbed as protein, so hepatic urea production rises and BUN climbs out of proportion to creatinine (BUN:creatinine >30) with a stable GFR. That is why a high urea points to an upper source, and why it should not be read as AKI.

DocT: AIMS65 (albumin <3 g/dL, INR >1.5, altered mental status, SBP ≤90, age ≥65) predicts in-hospital mortality, whereas Glasgow–Blatchford predicts the need for intervention. Full Rockall needs endoscopic findings, and MELD is a cirrhosis score, not a bleed score.

DocT: The restrictive trigger in upper GI bleeding is Hb <7 g/dL (Villanueva 2013) but <8 g/dL with ischaemic heart disease (ACG/ESGE), so an IHD patient at Hb 8.1 is not transfused yet. TRIGGER (2015) only showed that <8 vs <10 was feasible and safe.

DocT GT: Warfarin with INR 4.5–10 and no bleeding: hold 1–2 doses and recheck; low-dose oral vitamin K (1–2.5 mg) only if bleeding risk is high. INR >10 without bleeding → oral vitamin K 2.5–5 mg. PCC and IV vitamin K 5–10 mg are only for major bleeding and would over-correct a mechanical valve.
cross: Marrow keys FFP + vitamin K for a warfarin bleed in a patient with a recent thrombotic event (4F-PCC is prothrombotic and PCC trials excluded MI/stroke/TIA/DIC within 3 months). Truth: AHA/ESO still prefer 4F-PCC + IV vitamin K over FFP for life-threatening bleeding or ICH. If the stem stresses a recent MI/stroke and asks for the 'safest' agent, pick FFP + vitamin K; otherwise pick 4F-PCC.

lines: DocT + DocT GT: In NON-variceal bleeding, high-dose IV PPI works by holding gastric pH above 6 (pepsin inactive, clot stable), which H2 blockers cannot. Given before endoscopy (80 mg bolus ± 8 mg/h) it downstages ulcers (Lau, NEJM 2007) but does not cut rebleeding, surgery or death, so it must never delay the scope; REDUCE is a COPD steroid trial, not a PPI trial.

DocT GT: Intubate BEFORE endoscopy in variceal bleeding when there is encephalopathy or low GCS, massive ongoing haematemesis or an unprotected airway, because aspiration of blood is a leading cause of death. NIV is contraindicated (vomiting, low GCS) and nasal oxygen protects nothing.
cross: Marrow QB37-Q02 key: a first step other than antibiotics. Truth: in a cirrhotic variceal bleeder, vasoactive drug AND IV ceftriaxone 1 g/day (up to 7 days) are both guideline-mandated before endoscopy; antibiotics cut rebleeding and death. If 'IV ceftriaxone' is among the options and the vasoactive drug is already running, pick it.

lines: DocT: GAVE ('watermelon stomach': red stripes radiating from the pylorus in the ANTRUM) is not caused by portal pressure, so β-blockers and TIPS do not help; treat with argon plasma coagulation or band ligation. Portal hypertensive gastropathy is a mosaic 'snakeskin' pattern in the fundus/body and does respond to β-blockers.

DocT: Secondary prophylaxis after a variceal bleed = EVL every 2–4 weeks to eradication PLUS a non-selective β-blocker (propranolol or carvedilol), better than either alone (Baveno VII/AASLD). TIPS is for failure of this combination, or pre-emptive (within 72 h) in high-risk bleeders (Child C 10–13, or Child B >7 with active bleeding at endoscopy).

Marrow: Primary prophylaxis of large varices = NSBB (carvedilol preferred) or EVL if β-blockers are not tolerated. Portal vein thrombosis in cirrhosis → anticoagulate, usually with LMWH first; warfarin is hard to monitor because the baseline INR is already raised.
cross: DocT 16 key: C, TIPS first-line. Truth: EVL + NSBB is first-line secondary prophylaxis; TIPS is rescue or pre-emptive within 72 h in high-risk patients, and DocT's own explanation says so. If the stem is a stabilised patient after a first bleed, pick EVL + NSBB.

DocT keys 3 days of antibiotics after source control for intra-abdominal infection. Truth: STOP-IT (Sawyer, NEJM 2015) gave a fixed 4 ± 1 days (median 4). Pick 4 days if offered; otherwise the closest (3 days).

lines: DocT: Renal Doppler in HRS shows normal-sized, unobstructed kidneys with a raised resistive index (>0.70; DocT quotes >0.9) from intense renal arterial vasoconstriction, and the RI can rise before creatinine. ATN shows parenchymal change; obstruction shows hydronephrosis.

DocT GT: Stage 1A AKI in cirrhosis = monitor closely and remove risk factors (stop NSAIDs and nephrotoxins, taper diuretics and non-selective β-blockers, treat infection, replace losses). Terlipressin + albumin only once HRS-AKI criteria are met and AKI is beyond stage 1A, so terlipressin is the wrong pick at 1A.

DocT: Bubble echo: agitated saline reaching the left atrium after ≥3 cardiac cycles (typically 3–6) = intrapulmonary shunt (HPS); within <3 cycles = intracardiac shunt (PFO/ASD). The card's '3–4' is where the window starts, so a bubble at beat 5 or 6 still counts as HPS.

DocT GT: Platypnoea = breathlessness on sitting/standing, relieved lying flat; orthodeoxia = the matching SaO2 fall (≥4–5%) upright. Both point to HPS because the basal intrapulmonary shunts get more flow when upright. Orthopnoea is the reverse (worse lying flat); trepopnoea is worse lying on one side.

DocT GT: Hepatopulmonary syndrome is graded by room-air PaO2 (with an A–a gradient ≥15 mmHg, ≥20 if over 64): mild ≥80, moderate 60–79, severe 50–59, very severe <50 mmHg. PaO2 <60 earns MELD exception points for transplant, and <50 raises post-transplant mortality.

Marrow: If neither terlipressin nor noradrenaline is offered, midodrine + octreotide with albumin is the answer. Dialysis is only for refractory fluid overload, hyperkalaemia or acidosis, as a bridge to transplant, not as HRS treatment.
cross: Marrow QB40-Q07 key: midodrine + octreotide + albumin. Truth: terlipressin + albumin is first-line (noradrenaline in the ICU); midodrine/octreotide is the weaker fallback. If terlipressin or noradrenaline is offered, pick it; midodrine only when neither is.

lines: DocT: Non-response to terlipressin + albumin is the strongest predictor of death in HRS-AKI: non-responders survive weeks to months, and RRT is only a bridge to transplant. Baseline creatinine and bilirubin predict who will respond; ascites volume and ammonia are weak outcome predictors.

DocT: Hyponatraemia (especially Na <130) is an independent HE precipitant: astrocytes already loaded with glutamine have used up their organic osmolytes (myo-inositol), so low plasma osmolality swells them further. In a cirrhotic on furosemide with Na 122, name hyponatraemia as the precipitant; furosemide is its cause and ammonia the mediator.
cross: DocT 21 key: 'All of the above', including a high-fat meal. Truth: fat is not an HE precipitant (protein load/GI blood is), and in that stem the real trigger is the diuretic (hyponatraemia, hypokalaemia, volume loss). If 'all of the above' contains a non-precipitant, pick the diuretic-related option.

GT 148; GT4 Q101, same key A key: one option keyed though all four are recognised precipitants. Truth: infection (including SBP) is the commonest trigger in recent series; GI bleeding is the classic textbook answer. If asked 'commonest', pick infection; if asked 'classic', pick GI bleed.

lines: DocT + Marrow: Zinc deficiency is common in cirrhosis (poor intake, diuretic-driven urinary loss, malabsorption). Zinc is a cofactor for ornithine transcarbamylase (urea cycle) and muscle glutamine synthetase, so deficiency raises ammonia; replacement gives only a modest mental-state benefit.

DocT: Rifaximin to prevent recurrent HE = Bass, NEJM 2010: 299 cirrhotics after ≥2 episodes, 550 mg BD vs placebo for 6 months (91% also on lactulose); breakthrough HE 22% vs 46%, HE admissions 14% vs 23%. CONFIRM is the terlipressin-HRS trial, not an HE trial.

DocT GT: BCAA (leucine, isoleucine, valine) supplements improve nitrogen balance in malnourished or critically ill patients, but no trial shows lower mortality or shorter ventilation. Their encephalopathy benefit is limited to cirrhosis (fewer HE episodes, not lower mortality), so they are not routine ICU nutrition.

DocT: In a confused cirrhotic, a symmetrical non-focal exam with asterixis = metabolic (hepatic) encephalopathy. Raised tone, clonus and extensor plantars occur in West Haven grade 3 HE, so they do not by themselves point to a structural lesion; a FOCAL deficit does.

DocT GT: Bacterial infection is the commonest ACLF trigger (~1/3 of cases) and 40–60% of infections in cirrhosis progress to ACLF, so prevention covers every infection, not only SBP. Norfloxacin prophylaxis selects quinolone-resistant organisms and C. difficile and carries QT/tendon toxicity; rifaximin is minimally absorbed with few systemic effects.

DocT: First step for hypervolaemic hyponatraemia in cirrhosis is fluid restriction to 1–1.5 L/day once Na <125, with diuretics stopped; hypertonic saline only for severe symptoms or just before transplant. Correct by ≤8 mmol/L in 24 h (high osmotic-demyelination risk) and avoid tolvaptan in liver disease (FDA hepatotoxicity warning).

DocT GT: Long-term albumin (ANSWER 2018: 40 g twice weekly for 2 weeks, then 40 g weekly, in uncomplicated ascites on diuretics) improved 18-month survival (77% vs 66%) and cut SBP, HE, renal dysfunction and paracenteses. MACHT (wait-listed patients) was negative, and ATTIRE (in-hospital albumin to ≥3 g/dL) gave no benefit and more pulmonary oedema.

fix.t: d No serum-albumin target (ATTIRE 2021: no benefit, more pulmonary oedema). Give with LVP >5 L (6–8 g/L removed), SBP (1.5 g/kg d1, 1 g/kg d3), HRS-AKI.
fix.why: Replace albumin to keep serum albumin above 3 g/dL. ATTIRE showed no benefit from that target; albumin is for LVP, SBP, HRS.

lines: DocT: Autoimmune hepatitis presenting as ALF: steroids only in early ALF (no grade 3–4 HE), with transplant listing in parallel; no improvement in bilirubin/INR within ~7 days = steroid failure → urgent transplant. Do not escalate steroids or add azathioprine/MMF: they act slowly and add sepsis risk.

DocT + DocT GT: Hepatitis B is the exception to 'viral hepatitis = supportive': start tenofovir or entecavir at once in acute severe HBV/ALF, HBV reactivation, HBV-ACLF and decompensated HBV cirrhosis, whatever the HBV DNA. Reactivation under rituximab, chemotherapy or steroids can bring back IgM anti-HBc (so it does not prove new infection), and is prevented by screening HBsAg and anti-HBc and giving prophylactic entecavir/tenofovir.

DocT GT: Autoantibodies in autoimmune hepatitis: anti-LKM1 marks type 2 (children and young women, more often acute severe or fulminant) and is the most specific; ANA and anti-smooth-muscle mark the commoner type 1. Anti-mitochondrial = PBC; anti-centromere = limited scleroderma.

DocT GT: Judge the response in hepatic encephalopathy clinically, by clearing disorientation and asterixis (West Haven grade falling). Serum ammonia correlates poorly with grade in cirrhosis and is not used to monitor treatment (AASLD/EASL); EEG and bilirubin do not track it either.

DocT: MELD and 3-month mortality: ≤9 ~2%, 10–19 ~6%, 20–29 ~20%, 30–39 ~53%, ≥40 ~71%. Refer for transplant once MELD ≥15, where transplant survival benefit exceeds operative risk; so MELD 25 = high risk, evaluate for transplant.

DocT + Marrow: Sequence in septic shock with a surgical source: resuscitate and give antibiotics within 1 h, then source control as soon as the patient is stabilised (2026 target ≤6 h) — timely source control is the intervention most tied to survival. 'Antibiotics within 6 h' is wrong; bicarbonate does not treat the cause.

DocT + DocT GT: CIAOW (WSES worldwide observational study, ~2,000 complicated intra-abdominal infections): delayed source control >24 h, age, small-bowel perforation, ICU admission and immunosuppression independently predicted death — THE source-control-timing study (ProCESS = EGDT; SOAP II = dopamine vs norepinephrine).

Marrow: An abscess that is not shrinking (or is enlarging) after 48–72 h of appropriate antibiotics needs percutaneous drainage, with antibiotics continued — antibiotics penetrate abscess cavities poorly.
cross: DocT keys 'source control within 12 hours'. Truth: SSC 2026 suggests within 6 h (2021 said 'as rapidly as possible'). If both 6 h and 12 h are offered, pick 6 h; if only 12 h, it is still the best option.

lines: Marrow: SvO2 (normal ~65–75%) is a perfusion endpoint: LOW in hypovolaemic, cardiogenic and obstructive shock (low delivery, high extraction) and HIGH in distributive shock (impaired extraction); lactate and base deficit are the other endpoints.

DocT: Hypercalcaemia raises the depolarisation threshold, so it causes hyporeflexia and weakness (the mirror of hypocalcaemic hyperreflexia and tetany). Traps: bisphosphonates block osteoclasts not osteoblasts, NSAIDs are avoided because they cut renal blood flow and calcium excretion, and the QT is short rather than long.

DocT GT: Severe hypercalcaemia can produce J (Osborn) waves as well as a short QT, even at a normal temperature; with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy that points to sarcoidosis, where granulomas make calcitriol through 1-alpha-hydroxylase.

DocT: Diagnostic or banding endoscopy is a low-bleeding-risk procedure: AGA 2021, EASL 2022 and AASLD 2024 advise no prophylactic platelets, FFP or cryoprecipitate before it in cirrhosis whatever the count or INR, because transfusion raises portal pressure. A platelet target (~50,000) is considered only for high-risk procedures (polypectomy, liver biopsy).

DocT GT: Factor VIII (with von Willebrand factor) RISES in cirrhosis because it is made by endothelium and its clearance falls, while II, V, VII, IX, X and protein C fall. High VIII with low protein C is why cirrhotics clot despite a raised INR, and a low VIII points to DIC rather than liver failure.
cross: DocT 2 key: transfuse platelets to >50,000 before endoscopy. Truth: endoscopy is low-risk, and current cirrhosis guidance is to proceed without correction. If the procedure is low-risk (endoscopy, paracentesis, central line), pick 'proceed without intervention'; consider a platelet target only for high-risk procedures.

GT7 Q118 key: PCC lacks factor VII. Truth: only the old 3-factor PCC lacks VII; the 4-factor PCC used for warfarin reversal contains II, VII, IX and X plus proteins C and S (this card). If factor V or VIII is offered, pick it; pick VII only if the stem means 3-factor PCC.

fix.t: d No prophylactic platelets/TPO-RA for low-risk procedures at any count; high-risk procedure with <50,000: individualise (TPO-RA e.g. avatrombopag/lusutrombopag, or platelets). Transfuse for active bleeding.
fix.why: Platelets 20–50k before invasive procedures is outdated for low-risk procedures (AGA 2021, EASL 2022, AASLD 2024: no prophylactic products).
fix.src: AGA Clinical Practice Update 2021; EASL CPG 2022

lines: DocT: PLADO (NEJM 2010, 1,351 patients with hypoproliferative thrombocytopenia) compared prophylactic doses of 1.1, 2.2 and 4.4 x10^11/m2 at a trigger of 10,000: grade 2 or worse bleeding was the same (~70%) in all arms. The low dose used fewer platelets overall but needed more transfusions - dose does not change bleeding.

DocT GT: The 2019 TRALI definition splits it in two: type I = no ARDS risk factor, onset within 6 h, P/F <=300 (or SpO2 <90% on air), bilateral infiltrates, no left-atrial hypertension; type II = an ARDS risk factor or mild pre-existing ARDS that had been stable for 12 h before transfusion. Deterioration driven by the underlying risk factor is ARDS, not TRALI.

Marrow: An acute haemolytic transfusion reaction is a type II (antibody-mediated) reaction from ABO incompatibility - preformed IgM against transfused red cells: fever, hypotension, loin pain, oozing from DIC and AKI. Stop the transfusion, notify the blood bank and send the unit with samples; the first move in any suspected reaction is to stop it.

Marrow: Hold the two reflexes side by side: TACO is hypertensive with a high BNP and responds to an IV diuretic; TRALI is hypotensive and diuretics are harmful - give oxygen and lung-protective ventilation instead.
cross: GrandT1 Q43 keys TRALI type II for a trauma patient whose stem states there are NO ARDS risk factors. Truth: no risk factor defines type I, DocT's own explanation describes type I, and the later repeats (CGT1 Q116, GT8 Q53) key type I.
