Read the risk-factor sentence first: no risk factor = type I, risk factor present (or stable mild ARDS for 12 h) = type II.

AIM2 Q105 keys TRALI for sudden refractory hypoxaemia with bilateral fluffy opacities after trauma, but the stem never mentions a transfusion. Truth: TRALI needs a transfusion within 6 h; fat embolism (24-72 h after a long-bone fracture, with petechiae and confusion) fits the same picture. If a transfusion is stated or implied, pick TRALI; if a long-bone fracture with petechiae is given, pick fat embolism.

GT7 Q90 keys 6 g/dL as the haemoglobin below which transfusion benefits. Truth: that is the old ASA 'almost always indicated' figure; the trial-based restrictive threshold (TRICC, TRISS, AABB 2023) is 7 g/dL, 8 in cardiac surgery or active ischaemia. If 7 is offered pick 7; pick 6 only when it is the lowest option and the stem echoes the 'almost always' wording.

lines: DocT: TRISS (Holst, NEJM 2014; 998 septic-shock patients): transfuse at Hb ≤7 vs ≤9 — 90-day mortality 43% vs 45% (NS), same ischaemic events and life support, half the red cells; the 7 trigger holds even in shock with raised lactate, unlike Rivers' haematocrit-30% target.

DocT GT + Marrow: Suspected TTP (MAHA, platelets low, no other cause) gets plasma exchange started on suspicion plus steroids, with rituximab and caplacizumab as add-ons - send ADAMTS13 but never wait for it. The card's bare plasma exchange row understates current treatment.

DocT GT: A TMA appearing within days of a new drug (quinine, co-trimoxazole, gemcitabine, clopidogrel, tacrolimus or ciclosporin) with ADAMTS13 only mildly reduced (>10%) is drug-induced TMA, not TTP: stop or switch the drug, since plasma exchange gives no proven benefit. Refractory complement-mediated cases may need eculizumab.

DocT: Sepsis-associated DIC without bleeding or a planned procedure is treated by treating the cause only - no FFP for INR 2.4, no platelets at 62,000, no cryoprecipitate at fibrinogen 1.8 g/L. If bleeding: FFP 15-30 mL/kg for PT/APTT >1.5x, cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate below 1.5 g/L, platelets below 50,000.

fix.t: Treatment | TTP: plasma exchange started on suspicion + steroids + rituximab ± caplacizumab; aHUS: eculizumab/ravulizumab; STEC-HUS: supportive
fix.why: TMA treatment "plasma exchange; IVIG". Current: plasma exchange + steroids ± rituximab/caplacizumab, started on suspicion.

lines: DocT: In DIC the platelet count, and above all a falling trend, tracks ongoing consumption and correlates best with organ dysfunction and mortality: D-dimer is sensitive but non-specific, PT prolongs late, and fibrinogen is an acute-phase reactant that is often normal in sepsis-associated DIC. The ISTH sepsis-induced coagulopathy score uses platelets, PT and SOFA, without D-dimer.

DocT GT: Placental abruption releases tissue factor, driving systemic thrombin generation; fibrin microthrombi then consume platelets and factors (high INR, low platelets and fibrinogen, high D-dimer) and shear red cells into schistocytes. ITP gives isolated thrombocytopenia with a normal INR, and vitamin K deficiency spares platelets.

DocT Recall25: Bleeding on day 6 of ECMO with LOW fibrinogen and HIGH D-dimer is consumptive DIC from circuit contact activation of coagulation and fibrinolysis. HIT gives thrombosis with a platelet fall, not low fibrinogen; vitamin K deficiency and liver failure prolong the PT without a big D-dimer rise.
cross: Recall25 Q147 keys ATRA as the drug 'most commonly associated with DIC'. Truth: APL itself causes the hyperfibrinolytic DIC and ATRA corrects it within days (bleeding risk is highest before ATRA); ATRA's own complication is differentiation syndrome. If APL-linked drugs are the only fit, pick ATRA as the intended link, but do not learn ATRA as a cause of DIC.

lines: DocT GT: Every patient with HIT gets a full therapeutic-dose non-heparin anticoagulant even without thrombosis, because stopping heparin alone leaves a 25-50% thrombosis risk within 30 days. Options are argatroban, bivalirudin, fondaparinux (a pentasaccharide that barely binds PF4, renally cleared, avoided at CrCl <30, not reversed by protamine) or a DOAC.

DocT GT: Never start warfarin in acute HIT: it depletes protein C before prothrombin and causes venous limb gangrene or skin necrosis. Start it only once platelets recover (>=150,000), overlap with the non-heparin agent for at least 5 days, and give vitamin K if warfarin was already started.

DocT GT + Recall25 + Marrow: Toxic alcohols separate by their acid. Methanol -> formic acid -> retina and optic nerve (snowstorm vision, disc hyperaemia, blindness), putaminal necrosis, haemorrhagic pancreatitis; folinic acid speeds formate clearance. Ethylene glycol -> glycolic then oxalic acid -> urinary calcium oxalate crystals, hypocalcaemia, AKI at 24-72 h - the oxalate crystals and renal failure are the findings specific to ethylene glycol once the osmolal gap says 'toxic alcohol'.

DocT GT + Marrow: Give fomepizole empirically when a toxic alcohol is suspected and the level is delayed; a normal osmolal gap does not exclude it in a late presenter. A serum ethanol >=100 mg/dL already saturates alcohol dehydrogenase (10-20x higher affinity), so fomepizole can be deferred while ethanol stays high and started as it falls. Dialyse for visual signs, AKI or severe acidosis.

Marrow: COHb half-life is ~4 h on air, ~1 h on 100% O2, 20-30 min with hyperbaric O2; intubate if GCS <=8. In fire victims give hydroxocobalamin 5 g for suspected cyanide and avoid nitrites, whose methaemoglobin adds to the CO carriage deficit and worsens hypotension.
cross: Marrow keys high-flow oxygen for an unconscious carbon monoxide patient. Truth: 100% O2 is the core treatment, but it must be delivered through a protected airway. If GCS <=8 or the airway is unprotected, pick intubation with 100% O2; otherwise high-flow O2 is right.

lines: DocT: Voriconazole-first rests on Herbrecht (NEJM 2002; 277 patients): vs amphotericin B deoxycholate, response 53% vs 32% and 12-week survival 71% vs 58%. Fluconazole has no mould activity, and caspofungin is salvage, not primary therapy.

DocT GT: Acute GVHD severity (MAGIC/Glucksberg grade I-IV) is set by skin rash area, stool volume and bilirubin, with grade III-IV and extensive gut disease carrying far higher mortality. It is T-cell driven, diagnosed on skin or GI biopsy (not liver), and treated with methylprednisolone 2 mg/kg, topical steroid alone only for isolated grade I skin.

DocT: Acute GVHD hits skin, gut and liver; lung GVHD is chronic (bronchiolitis obliterans). Rash with fever and non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema at neutrophil recovery (day 7-30) is engraftment syndrome, which is also steroid-responsive, so choose GVHD only when engraftment syndrome is not offered.

DocT: When Pseudomonas is resistant to the empirical β-lactam, switch to an active one (e.g. meropenem); a short aminoglycoside double cover is acceptable in shock. Drop the aminoglycoside after 48–72 h once susceptibilities are known: β-lactam monotherapy matches combination for mortality with less nephrotoxicity (Cochrane; SSC).

DocT: Owl's-eye intranuclear inclusions on BAL cytology or biopsy mean tissue-invasive CMV pneumonitis even when blood CMV PCR is negative, because lung disease can be compartmentalised. Treat with IV ganciclovir 5 mg/kg 12-hourly.

DocT GT: β-D-glucan is a pan-fungal marker (Candida, Aspergillus, very high in Pneumocystis) but is NOT raised by Cryptococcus or Mucorales. False positives: IVIG, albumin, cellulose dialysis membranes, surgical gauze, Gram-negative bacteraemia and older batches of piperacillin-tazobactam/amoxicillin-clavulanate.
cross: GT 148 key: meropenem as a cause of false-positive β-D-glucan. Truth: meropenem is not a recognised cause; the drug culprits are older β-lactam/β-lactamase-inhibitor batches, plus IVIG, albumin, haemodialysis membranes and gauze. If IVIG, albumin or haemodialysis is offered, pick it; meropenem is only DocT's answer by elimination.

lines: Marrow: Enzyme inducers (rifampicin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, dexamethasone, efavirenz, nevirapine) lower caspofungin levels, so raise the maintenance dose from 50 to 70 mg/day.

DocT + DocT GT: TB pattern follows cell-mediated immunity: HIV with CD4 >200 looks like reactivation (upper-lobe cavities); CD4 <200 or a transplant recipient looks primary (lower/middle-lobe consolidation, hilar nodes, miliary, few cavities, often smear-negative). Start ART within 2 weeks of HRZE if CD4 <50, otherwise by 8 weeks, delaying it in TB meningitis (IRIS); in transplant recipients rifampicin induces tacrolimus/ciclosporin, so raise doses and follow levels.
Marrow: The compensatory anti-inflammatory response (CARS) is driven by IL-4 and IL-10, which suppress TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6 and IL-8 — the basis of late immunoparalysis and nosocomial infection.

DocT GT: Let PaCO2 rise gradually, about 10 mmHg/h up to ~80 mmHg over the first day, so intracellular buffering keeps pH ≥7.20; faster rises cause abrupt acidosis, raised ICP and haemodynamic instability. Oxygenation target stays SpO2 88–95% — never accept 75%.

Marrow: Harms of permissive hypercapnia: cerebral vasodilation with raised ICP (avoid in brain injury), hypoxic-pulmonary-style vasoconstriction with RV strain, sympathetic surge and arrhythmias, depressed contractility, and a right-shifted O2 dissociation curve.
cross: Marrow keys 'continue current settings' at pH 7.27 on RR 18. Truth: ARDSNet raises RR (up to 35) whenever pH <7.30; VT increase or bicarbonate only if pH <7.15 at RR 35. If 'increase RR' is offered, pick it; pick 'continue' only if no rate option exists.

Marrow keys 'severe sepsis' for infection with organ dysfunction (the Sepsis-2 answer). Truth: Sepsis-3 removed severe sepsis — infection with a SOFA rise ≥2 is simply sepsis. If the stem says Sepsis-3, pick sepsis; if it uses SIRS-era definitions, severe sepsis.

lines: Marrow: In a stable, non-bleeding patient transfuse ONE unit at Hb <7 (over ~2–4 h) and recheck before the next — each unit raises Hb by ~1 g/dL.
DocT: Persistent MODS beyond 48–72 h carries mortality above 50%; Ferreira (JAMA 2001): a SOFA rising over the first 48 h predicts ≥50% mortality whatever the start, a falling SOFA <27%.
cross: DocT keys SOFA as the prognostic score in a sepsis stem. Truth: APACHE II also predicts mortality; SOFA is picked because Sepsis-3 is built on it and its 48–72 h trend carries prognosis. If the stem frames sepsis or organ-failure trend, pick SOFA.
DocT calls a SOFA of 5 'poor prognosis'. Truth: 5 is moderate dysfunction (admission mortality ~10–20%). Choose the option that reads it as moderate when available.

lines: DocT GT: Uncomplicated Gram-negative CLABSI (Pseudomonas included) with the line out and no metastatic focus: 7 days is enough (Yahav 2019 RCT, 7 vs 14 days non-inferior). 14 days is the minimum for S. aureus; 4–6 weeks for endocarditis, osteomyelitis or septic thrombosis.

DocT: Candidaemia with liver abscesses: echinocandin (caspofungin 70 mg then 50 mg/day) or liposomal AmB, drain the abscesses and treat until the lesions resolve (not just 14 days); step down to fluconazole after 5–7 days if susceptible, stable and cultures clear.
cross: DocT keys 'stop antibacterials and switch to liposomal AmB'. Truth: IDSA 2016 gives echinocandin or L-AmB equally; switching to caspofungin with continued drainage is at least as correct, and stopping antibacterials is unjustified. If caspofungin + drainage is offered, it is defensible.

lines: DocT + DocT GT: Oseltamivir (a neuraminidase inhibitor that stops virion release) is started at once in every hospitalised, severe or high-risk patient whatever the symptom duration or rapid-test result; the 48-h rule applies only to uncomplicated outpatients. Give 75 mg BD for 5 days (longer if immunocompromised); double dose adds nothing.

DocT GT: High-risk groups for treatment: age ≥65, pregnancy and up to 2 weeks postpartum (6 weeks is outside), immunosuppression (steroids, TNF-α blockers, chemotherapy, HIV CD4 <200), chronic heart, lung, liver, kidney, metabolic or neurological disease, BMI ≥40, nursing-home residents.

DocT: Suspected avian influenza (H5N1/H7N9) with severe pneumonia → oseltamivir empirically at once and RT-PCR on a lower-respiratory sample, because rapid antigen tests miss novel strains. Neuraminidase inhibitors stay active against most H5N1, and routine steroids prolong shedding and raise mortality.

Marrow: Start IV aciclovir on suspicion of HSV encephalitis, before PCR or MRI results. Red cells in an atraumatic CSF (haemorrhagic temporal necrosis) support HSV, and a PCR taken in the first 72 h can be falsely negative, so repeat it rather than stop.
cross: DocT 22 key: 21 days. Truth: IDSA 2008 gives 14–21 days; UK 2012 gives 14 days if immunocompetent and 21 if immunocompromised (this card). If the patient is immunocompetent, 14 days is equally right; pick 21 only if immunosuppressed or if '14–21 days' is not offered.

lines: DocT: At CD4 <50, the viral CNS opportunist with high CSF protein and LOW glucose is CMV ventriculoencephalitis, confirmed by CSF CMV PCR (not an antigen test) and treated with ganciclovir + foscarnet. CSF EBV DNA in advanced HIV mainly flags primary CNS lymphoma; JC virus (PML) gives non-enhancing white-matter lesions with bland CSF and no oedema.
cross: DocT 1 key: EBV encephalitis. Truth: EBV encephalitis is rare; CD4 20 + low CSF glucose + diffuse oedema fits CMV ventriculoencephalitis, and a positive CSF EBV PCR in advanced HIV means primary CNS lymphoma. If a CMV option is offered (even one spoiled by 'antigen test'), pick CMV.

lines: DocT + DocT GT: Blood cultures miss ~50% of invasive candidiasis and take days, so add non-culture tests: (1→3)-β-D-glucan (pan-fungal, high NPV; misses Cryptococcus and Mucorales; false positives from albumin/IVIG, cellulose dialysis membranes, gauze) and PCR/T2Candida. Galactomannan is Aspergillus-only; they rule OUT and target therapy, not a trigger for empirical antifungals.

Marrow: Candida in respiratory samples is almost always colonisation — true Candida pneumonia is rare and needs histology — so it is no reason to start antifungals; immunosuppression (e.g. chemotherapy) is the real risk factor for invasive disease.
cross: DocT keys pre-emptive echinocandin for a Candida colonisation index ≥0.5 (older IDSA 2016 thinking). Truth: EMPIRICUS and INTENSE were negative and SSC 2026 suggests against empirical or biomarker-triggered antifungals. If 'no antifungal, monitor' is offered for a stable patient, it has the better evidence; pick echinocandin only for a shocked high-risk patient.

lines: Marrow: Pentamidine for PCP TREATMENT is IV (4 mg/kg daily) for severe disease failing or intolerant of TMP-SMX; aerosolised pentamidine is for prophylaxis only (poor upper-lobe distribution, no systemic cover).

fix.t: Pentamidine | 4 mg/kg IV once daily | IV only (aerosolised 300 mg monthly = prophylaxis only) | Alt (severe)
fix.why: Pentamidine "IV / aerosol" for PCP treatment. Aerosolised is prophylaxis only; treatment is IV.

fix.t: Pentamidine "600 mg daily" is not a standard dose (4 mg/kg once daily IV); the card also omits steroids when PaO2 <70 mmHg.

lines: DocT: The opportunist after severe influenza is influenza-associated pulmonary aspergillosis (~19% of ICU influenza patients, even immunocompetent; ~50% mortality): BAL galactomannan, then voriconazole. PJP needs T-cell immunosuppression; secondary bacterial pneumonia (S. aureus, pneumococcus) is the other classic post-influenza complication.
cross: DocT 9 key: PJP after recovered severe influenza in an immunocompetent 25-year-old. Truth: no recognised link; the established complications are influenza-associated aspergillosis and secondary bacterial pneumonia. If galactomannan/aspergillosis is offered, pick it.

lines: DocT: Fever + rash with crippling symmetrical small-joint polyarthralgia, platelets only mildly low and a stable haematocrit = chikungunya, not dengue: no plasma leak, so care is supportive (paracetamol) and the arthritis can last months. Dengue's clues are retro-orbital pain, myalgia and a day 4–5 leak with rising haematocrit; avoid NSAIDs until dengue is excluded.

Marrow: CNS involvement is common in leptospirosis: CSF pleocytosis in 50–90% in the immune phase (aseptic meningitis), whereas fewer than 10% develop icteric Weil's disease. Conjunctival suffusion + biphasic fever + aseptic meningitis = leptospirosis.

DocT: For RMSF and all rickettsioses, doxycycline 100 mg BD is the drug of choice at every age, including children <8 (short courses do not stain teeth) and life-threatening disease in pregnancy. Unlike scrub typhus, RMSF has no reliable alternative: azithromycin is unproven and chloramphenicol carries higher mortality.

DocT: Rocky Mountain spotted fever (R. rickettsii, tick) has no eschar: the rash starts on wrists and ankles on day 2–5, spreads centrally and to palms and soles, turns petechial, and leads to vasculitic multi-organ failure (~20–30% mortality untreated). Start doxycycline on suspicion; delay beyond day 5 raises mortality.

DocT GT: Artesunate needs no dose change in malarial AKI or on dialysis (converted to dihydroartemisinin, not renally cleared); quinine accumulates, so its maintenance dose is cut by a third after 48 h. Malarial AKI is mostly falciparum (sequestration, haemolysis, rhabdomyolysis), and hyponatraemia is commoner than hypernatraemia.

DocT + Marrow: Severe CAP = β-lactam + macrolide (ceftriaxone + azithromycin). Add MRSA or Pseudomonas cover only for validated risk factors (prior respiratory isolation, or hospitalisation with IV antibiotics in the last 90 days) or for Gram-positive cocci in clusters, necrotising/cavitary or post-influenza pneumonia (ATS/IDSA 2019). Nursing-home residence alone (old 'HCAP') no longer qualifies, and cefepime + vancomycin misses atypicals.

DocT GT: A negative MRSA nasal PCR/culture has ~96–99% negative predictive value for MRSA pneumonia (CAP and HAP/VAP), so anti-MRSA cover can be withheld or stopped. A positive swab has poor positive predictive value and says nothing about Pseudomonas or Enterobacterales.

DocT GT: A non-severe penicillin allergy (rash, not anaphylaxis) does not bar ceftriaxone + clarithromycin in severe CAP, because cephalosporin cross-reactivity is ~1–2% and side-chain dependent. Co-amoxiclav is a penicillin; true anaphylaxis calls for a respiratory fluoroquinolone.
cross: DocT 1; GT6 Q67 key: ceftriaxone + azithromycin alone in septic shock with Gram-positive clusters. Truth: ATS/IDSA 2019 would add vancomycin or linezolid; that option is not offered, so the key is least wrong. If an MRSA-covering combination is offered with clusters on Gram stain, pick it.

Marrow QB12-Q06 key: cefepime + vancomycin for a nursing-home COPD patient in shock. Truth: HCAP is retired; nursing-home residence alone does not justify MRSA/Pseudomonas cover. If the stem gives prior MRSA/Pseudomonas isolation or recent hospitalisation with IV antibiotics, pick broad cover; otherwise pick β-lactam + macrolide.

lines: DocT: For MSSA bacteraemia switch vancomycin to an anti-staphylococcal beta-lactam (nafcillin/oxacillin 2 g 4-hourly or cefazolin 2 g 8-hourly): vancomycin kills MSSA more slowly with ~1.5–2× the failure and mortality. Keep vancomycin for true beta-lactam anaphylaxis; ceftriaxone is inadequate for S. aureus endocarditis.

DocT GT: Daptomycin, the card's alternative when vancomycin MIC ≥2, is inactivated by pulmonary surfactant, so it fails in pneumonia (including septic pulmonary emboli from MRSA bacteraemia). Treat lung involvement with linezolid, vancomycin or ceftaroline.

DocT GT: Empirical line-sepsis cover (Gram-positive cocci in clusters) in a beta-lactam-allergic patient = an anti-MRSA agent (vancomycin; daptomycin or linezolid as alternatives) + NON-beta-lactam Gram-negative cover (fluoroquinolone, aminoglycoside or aztreonam); ceftriaxone, pip-tazo and ampicillin are all beta-lactams. Linezolid is bacteriostatic, so switch to vancomycin or daptomycin once S. aureus bacteraemia is confirmed.
cross: DocT keys linezolid for MRSA bacteraemia in a haemodialysis patient. Truth: vancomycin (dosed to levels) or daptomycin (q48h on HD) is first line; linezolid is bacteriostatic and salvage only. Pick vancomycin or daptomycin.

lines: DocT: MERINO (JAMA 2018; ceftriaxone-resistant E. coli/Klebsiella bacteraemia): 30-day mortality 12.3% on piperacillin-tazobactam vs 3.7% on meropenem, so pip-tazo is not a carbapenem substitute for ESBL bacteraemia (inoculum effect, co-carried OXA-1).

fix.t: AmpC | Inducible chromosomal (moderate–high risk): Enterobacter cloacae, Klebsiella aerogenes, Citrobacter freundii (low risk: Serratia, Morganella, Providencia); plasmid AmpC: E. coli, K. pneumoniae
fix.why: Inducible AmpC organisms listed as E. coli, A. baumannii, Klebsiella. Classic ones are Enterobacter, Citrobacter, Serratia.

fix.t: ESBL row lists P. aeruginosa, A. baumannii and S. maltophilia as ESBL pathogens — atypical; ESBLs are mainly an Enterobacterales problem.

lines: DocT + DocT GT: Necrotising soft-tissue infection (incl. Fournier's): empirical vancomycin or linezolid (MRSA) + pip-tazo or a carbapenem + clindamycin (switches off toxin synthesis), IDSA 2014. DocT keys 'pip-tazo + clindamycin', which omits MRSA cover but is the best option offered; surgery still decides survival.

DocT (×2) + Marrow: Trigger for emergency exploration = 'cellulitis' advancing despite 48 h of antibiotics with pain out of proportion, woody induration beyond the erythema, numbness at the edge, crepitus, bullae or shock (sea-water abrasion = Vibrio vulnificus: add doxycycline + ceftazidime). MRI must not delay theatre; antibiotics, IVIG or HBO alone are wrong.

DocT GT (×4): Gas in the renal parenchyma on CT/X-ray in a diabetic (~90%) or obstructed patient with fever, flank pain and AKI = emphysematous pyelonephritis (E. coli, Klebsiella). Resuscitate, IV antibiotics, glycaemic control and percutaneous drainage or relief of obstruction FIRST; nephrectomy only for extensive gas (Huang–Tseng 3–4 with shock) or failed drainage. Gas confined to the collecting system = emphysematous pyelitis (better prognosis).

DocT: In a stable patient with MDR Pseudomonas CAUTI, amikacin alone (15 mg/kg once daily for 5–7 days) is acceptable: ~90% is excreted unchanged, so urinary levels far exceed the MIC, and it spares meropenem and colistin. This holds only in the urinary tract, not for bacteraemia or pneumonia, and the catheter must be changed.

DocT GT: When two antipseudomonal agents are needed they must come from different classes: an antipseudomonal β-lactam (pip-tazo, cefepime, ceftazidime, meropenem/imipenem, aztreonam) PLUS a fluoroquinolone (cipro/levo) or an aminoglycoside, e.g. cefepime + ciprofloxacin. Two β-lactams add no cover, and ceftriaxone and ertapenem do not cover Pseudomonas at all.

DocT: The dexamethasone course is 0.15 mg/kg 6-hourly for 4 days (de Gans 2002), not 5. The mortality benefit is in pneumococcal meningitis, so many guidelines stop it once another organism (e.g. meningococcus, Gram-negative diplococci) is confirmed.

fix.t: Dose: dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg (10 mg adult) 6-hourly for 4 days (IDSA: 2–4 days); stop if not pneumococcal/Hib.
fix.why: Dexamethasone for 5 days in bacterial meningitis. Standard course is 4 days (0.15 mg/kg 6-hourly, de Gans).

lines: DocT + DocT GT: Stroke lysis trials by window: NINDS 0–3 h, ECASS III 3–4.5 h, IST-3 up to 6 h (included >80 y); WAKE-UP (2018) selects unknown-onset stroke by DWI+/FLAIR– mismatch (dates onset <4.5 h); EXTEND (2019) 4.5–9 h or wake-up by perfusion mismatch (PWI > DWI = salvageable penumbra, also the basis of DAWN/DEFUSE-3 thrombectomy).

DocT GT: Lytics by fibrin specificity and half-life: alteplase fibrin-specific, t½ ~4–6 min (needs infusion); reteplase ~15 min (double bolus); tenecteplase most fibrin-specific, t½ ~20 min (single bolus). Streptokinase acts indirectly via a streptokinase–plasminogen complex, is not fibrin-specific and is antigenic; urokinase is direct but not fibrin-specific.

DocT: Arrest in pregnancy with a dilated RV and septum bowing into the LV on POCUS = massive PE: lyse during CPR (alteplase 50 mg bolus) — pregnancy is only a relative contraindication and is overridden in arrest. From 20 weeks resuscitative delivery by 5 min runs alongside lysis, not instead (D wrong).

DocT (×2) + DocT GT: Imaging beats the clock. Wake-up stroke: DWI-positive/FLAIR-negative dates the infarct to <4.5 h (WAKE-UP 2018: mRS 0–1 53% vs 42%), and a perfusion mismatch selects alteplase up to 9 h (EXTEND 2019). LVO (ICA/M1) at 6–24 h with a small core → thrombectomy by clinical–core mismatch (DAWN, 6–24 h) or perfusion mismatch (DEFUSE-3, 6–16 h); hemicraniectomy treats malignant oedema, not the occlusion.

Marrow + DocT GT: Non-contrast CT first to exclude haemorrhage before any lytic or antithrombotic; DWI MRI is the most sensitive test for hyperacute ischaemia (~90% vs ~40% for early CT), and CT perfusion misses small, lacunar and posterior-fossa infarcts. Amaurosis fugax → carotid duplex or CTA.

Marrow: Suspected basilar occlusion (coma, quadriplegia, locked-in) → straight to angiography for thrombectomy; premedicate a contrast allergy rather than waiting for MRI, because untreated basilar occlusion is nearly always fatal.
cross: DocT GT keys the 'first-generation Merci retriever' for thrombectomy at 6 h in a lysis-ineligible patient. Truth: Merci (2004) is obsolete; current thrombectomy uses stent retrievers (Solitaire, Trevo) or contact aspiration. Pick a stent retriever if offered; otherwise Merci is the least-wrong option.

lines: DocT: Beyond 6 h (up to 24 h) thrombectomy is chosen on imaging mismatch, not the clock: DAWN (6–24 h) used a small core with a high NIHSS; DEFUSE-3 (6–16 h) used core <70 mL with mismatch ratio ≥1.8, both for ICA/M1 occlusion. 'NIHSS <6' is wrong — both trials needed NIHSS ≥6.

DocT: In stroke, pregnancy is only a RELATIVE contraindication to alteplase (~70 kDa, does not cross the placenta; AHA 2019 allows it when benefit outweighs uterine-bleeding risk); thrombectomy is preferred only when CTA shows a large-vessel occlusion.

DocT GT: AHA stroke rules add arterial puncture at a NON-compressible site within 7 days (e.g. femoral puncture above the inguinal ligament) as a contraindication to alteplase; a radial puncture, INR ≤1.7 and platelets ≥100,000 do not bar lysis.
cross: DocT keys thrombectomy for a pregnant woman with an MCA infarct on CT, without a CTA. Truth: thrombectomy needs a demonstrated LVO; IV alteplase may be given in pregnancy when benefit outweighs risk. If the stem shows an LVO, pick thrombectomy; if not, alteplase is equally defensible.

DocT GT keys 'after 48 hours' for starting aspirin after stroke alteplase, while its own explanation says 24 h. Truth: AHA 2019 — no antiplatelet or anticoagulant for 24 h; start after the 24-h CT/MRI excludes haemorrhage. Pick 'after 24 h with repeat imaging'.

DocT keys PCC for symptomatic ICH after alteplase. Truth: AHA/ASA 2019 — stop the infusion, cryoprecipitate 10 U (fibrinogen ≥150–200) + TXA 1 g (or aminocaproic acid); PCC is for warfarin/Xa-inhibitor bleeds. If cryoprecipitate or TXA is offered, pick it; PCC only as least-wrong.

DocT keys a target SBP <160 in acute ICH. Truth: AHA/ASA 2022 for SBP 150–220 → target 140 (range 130–150) is safe and may improve function; INTERACT3 bundle also <140. If 'labetalol, <140' is offered, pick it.

lines: DocT GT: Antiplatelet-related platelet dysfunction in SAH/ICH needing surgery → desmopressin 0.4 µg/kg IV (releases vWF and factor VIII, restores adhesion). Platelet transfusion is not routine (PATCH: worse outcome in ICH on antiplatelets); aspirin is withheld until the aneurysm is secured.

cross: DocT keys 'observe and monitor ICP' for a mild lobar ICH on antiplatelets. Truth: no platelet transfusion (PATCH: more death/dependency) is correct, but an alert patient needs BP control and supportive care, not an ICP monitor (GCS ≤8, IVH/hydrocephalus, herniation). Pick 'observe' over platelet transfusion.

lines: DocT: Strongest predictors of haematoma expansion = early time from onset, baseline volume, CTA spot sign and anticoagulation/coagulopathy (INR >1.5). High SBP is a weak, inconsistent predictor (INTERACT2/ATACH-II lowered BP with little effect on growth).
cross: DocT keys SBP >180 as the predictor of expansion. Truth: INR >1.5/anticoagulation, time from onset, volume and spot sign predict far better (AHA 2022). If INR >1.5 is offered, pick it.

lines: DocT: An alert (GCS 15) lobar ICH without shift or hydrocephalus is observed with supportive care; ENRICH (2024), which made minimally invasive evacuation of 30–80 mL lobar bleeds work, enrolled only GCS 5–14.

DocT: Haematoma growth on repeat CT WITHOUT clinical decline → tighter medical care (SBP ~140, reverse anticoagulant, frequent neuro checks) and a neurosurgical opinion, not automatic craniotomy (no functional benefit in supratentorial ICH; reserved as life-saving for deterioration).
cross: DocT keys 'plan craniotomy' for haematoma expansion alone. Truth: AHA 2022 reserves craniotomy for the deteriorating patient; the stem gives no clinical decline. Pick medical optimisation + neurosurgical review if offered.

lines: DocT: Blood in the basal cisterns, Sylvian fissures and sulci = SAH (~85% aneurysmal); blood only in the cisterns in front of the midbrain/pons = perimesencephalic non-aneurysmal SAH (CTA negative, rarely rebleeds). Parenchymal hyperdensity = ICH.

cross: DocT GT keys cerebral autoregulation as MAP 60–150 mmHg. Truth: classic texts give 50–150 (the card), newer data 60–150 with much narrower individual plateaus; chronic hypertension shifts the whole curve right. If only one range is offered pick it; if both, pick 60–150 for DocT.

lines: DocT + Marrow + DocT GT (×4): Uncal herniation = medial temporal lobe over the tentorium → ipsilateral CN III palsy (superficial parasympathetic fibres fail first: blown pupil, then ptosis and a down-and-out eye) + contralateral hemiparesis. Kernohan notch (opposite peduncle crushed on the tentorium) gives IPSILATERAL hemiparesis, a false-localising sign. Fixed dilated pupils in coma mean structural herniation: metabolic coma keeps pupils reactive, pontine bleeds and opioids give pinpoint pupils.

DocT GT (×4): Tonsillar herniation (posterior fossa mass) compresses the medulla: sudden coma, irregular breathing then apnoea, Cushing triad, flaccid quadriplegia, fixed pupils, cardiovascular collapse. Central herniation progresses rostro-caudally with posturing.

DocT + DocT GT (×3): Herniation types = subfalcine (commonest, = midline shift on CT; cingulate under the falx compresses the ACA → contralateral LEG weakness), uncal, central transtentorial (early diencephalic stage: small reactive pupils, roving eyes, Cheyne–Stokes, decorticate; then midposition pupils, decerebrate, Duret haemorrhages), upward (posterior fossa mass, often after an EVD: vomiting, upgaze palsy, small pupils), tonsillar and external (through a craniectomy). 'Transcerebellar' is not a type.
cross: Marrow keys IPSILATERAL hemiparesis (Kernohan notch) for uncal herniation. Truth: the expected finding is CONTRALATERAL hemiparesis; Kernohan is the false-localising exception. If the stem stresses a false-localising sign or the opposite peduncle, pick ipsilateral; otherwise contralateral.

lines: DocT: Thalamic haemorrhage gives contralateral hemiparesis and hemisensory loss by compressing the adjacent posterior limb of the internal capsule. Homonymous hemianopia = occipital, ipsilateral ataxia = cerebellar, global aphasia = dominant MCA cortex.

DocT: Pinpoint but REACTIVE pupils localise to the pons (descending sympathetic fibres cut, parasympathetic intact): pontine haemorrhage or basilar occlusion. Opioids and organophosphates mimic it, so exclude drugs first.

DocT GT: Cerebellar haemorrhage usually starts in the dentate nucleus (superior cerebellar artery branches): sudden vertigo, vomiting, inability to walk, ipsilateral gaze and facial palsy in an awake patient, then sudden coma from brainstem compression or hydrocephalus. Evacuate if >3 cm, deteriorating, or with brainstem compression/hydrocephalus.

DocT: Strictly lobar/cortical microbleeds on GRE/SWI (± cortical superficial siderosis) at age ≥50 = probable cerebral amyloid angiopathy (Boston 2.0); deep microbleeds (basal ganglia, thalamus, pons) = hypertensive arteriolopathy. CAA predicts recurrent lobar ICH and makes antithrombotics and lysis riskier.
Marrow: Bilateral or parasagittal lobar haemorrhage in a young woman (OCP, pregnancy, puerperium) = cerebral venous thrombosis until proven otherwise; get CT/MR venography.
DocT: CT never diagnoses brain death: diffuse grey–white loss with effaced sulci and cisterns only supplies the 'known irreversible cause'; brainstem testing and the apnoea test still decide death.

DocT: After midazolam/fentanyl infusions wait at least 5 elimination half-lives before testing, longer after prolonged infusion, in renal/hepatic failure or hypothermia (midazolam's active metabolite accumulates in AKI); if you cannot wait, use an ancillary flow study.

DocT: In aSAH the EVD is the ICP monitor of choice because it also drains CSF for hydrocephalus (up to 20%, often in the first 24 h), usually the reason to monitor; jugular oximetry and TCD give no ICP number. A GCS 13 patient without hydrocephalus needs no monitor.

cross: DocT keys mannitol as the 'most appropriate initial' step for raised ICP. Truth: head-up 30°, midline, sedation, normocapnia and CPP come first (SIBICC/BTF); mannitol is the first DRUG. If a positioning/basic-measures option is offered, pick it.

lines: DocT (×3): With compressed or small ventricles (after craniotomy, ASDH with shift, diffuse swelling in DAI) a parenchymal probe is the practical ICP device. Evacuate an ASDH first if >10 mm or shift >5 mm (any GCS); in DAI ICP can be high with no shift, so absent shift does not remove the indication. New confusion (GCS 14) after craniotomy needs a CT, not a monitor.
cross: DocT keys the EVD in post-craniotomy, ASDH and DAI items. Truth: EVD is the gold-standard device in general, but compressed ventricles make a parenchymal probe the usual choice. If the question asks 'gold standard', pick EVD; if it asks the practical device with small ventricles, pick parenchymal.

lines: DocT: Routine ICP monitoring is NOT recommended in ischaemic stroke, even malignant MCA infarction (AHA 2019; NCS 2015): lateral shift causes herniation while global ICP is still normal, and hemicraniectomy is decided clinically and on CT.
cross: DocT keys an EVD for monitoring malignant MCA infarction. Truth: no invasive monitor is recommended, and an EVD is a poor choice with compressed ventricles and no hydrocephalus. If 'clinical + CT monitoring' is offered, pick it.

fix.t: Malignant infarction: NOT routine — follow clinical exam + imaging (ICP may stay normal despite herniation); CNS infection
fix.why: Lists malignant infarction as an ICP-monitoring indication. AHA 2019 does not recommend routine ICP monitoring there.
fix.src: AHA/ASA 2014 swelling statement (Wijdicks); NCS LHI guideline 2015

lines: Marrow + DocT GT (×2): Doses (options differ only by dose): levetiracetam 60 mg/kg, max 4500 mg (ESETT; renal, extra dose after HD, no levels); midazolam 0.2 mg/kg → 0.05–2 mg/kg/h; propofol 1–2 mg/kg → 20–200 µg/kg/min (≈1–10 mg/kg/h); pentobarbital 5–15 mg/kg → 0.5–5 mg/kg/h; ketamine up to ~5 mg/kg/h; phenobarbital 20 mg/kg at 50–75 mg/min.

DocT GT (×3): Systemic effects of GCSE: the seizure drives a catecholamine surge (hypertension, tachycardia, hyperthermia, lactic acidosis, hyperglycaemia) that settles once seizures stop, so don't chase the BP; the drugs (benzodiazepines, propofol, barbiturates, fosphenytoin) cause the hypotension. Prolonged GCSE adds arrhythmias, stress cardiomyopathy, NEUROGENIC PULMONARY OEDEMA, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalaemia, AKI and aspiration; CPM, CVT and PRES cause seizures but are not their consequences.

DocT (×2) + DocT GT: Why other drugs still work: in prolonged seizures GABA-A receptors are internalised while NMDA receptors move to the synapse, so ketamine (NMDA antagonist) is added early in refractory SE; being sympathomimetic it supports BP and lowers vasopressor needs, and with controlled ventilation it does not meaningfully raise ICP. Levetiracetam acts on SV2A (unaffected by internalisation); phenytoin blocks voltage-gated Na+ channels.

DocT + DocT GT: NCSE = impaired consciousness without convulsions + epileptiform EEG. Salzburg: discharges >2.5 Hz, or ≤2.5 Hz/rhythmic delta with clinical or EEG improvement after IV benzodiazepine, subtle ictal signs or evolution. Found in 8–10% of comatose and 10–30% of unexplained altered-consciousness ICU patients; twitching is a minority sign, so only (continuous 24–48 h) EEG finds it.

DocT: EEG patterns: NCSE = rhythmic/periodic discharges >2.5 Hz or evolving, improving after benzodiazepine; metabolic encephalopathy = diffuse theta–delta slowing ± triphasic waves without evolution; brain death = electrocerebral silence; absence = generalised 3-Hz spike-and-wave lasting seconds (children).

DocT: FIRES = new-onset refractory SE (NORSE) 24 h–2 weeks after a febrile infection, mostly in school-age children; MRI and CSF are often normal and antiseizure drugs fail. Ketogenic diet is the most consistently effective therapy (start within days), with anakinra (IL-1 blockade) as the 2022 consensus add-on.

DocT GT: The ketogenic diet works in SRSE through induced ketosis: a 4:1 fat:(protein + carbohydrate) enteral formula with no glucose-containing infusions gives ketonuria and serum beta-hydroxybutyrate ≥2 mmol/L within 2–3 days (ketones raise GABA synthesis, stabilise neuronal energy). Watch acidosis, hypoglycaemia and hypertriglyceridaemia; avoid combining with propofol.

DocT GT: Super-refractory SE (≥24 h after starting anaesthetic infusions, or recurrence on weaning) also uses ketamine, inhaled anaesthetics, magnesium and neuromodulation: vagus nerve stimulation, DBS, ECT, or resective surgery. Continuous diazepam, rectal topiramate and nimodipine infusion are not SRSE therapies.

DocT: PLEDs (now LPDs) mark an acute focal cortical lesion (stroke, HSV encephalitis, abscess, tumour) and sit on the ictal–interictal continuum: about half have seizures, so they push toward NCSE and continuous EEG, though alone they do not prove NCSE. Metabolic encephalopathy gives generalised periodic or triphasic waves.
Marrow: Decerebrate or decorticate posturing needs an intact brainstem, so it EXCLUDES brain death; spinal reflexes, sweating, tachycardia and normal BP without pressors remain compatible with it.
Marrow: EEG for brain death = electrocerebral silence (no activity >2 µV) on a full montage for ≥30 min, off sedation and normothermic.

Marrow (×2): ECMO is not a contraindication to the apnoea test: cut sweep gas to 0.5–1 L/min to let PaCO2 rise, keep oxygenating through the oxygenator and CPAP 10 on the ETT, and confirm the PaCO2 threshold on post-oxygenator and patient gases.

DocT: Hyponatraemia is the commonest electrolyte cause of metabolic encephalopathy in hospital (about a third of ICU admissions are hyponatraemic), though sepsis-associated encephalopathy is the commonest ICU encephalopathy overall; hypercalcaemia, hyperglycaemia and uraemia do it less often.
Marrow: Promote carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine to the front of the SIADH drug list, with the elderly at highest risk - they raise renal ADH sensitivity rather than only central release.

DocT: Sudden severe ('thunderclap') headache with meningism is SAH until proven otherwise, so CT comes first. If bacterial meningitis is the worry and CT must precede LP, take blood cultures and give dexamethasone + antibiotics BEFORE the scan (IDSA/ESCMID).

DocT GT: Suspected bacterial meningitis → blood cultures, then empirical antibiotics + dexamethasone at once; never delay them for CT, LP or work-up of a complication. New polyuria with hypernatraemia here = central DI, a meningitis complication, confirmed later with urine osmolality and sodium.

DocT Recall25: Before an LP, correct platelets below 40–50 ×10⁹/L and an INR above 1.5 (platelets, FFP or PCC), because a spinal epidural haematoma can cause paraplegia. Start empirical antimicrobials while correcting; never wait for the LP.
cross: DocT 9 key: CT head first. Truth: right if the stem reads as SAH; if it reads as bacterial meningitis, cultures + dexamethasone + antibiotics come before CT (option D). If fever/photophobia/Brudzinski dominate, pick antibiotics before CT; if the onset is thunderclap, pick CT.

Marrow QB26-Q09 key: straight to LP, no CT. Truth: seizures, GCS ≤12, focal signs or papilloedema each mandate imaging before LP (this card); antibiotics go first so the scan causes no delay. If any of the four indications is in the stem, pick imaging before LP.

lines: DocT: At a sodium of 110 the clinical answer is seizures and coma: cerebral oedema and raised intracranial pressure are the mechanism, not a sign at the bedside. Severity is graded by symptoms, not the number - moderate means nausea, confusion and headache; severe means vomiting, seizures, GCS <=8 or cardiorespiratory distress.

DocT: In chronic pancreatitis hypocalcaemia has two routes - vitamin D malabsorption from steatorrhoea and alcohol-related hypomagnesaemia blocking PTH release. It presents with confusion, seizures, tetany and a long QT, and calcium will not hold until magnesium is replaced.

DocT: Naloxone-associated pulmonary oedema (~1-3% of reversals) is non-cardiogenic: abrupt reversal gives a catecholamine surge that raises pulmonary capillary pressure while the waking patient gasps against a closed glottis. It is not heroin alveolar toxicity or myocardial depression, which is why naloxone is titrated to breathing rather than full wakefulness.

DocT: Naloxone restores breathing, not consciousness. Persistent drowsiness once RR >=12 means a second cause: co-ingested sedative (benzodiazepine, alcohol, gabapentinoid, xylazine), hypoglycaemia, head injury or hypoxic brain injury. Titrate to RR >=12 and airway reflexes, then look for that second agent.

cross: DocT keys hypomagnesaemia as the electrolyte cause of neuronal excitability and confusion. Truth: hypomagnesaemia does cause hyperexcitability by lifting the Mg block on NMDA channels, but hyponatraemia is the commonest electrolyte cause of encephalopathy and DocT keys it as such elsewhere in the same module. If the question asks for neuronal excitability, pick magnesium; if it asks for the commonest cause of confusion, pick sodium.

lines: DocT GT (×2): Uterotonics in asthma: carboprost (PGF2α) bronchoconstricts, so it is the one contraindicated; misoprostol (PGE1), dinoprostone (PGE2, a bronchodilator) and oxytocin are safe. Ergometrine is barred by hypertension or pre-eclampsia, and only rarely provokes bronchospasm.
cross: DocT keys carboprost as the second uterotonic. Truth: ergometrine is equally valid when there is no hypertension (RCOG GTG 52, WHO 2023). Carboprost is right only because the stem says no asthma; if the stem mentions asthma pick ergometrine, if hypertension pick carboprost.

In an ASTHMATIC with atony, DocT GT keys misoprostol as the next drug (CGT4 Q66, although methylergonovine is safe if normotensive) and lists methylergonovine as the drug to AVOID when carboprost is not among the options (CGT6 Q89). Truth: carboprost is the drug to avoid in asthma. For 'avoid', pick carboprost if offered, else methylergonovine; for 'next drug', pick methylergonovine if BP is normal, misoprostol if DocT offers no ergot.

lines: DocT GT: A positive FAST changes management only together with the haemodynamics: unstable plus free fluid goes straight to laparotomy with no CT, stable goes to contrast CT. FAST needs roughly 200 mL (100-250 mL) of free fluid to be visible, so a negative FAST does not exclude injury.

DocT (×2): Placenta accreta spectrum on USG/MRI = loss of the retroplacental clear zone, placental lacunae, interrupted/bulging bladder line, dark T2 bands; with praevia the risk climbs with each caesarean (~3% → 11% → 40% → 60%). Planned caesarean hysterectomy at 34–36 weeks with the placenta left in situ (peeling it tears the invaded bed); B-Lynch, iliac ligation and embolisation are for atony.

DocT (×2): Uterine artery embolisation = for the STABLE woman with ongoing PPH after uterotonics when IR is available (~90% success, fertility kept); a contrast blush on angiography → embolise in the same sitting. Unstable or failed embolisation → laparotomy.
DocT: Early cord clamping is NOT part of active management of the third stage: WHO delays clamping 1–3 min, and the uterotonic within 1 min of birth carries almost all the benefit.
cross: DocT GT1 keys internal iliac ligation, but the GT3 repeat keys compression sutures for atony after failed uterine artery ligation. Truth: B-Lynch/compression sutures are quicker, uterus-sparing and treat atony; internal iliac ligation is demanding with ~40–60% success. Pick compression sutures.

lines: DocT + Marrow + DocT GT: Uterine inversion = collapse right after delivery, vaginal mass, no fundus palpable; shock out of proportion to blood loss (vagal bradycardia). Stop uterotonics, resuscitate, replace at once with the placenta left in situ (Johnson manoeuvre); if the ring is tight give a tocolytic (terbutaline, MgSO4, GTN) or GA, then oxytocin after reduction.

DocT: Day-2 heavy bleeding with a bulky tender uterus and open os = retained products: ultrasound shows an echogenic intracavitary mass WITH colour-Doppler flow (subinvolution lacks it). Uterotonic, antibiotics and evacuation.

cross: DocT keys expectant management (admit, pelvic rest, steroids, cross-match) for placenta praevia with a small painless bleed. Truth: ACOG/SMFM 2021 plan caesarean at 36+0 to 37+6 weeks, or 34+0 to 35+6 with recurrent bleeding, so at 36 weeks with a second bleed caesarean is the current-guideline answer. Pick expectant care only before 34 weeks with a single stable bleed.

lines: DocT Recall25: HELLP with hypotension and a falling Hb means a subcapsular liver haematoma (crescentic collection under the capsule on CT). Unruptured and stable: embolisation or conservative care with delivery; ruptured (free fluid, shock): resuscitate with blood products and do emergency caesarean with laparotomy for the liver (packing, embolisation) - not steroids or expectant care.

DocT + DocT GT: In severe pre-eclampsia, magnesium and treatment of BP ≥160/110 within 30–60 min run in parallel. With pulmonary oedema furosemide IS indicated (the 'avoid diuretics' rule is for oedema without lung congestion).
cross: DocT and DocT GT key magnesium as the 'initial' step with BP 180/110 and pulmonary oedema. Truth: urgent BP control (labetalol/hydralazine; nitroglycerin with pulmonary oedema) and furosemide are equally initial (ACOG 2020). If one first step is asked, magnesium is the least-wrong answer.

Marrow keys volume expansion first (dated Oxford Handbook answer). Truth: current practice restricts fluid to ≤80 mL/h; delivery is definitive with magnesium + antihypertensives. Pick fluid restriction if offered.

lines: DocT: HELLP with severe RUQ or shoulder-tip pain and very high AST → suspect subcapsular liver haematoma (~1% of HELLP) and image now; rupture → sudden shock, maternal mortality 30–50%. Unruptured: deliver, transfuse, avoid abdominal pressure; ruptured: laparotomy with packing or embolisation.

DocT: HELLP normally improves within 48–72 h of delivery; platelets still falling and haemolysis worsening after that suggest TTP or aHUS unmasked by pregnancy. Send ADAMTS13 and start plasma exchange (ASFA category I for TTP, only III for HELLP).
Marrow: RUQ/epigastric pain in HELLP = hepatic swelling stretching Glisson's capsule, which carries the risk of subcapsular haematoma and rupture.

DocT + DocT GT (×3): Over 90% of eclamptic seizures show PRES: bilateral symmetric parieto-occipital T2/FLAIR hyperintensity WITHOUT diffusion restriction (vasogenic oedema). An infarct restricts on DWI; CVT shows venous infarcts or empty-delta sign. Up to a third of eclampsia is postpartum (up to ~6 weeks); 'hypertensive encephalopathy' is the clinical term, PRES the radiological answer.
Marrow: Magnesium is contraindicated in myasthenia gravis (blocks ACh release, can precipitate crisis); use levetiracetam for eclampsia prophylaxis instead.

DocT: Shock in pregnancy follows the non-pregnant rule — norepinephrine first; phenylephrine (B) is for spinal-anaesthesia hypotension at caesarean, not established shock, and dopamine (A) causes more arrhythmias.

DocT: Paediatric septic shock persisting after 40–60 mL/kg of fluid needs adrenaline or norepinephrine, peripherally if needed (SSC Children 2020): warm shock (bounding pulses, flash refill, low diastolic) → norepinephrine; cold shock (mottled, slow refill) → adrenaline. Milrinone or nitroprusside only for cold shock with high SVR once BP is restored.

DocT: Absent end-diastolic flow in the umbilical artery = placental resistance so high (~60–70% of villous vessels obliterated) that diastolic flow stops (uteroplacental insufficiency, not cord thrombosis). AEDF → steroids and delivery by ~34 weeks; reversed EDF by ~30–32 weeks.

DocT: Evidence for resuscitative delivery is observational only: Katz, Dotters and Droegemueller 1986 (the '4-minute rule': start at 4 min, deliver by 5 min, because the gravid uterus cuts CPR output to ~30%), then Katz 2005 and Einav 2012 case reviews where ROSC often followed delivery. No RCT exists; MOMS = fetal myelomeningocele surgery, ALPS = late-preterm steroids, PROWESS = drotrecogin alfa.

DocT: Resuscitative hysterotomy uses a vertical midline incision from just above the symphysis to the umbilicus (fastest, best exposure), then a classical vertical uterine incision, done where the patient lies with CPR and uterine displacement continuing. Supra-umbilical or xiphoid incisions miss the uterus.
cross: DocT keys a 'HELP trial' as the evidence for resuscitative delivery. Truth: no such trial exists — the evidence is Katz 1986/2005 and the Einav 2012 review. If Katz or a case series is offered, pick it; otherwise eliminate MOMS, ALPS and PROWESS.

lines: DocT: Obstetric haemorrhage is the commonest cause of maternal cardiac arrest (~38% in AHA pooled data), so treat PEA in pregnancy as hypovolaemia first: wide-bore lines above the diaphragm, massive transfusion, uterotonics, obstetrician to theatre; eclampsia itself rarely arrests the heart.
cross: DocT keys 'give magnesium promptly as part of ACLS' in an eclampsia-related arrest. Truth: the AHA maternal arrest algorithm says if on IV magnesium, STOP it and give calcium chloride or gluconate; seizure prophylaxis resumes after ROSC. If she was already on magnesium, pick calcium.

lines: DocT GT: The 1 mg arrest dose is 10 mL of 1:10,000 (0.1 mg/mL). 1:1000 is 1 mg/mL (the IM anaphylaxis strength, 0.5 mL), so 10 mL of 1:1000 would be a tenfold overdose.

Marrow: Suspect tension pneumothorax in arrest with unilateral absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation (late) or rapidly rising airway pressures on the ventilator: decompress immediately (needle or finger thoracostomy) without imaging, then place a chest tube.

DocT: In arrest, an effusion seen on POCUS at the rhythm check is treated as tamponade and drained at once (subxiphoid, ultrasound-guided) during CPR, because compressions cannot fill a compressed heart. Thrombolysis (B) is for a dilated RV.

cross: DocT keys amiodarone + magnesium for maternal refractory VF with eclampsia. Truth: AHA lists amiodarone OR lidocaine, so lidocaine + magnesium is equally correct (fetal thyroid risk is irrelevant in arrest). If only one antiarrhythmic + magnesium pair is offered, pick it; with both, pick the keyed amiodarone.

lines: DocT GT: VF is the one rhythm that can never perfuse: chaotic ventricular activity gives zero output by definition (asystole is the other always-pulseless rhythm). VT, AF with RVR and junctional rhythm can each carry a pulse, so VT is shockable only when pulseless; with a pulse it is synchronised cardioversion or drugs.

DocT: AFE stays a clinical diagnosis (SMFM 2016: sudden arrest or hypotension + hypoxia + overt DIC within 30 min of the placenta, no fever). Serum markers that get asked (zinc coproporphyrin, sialyl-Tn, low C3/C4) are research tests; D-dimer and troponin are non-specific.

DocT: Collapse with coagulopathy during caesarean → TEE/TTE at the table: acute RV dilatation, septal shift, severe TR and an under-filled LV support AFE and steer therapy (inotrope or pulmonary vasodilator, not fluid). CTPA means moving an unstable, bleeding patient.

DocT: Collapse with an acutely dilated RV right after delivery is AFE until proven otherwise, even in APS: supportive care (oxygen/intubation, noradrenaline, inotrope or inhaled pulmonary vasodilator). Blind heparin or lysis is wrong because AFE brings DIC onto a uterus that has just bled; lyse only for confirmed massive PE or arrest.
Marrow: Pyelonephritis in pregnancy: admit, IV ceftriaxone, keep urine >50 mL/h, switch to oral once afebrile, discharge after 24 h afebrile, 7–10 days in total.

Marrow: Listeria in pregnancy: unpasteurised dairy/deli meat, flu-like or GI illness, Gram-positive rods with tumbling motility; can cause miscarriage, preterm labour and neonatal sepsis. Treat with ampicillin (cephalosporins do not cover Listeria).

DocT: Bilateral infiltrates after AFE are pulmonary oedema of mixed origin: early capillary leak (non-cardiogenic) and phase-2 LV failure (cardiogenic). DocT's key says 'cardiogenic' while its explanation says non-cardiogenic; pick the AFE-oedema option over pneumonia, PE or atelectasis.

DocT: In thrombotic antiphospholipid syndrome, especially triple-positive or after an arterial event, warfarin (INR 2–3) beats a DOAC: TRAPS (rivaroxaban vs warfarin) stopped early with thrombosis 12% vs 3%, mostly strokes and MI. Indefinite LMWH is the fallback for warfarin failure or pregnancy.
DocT: The paediatric GCS keeps the 3–15 scale and ≤8 still means secure the airway, but it has NOT been validated for prognosis in infants and young children: use it for trend and triage only.

DocT: Paediatric compressions: rate 100–120/min (as adults); depth at least one-third of the AP chest diameter — about 4 cm in infants, 5 cm in children; adolescents use the adult 5–6 cm. Ratio 30:2 with one rescuer, 15:2 with two.

DocT GT: Isopropanol is the toxic alcohol that breaks the high-gap rule: ADH converts it to acetone, so there is ketosis without acidosis - normal pH, positive ketones, raised osmolal gap, fruity breath, often haemorrhagic gastritis. It is 2-4 times as CNS-depressant as ethanol and lasts 2-4 times longer, so coma persists with a normal pH, and fomepizole is not needed.

DocT GT: Proximal (type 2) RTA lowers the bicarbonate reabsorption threshold to ~15-18 mmol/L: above it bicarbonate spills and urine is alkaline; once plasma HCO3 falls below it the intact distal nephron acidifies and urine pH drops below 5.5. Distal type 1 keeps urine pH >5.5 at any HCO3; type 2 causes are Fanconi, acetazolamide, myeloma and tenofovir.
cross: GT6 Q69 (repeated as GT7 Q83) keys type 2 RTA as the one cause that is NOT high-anion-gap. Truth: a pancreatic or small-bowel fistula also loses bicarbonate and is normal-gap, so two options are correct. If both appear, pick proximal RTA as DocT does, knowing fistula is normal-gap too.

lines: DocT (×2): APACHE II bands (Knaus 1985, hospital mortality): 0–4 ≈ 4%, 10–14 ≈ 15%, 20–24 ≈ 40%, 25–29 ≈ 55%, 30–34 ≈ 75%, >34 ≈ 85%. So 20 = severe, 25 ≈ one in two dies; GCS 10 alone adds 5 points (15 − GCS). In pancreatitis APACHE II >8 already marks severe disease.

DocT GT: The general ICU mortality-prediction systems are APACHE (II–IV), SAPS (II/3) and MPM0 (II/III), all from admission data for case-mix adjustment. BISAP is pancreatitis-specific and TRISS trauma-specific (RTS + ISS + age).
DocT: APACHE II's output is predicted hospital mortality, hence the score for overall severity in septic shock; MELD, Child-Pugh and CHA2DS2-VASc are organ- or disease-specific distractors.
cross: DocT keys APACHE II where SAPS II is also offered. Truth: both are general admission severity/mortality scores; nothing in the stem separates them. Pick APACHE II (the classic answer) unless the stem gives a SAPS-specific feature.

lines: DocT + DocT GT: After decompression, keep the abdomen open with temporary closure (negative-pressure preferred, WSACS 2013) and close the fascia as early as physiology allows: DocT keys 48–72 h, WSES 2018 says ideally within 4–7 days. Closure rates fall and fistula, infection and 'frozen abdomen' risk rise each day; TAC prevents recurrent ACS rather than causing it.
cross: DocT 3; CGT4 Q33; GT6 Q105 key: 'decompressive laparotomy after failure of conservative measures'. Truth: IAP 26 + oliguria + hypotension from a perforated ulcer = ACS with an unsourced perforation, so immediate laparotomy (source control + decompression) is right, as DocT's own explanation and its identical Q11 say. If ACS has a surgical cause, pick immediate laparotomy over a conservative trial.

DocT 9 key: minimise PEEP in IAH. Truth: WSACS 2013 makes no such recommendation; PEEP is set by best compliance or transpulmonary pressure, often higher to offset IAP-driven atelectasis (this card). If 'titrate PEEP to compliance/oesophageal pressure' is offered, pick it.

lines: DocT: For mortality prediction in a comorbid admission (COPD, prior MI) APACHE II beats SAPS II, whose only chronic-disease items are AIDS, metastatic cancer and haematological malignancy; SOFA has no age or comorbidity points at all.

cross: DocT 12 key: MELD as the prognostic tool in paracetamol ALF. Truth: King's College criteria are the standard (pH <7.30, or INR >6.5 + creatinine >3.4 mg/dL + grade 3–4 HE; lactate as add-on); MELD >33 is a secondary marker. If KCC is offered, pick it; otherwise MELD is least wrong.

lines: DocT: APACHE II uses serum HCO3 in place of arterial pH only when no ABG is available (≥52 = 4 points … <15 = 4); it includes chronic health points and is a general, not neurological, score.

DocT (×4) + DocT GT: Recovery from CO, then 2–40 days later parkinsonism, cognitive decline, mutism or incontinence = delayed neuropsychiatric sequelae. MRI: BILATERAL GLOBUS PALLIDUS lesions + diffuse white-matter demyelination (pallidus has high O2 demand and watershed supply). Not Wernicke, not peripheral neuropathy; cortical laminar necrosis suggests global hypoxia instead. About 50–75% recover within a year.

DocT (×2) + DocT GT + Recall25: Peak COHb predicts outcome poorly (it falls in transport and on O2); sequelae are predicted by loss of consciousness, age ≥36, exposure ≥24 h and COHb ≥25% (Weaver 2007). HBO (Weaver 2002, DocT's 'COMA trial': 3 sessions in 24 h cut cognitive sequelae 46% → 25%; Scheinkestel 1999 negative) is chosen by the PATIENT, not the level: LOC or neurological signs, pH <7.1–7.2, cardiac ischaemia, pregnancy or COHb >25% (drowsy with pH 7.15 at COHb 12% → HBO).

DocT (×2): CO is cardiotoxic (binds myoglobin, blocks complex IV): myocardial injury in about a third of moderate–severe cases raises long-term mortality (Henry 2006), so ECG and troponin in every patient. A STEMI pattern in a patient with CAD still needs urgent angiography; give 100% O2 throughout and HBO after reperfusion if indicated.
cross: DocT (and DocT GT) key exposure DURATION as the best predictor of CO sequelae. Truth: loss of consciousness and age predict as strongly (Weaver 2007), and acidosis predicts severity. If LOC is offered, it is equally defensible; otherwise pick duration.

DocT keys HBO for ST elevation in CO poisoning with CAD. Truth: STEMI guidance puts primary PCI first; HBO cannot open an occluded coronary and the chamber delays the cath lab. If 'immediate angiography' is offered, pick it.

lines: DocT: In a COPD exacerbation the systemic steroid is prednisolone 40 mg/day for 5 days (REDUCE: 5 days as good as 14); oral works as well as IV, so 'high-dose IV corticosteroids' is not the GOLD choice. Order: inhaled SABA ± ipratropium, O2 to 88–92%, steroid, antibiotic if sputum is purulent, NIV if pH <7.35 with PaCO2 >45.
cross: DocT keys high-dose IV steroids as the best initial therapy for AECOPD. Truth: GOLD 2025 first-line is inhaled SABA ± SAMA, then oral prednisolone 40 mg × 5 days; with purulent sputum antibiotics are equally indicated. If inhaled bronchodilator is offered, pick it; otherwise DocT's steroid key is least wrong.

lines: DocT: The FEV1 grade (GOLD 1–4) does not choose the inhaler — the ABE group does. A (0–1 moderate exacerbation, none admitted, mMRC 0–1/CAT <10) → one bronchodilator; B (mMRC ≥2/CAT ≥10) and E (≥2 moderate or ≥1 hospitalised) → LABA + LAMA. One admission = E → discharge on LABA + LAMA; add ICS (C) only if eosinophils ≥300/µL, because ICS adds pneumonia risk.

DocT GT: Airway mast-cell subtype tracks asthma severity: normal lung and MILD asthma keep subepithelial mast cells almost all tryptase-only (MCT); only SEVERE asthma shows fewer submucosal mast cells that are mainly tryptase + chymase (MCTC). The false option puts the reduced MCTC pattern in mild asthma.

DocT GT: In hypercapnic AECOPD, reduced consciousness is only a RELATIVE contraindication to NIV: a drowsy but rousable patient can have a closely watched trial, because CO2 narcosis often clears within 1–2 h. Coexisting cardiogenic pulmonary oedema is an extra indication for NIV, not a contraindication.

DocT Recall25: COPD with pH 6.9 and PaCO2 110 is life-threatening: immediate intubation is the keyed answer (pH <7.1 is outside the safe NIV range). The NIV rule still holds for less severe acidosis: pH 7.25–7.35 = NIV; below 7.25 NIV only with intubation immediately at hand.
cross: DocT keys intubation for AECOPD with pH 7.28, RR 30, anxious but awake. Truth: GOLD 2025 / ERS-ATS 2017 — NIV first for pH ≤7.35 with PaCO2 >45; intubate for NIV failure or intolerance, arrest, falling consciousness, uncleared secretions, shock, or pH <7.25 DESPITE NIV. If NIV is offered and none of those apply, pick NIV.

lines: DocT: A normal pH and baseline PaCO2 on the ventilator only make the COPD patient ready to TEST: run an SBT (PS 5–8, CPAP or T-piece, 30–120 min) and extubate to NIV only after a pass. Extubating straight to NIV (B) skips the SBT; continuing full ventilation (C) prolongs it.
Marrow: Ventilated COPD: in-hospital mortality ~10–30% and 1-year mortality ~40–60%; poor-prognosis markers are hypercapnia, low BMI, low albumin, older age and chronic steroid use.

DocT GT: On CXR the most specific sign of pneumomediastinum is the continuous diaphragm sign (air under the heart joining both hemidiaphragms); also ring-around-the-artery and the Naclerio V sign. A supine pneumothorax gives the deep sulcus sign instead; in ventilated patients pneumomediastinum often precedes pneumothorax (Macklin effect).

DocT GT: Catamenial pneumothorax = recurrent, usually RIGHT-sided pneumothorax within 72 h of menses from thoracic endometriosis (diaphragmatic defects/implants); high recurrence, so VATS repair of the diaphragm with pleurodesis plus hormonal suppression (GnRH analogue).

Marrow: Subclavian cannulation carries a higher pneumothorax risk than internal jugular; desaturation or air aspiration during attempts → abort and get a chest X-ray before trying the other side (bilateral pneumothorax risk).

Marrow: Needle decompression is only temporising; definitive treatment is a chest drain in the 5th intercostal space, mid-axillary line, just above the rib (triangle of safety). Surgical emphysema with respiratory distress = pneumothorax until proven otherwise.
cross: Marrow keys immediate decompression for a pneumothorax with stable vitals. Truth: stable vitals mean simple pneumothorax — chest X-ray, then a drain; decompression without imaging is only for tension (hypotension, hypoxia, shift). If stable, pick imaging then drain; if unstable, decompress at 4th–5th ICS MAL.

lines: DocT: Weeks of breathlessness with hypoxaemia (PaO2 ~63 mmHg), LOW PaCO2 and a CLEAR chest on auscultation = pulmonary embolism (recurrent/chronic); dead space and V/Q mismatch drive hyperventilation. Fibrosing alveolitis gives velcro crackles and clubbing; atypical pneumonia gives fever and crackles.

DocT GT: Westermark sign = focal oligaemia distal to a pulmonary embolus (specific, not sensitive); other PE film signs: Hampton hump (pleural-based wedge infarct) and Fleischner/Palla sign (enlarged central PA). Generalised oligaemia suggests PAH or pulmonary stenosis; unilateral hyperlucency with emphysema suggests Macleod syndrome.

DocT GT: After VTE in pregnancy continue anticoagulation for at least 6 weeks postpartum and ≥3 months in total. Warfarin (INR 2–3, overlapped with heparin) and LMWH are both safe in breastfeeding, so switching to warfarin postpartum is standard; DOACs are avoided while breastfeeding and aspirin alone is not treatment.

DocT + Marrow: CTEPH (PH group 4) follows incomplete resolution of emboli — classically multiple small, recurrent, often silent emboli that remodel the arteries — not one massive saddle embolus, air or fat. Suspect it when dyspnoea persists >3 months after PE; V/Q scan is the screening test (a normal scan excludes it).

Marrow: CTEPH treatment = lifelong anticoagulation + pulmonary endarterectomy if operable (potentially curative); inoperable or distal disease → balloon pulmonary angioplasty and riociguat, transplant as the last option.
Marrow: Criteria for ICU/ventilation in neuromuscular weakness: majors = PaCO2 >48, PaO2 <56 on air, VC <15 mL/kg, NIF weaker than −30 cmH2O; intubate with 1 major or 2 minor criteria.

DocT: Vital capacity = TV + IRV + ERV (maximal exhalation after maximal inspiration, normal ~60–70 mL/kg), which is why <20 mL/kg signals failure. RV, FRC and TLC cannot be measured by spirometry (need helium dilution or plethysmography).

DocT: The curve shifts RIGHT (lower affinity, more unloading, P50 >27 mmHg) with high PCO2, acidosis (Bohr), high 2,3-DPG and fever - the conditions of working tissue. It shifts LEFT with alkalosis, low PCO2, hypothermia, low 2,3-DPG (stored blood, hypophosphataemia), HbF, carbon monoxide and methaemoglobin.

Marrow: BTS life-threatening asthma also includes PaO2 <8 kPa, cyanosis, silent chest, poor respiratory effort, exhaustion, altered consciousness, arrhythmia and hypotension (besides PEF <33%, SpO2 <92%, normal PaCO2); a RAISED PaCO2 or need for ventilation = near-fatal.

DocT GT: In acute asthma a 'normal' PaCO2 (≥40, or ~35 in pregnancy where normal is 28–32) with exhaustion, altered sensorium or PaO2 <60 signals impending arrest → intubate (ketamine RSI, most experienced operator, left uterine displacement if pregnant). Magnesium and adrenaline are adjuncts, not substitutes.

DocT: On a lab flow–volume loop, obstruction (asthma, COPD, chronic bronchitis) shifts the loop LEFT to high volumes with a scooped expiratory limb and FEV1/FVC <0.7 (flow-limited); restriction (fibrosis, sarcoidosis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis) gives a narrow tall 'witch's hat' shifted RIGHT with normal or high FEV1/FVC (volume-limited).

cross: DocT keys PRVC as 'pressure-support breaths with a volume target'. Truth: PRVC breaths are time-cycled PRESSURE-CONTROL breaths whose pressure is adjusted breath by breath to deliver the set VT; the flow-cycled volume-targeted pressure-support version is Volume Support. If an option says 'fixed target VT with breath-by-breath pressure adjustment', pick it.

lines: DocT + DocT GT: HFOV holds a constant HIGH mean airway pressure (CPAP-like, for oxygenation) and superimposes oscillations at 3–15 Hz (180–900/min) with ACTIVE expiration, VT 1–3 mL/kg — below dead space — keeping the lung open without cyclic stretch. CO2 clears with amplitude (ΔP) and, paradoxically, LOWER frequency; 'low inspiratory pressures' (A) is wrong.

DocT + DocT GT: High-frequency JET ventilation pulses small jets (VT ~2–5 mL/kg) at 100–200/min with PASSIVE expiration; its real niche is a large bronchopleural fistula and airway surgery, where small volumes cut leak flow. 'Minimises VILI in ARDS' is the theory DocT keys, not a proven benefit.

Marrow + DocT + DocT GT: HFOV moves gas by five mechanisms: bulk convection (proximal units), pendelluft (between units with different time constants), Taylor (augmented) dispersion, asymmetric coaxial flow (central inflow, peripheral outflow) and molecular diffusion (alveoli). Neither HFOV nor HFJV improves adult ARDS survival.

DocT GT: Oxygen-induced hypercapnia in COPD is mainly worse V/Q matching: high FiO2 releases hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, reperfusing poorly ventilated units and raising dead space. The Haldane effect adds ~20–25%, loss of hypoxic drive the least, and CO2 production does not change; hence controlled O2 to SpO2 88–92% via Venturi.

DocT GT: Interface in acute NIV: start with an oronasal (full-face) mask, because mouth-breathing makes a nasal mask leak and lose pressure and CO2 clearance. A mouth leak on a nasal mask → switch to full-face; over-tightening only causes nasal-bridge ulcers. Total-face mask or helmet for intolerance or skin breakdown.
cross: DocT GT (GT8 Q2, CGT1 Q54) keys the Haldane effect as the cause of the PaCO2 rise after O2 in COPD. Truth: physiological studies (Aubier, Robinson) attribute most of it to worsened V/Q and dead space; Haldane is a contributor. If V/Q mismatch/dead space is offered, it is the better answer; for DocT papers pick Haldane.

lines: DocT GT: For a hypoxaemic, mildly confused patient who keeps pulling off a face mask (e.g. multiple rib fractures), heated humidified HFNC is the next step: better tolerated than mask CPAP/NIV, reliable FiO2 up to 1.0 at 40–60 L/min, small PEEP and dead-space washout. A non-rebreather is no better tolerated and gives an unreliable FiO2.

DocT GT: HFNC (up to 60 L/min) matches the patient's peak inspiratory flow, so FiO2 stays stable; it washes out nasopharyngeal dead space and adds ~1 cmH2O PEEP per 10 L/min with the mouth closed. Respiratory rate and work of breathing fall, but tidal volume is unchanged or rises, so 'reduces tidal volume' is false.
cross: DocT keys 'positive pressure to maintain airway patency' as HFNC's main mechanism. Truth: dead-space washout, a reliable FiO2 and lower work of breathing come first; PEEP is only ~1 cmH2O per 10 L/min, and only with the mouth closed. If dead-space washout is offered, pick it.

lines: DocT GT: In emphysema lost elastic recoil lets small airways collapse in expiration. Pursed-lip breathing adds back-pressure at the mouth, moving the equal-pressure point toward cartilage-supported airways so small airways stay splinted open; on the ventilator the equivalent is expiratory retard or extrinsic PEEP (to ~80% of auto-PEEP).

DocT GT: Spontaneous breathing gives a sinusoidal (sine-wave) inspiratory flow, rising to a mid-inspiratory peak and falling smoothly. Ventilator patterns differ: square (constant flow, volume control) and decelerating ramp (pressure control and pressure support).

DocT GT: Inverse-ratio ventilation (I:E ≥1:1, of which APRV is the extreme form) raises mean airway pressure and oxygenation without raising plateau pressure; it is a rescue step (watch auto-PEEP and haemodynamics). Raising VT, dropping PEEP or chasing normocapnia worsen VILI; prone positioning (P/F <150) is the evidence-based escalation.

Marrow: Fix a long time constant (gas trapping) by raising inspiratory flow (square wave) to shorten Ti and lengthen Te, and lowering rate or VT; a longer Ti or more applied PEEP (in a passive patient) worsens trapping.

DocT GT: In pressure control the airway pressure is fixed, so peak = set pressure and peak − plateau cannot give resistance (D wrong). Compliance = VT ÷ (Pinsp − PEEP) is valid only while the patient is passive; once he breathes, his muscle pressure adds to the ventilator's, so oesophageal (pleural) pressure is needed for true lung compliance.

DocT + DocT GT: Inverse-ratio ventilation (I:E >1:1) raises mean airway pressure without raising VT or Pplat — DocT's key when prone is not offered — but it has no mortality benefit and brings auto-PEEP, hypotension and deep sedation; at P/F <150 the evidence-based step is prone ≥16 h/day (PROSEVA 32.8% → 16.0%). pH 7.22 at Pplat 30 is acceptable permissive hypercapnia; don't chase PaCO2 <40 (C).
cross: Marrow keys 'increase RR' to correct ventilation in a COPD patient with pH 7.30 and PaCO2 48. Truth: RR and VT set ventilation, but in COPD a faster rate shortens expiratory time and builds auto-PEEP, and PaCO2 48 at pH 7.30 implies a metabolic component. If auto-PEEP or airflow limitation is described, pick prolonging expiration over raising RR; otherwise RR is the keyed answer.

Recall25 keys 'decreases mean airway pressure' as the effect of inverse-ratio ventilation. Truth: IRV RAISES mean airway pressure (DocT's own explanation says so), a letter error. Pick 'increases mean airway pressure'.

lines: DocT: Ineffective efforts in COPD come from auto-PEEP: the patient must first generate a pressure equal to PEEPi before any trigger can sense the effort, so switching from pressure to flow triggering gains only ~1 cmH2O. A higher inspiratory flow (80 L/min) shortens Ti and lengthens expiration, attacking PEEPi directly; PEEP 0 makes triggering worse.
Marrow: On NIV, auto-PEEP cannot practically be measured during active breathing, so add external PEEP (EPAP) empirically, titrating up until ineffective efforts disappear.
cross: DocT keys 'switch to flow triggering' for ineffective efforts in COPD. Truth: the threshold load is PEEPi; reduce it (higher inspiratory flow, shorter Ti, less support) or offset it with external PEEP. If a higher inspiratory flow or external PEEP is offered, pick it.

lines: DocT GT: Proportional modes (PAV, NAVA) scale support to the patient's own effort, so the diaphragm keeps working and the over-assist disuse atrophy of fixed pressure support (ventilator-induced diaphragm dysfunction from ~48 h) is avoided. They guarantee neither VT nor rate and do not replace the SBT.

DocT GT: Do not replace or guidewire-exchange CVCs at fixed intervals to prevent CLABSI: infection does not fall and mechanical complications rise. Replace a line only for a clinical indication and remove it as soon as it is not needed (the bundle's daily review).

cross: DocT and Marrow key central venous access/CVP before starting vasopressors (EGDT logic). Truth: SSC 2021/2026 start norepinephrine peripherally without waiting for a central line, guide fluids with dynamic tests (PLR, capillary refill, lactate) and place an arterial line as soon as practical. If peripheral norepinephrine or an arterial line is offered, pick it.

lines: DocT: A balloon left inflated (or a tip migrated into permanent wedge) occludes the PA branch → infarction, and is the main route to PA rupture, heralded by haemoptysis. Inflate (≤1.5 mL) only to advance or briefly wedge, then deflate; never withdraw or flush with the balloon up. Knotting (A) comes from over-advancing.

Marrow: PE with a filter already in place → image the filter (Doppler US/CT) for filter thrombus or IVC occlusion and continue anticoagulation if possible; a retrievable filter with thrombus may need thrombectomy before removal.

DocT: Match the probe to depth and window: pleural fluid/consolidation, abdomen and FAST → curvilinear 2–5 MHz (deep, wide field); pleural line and sliding, vessels, ONSD and the cricothyroid membrane → linear 5–15 MHz (sharp but ≤6 cm deep). The phased array fits between ribs for the heart but has a narrow near field — second choice for pleural fluid.

DocT GT: A lung pulse (heartbeat transmitted through apposed but unventilated pleura) with absent sliding means the lung is not ventilated but the pleurae touch — it excludes pneumothorax just as B-lines do. Right after intubation this is right-mainstem intubation → withdraw the tube; only a lung point confirms pneumothorax.

DocT: The sinusoid sign (M-mode: the lung line swings toward the pleural line on inspiration) proves FREE-FLOWING, low-viscosity fluid — but not a transudate; septated or viscous collections (empyema, organised haemothorax) damp the swing.

DocT GT: Lung ultrasound separates ARDS from cardiogenic oedema: ARDS gives non-homogeneous B-lines with spared areas, an irregular thickened pleural line, small subpleural consolidations and reduced sliding; cardiogenic oedema gives homogeneous bilateral B-lines from the bases with a smooth pleural line and often effusions.

Marrow (×2): A tip in the SVC or at the cavo-atrial junction is usable, even if 3 cm above it; never re-advance an exposed catheter (even sterile-looking) — rewire or replace; CXR after IJ/SCV for tip and pneumothorax. Femoral access: reverse Trendelenburg (± hip abduction/external rotation) distends the femoral vein, Trendelenburg distends IJ/subclavian.

DocT: Lung ultrasound adds a third PE window — small pleural-based wedge-shaped hypoechoic consolidations (infarcts); with RV overload and a non-compressible vein, multiorgan POCUS is far more specific than any single window. A negative leg scan does not exclude PE.

DocT Recall25: Acute PE strains the RIGHT heart (RV dilatation, McConnell sign, Westermark oligaemia on CXR). Left atrial enlargement is a chronic left-sided finding (mitral disease, LV dysfunction) and is the one feature NOT expected in acute PE.

DocT: Ultrasound confirms tube position too: linear probe transverse at the suprasternal notch shows one air–mucosa line (tracheal); a second air line beside it ('double tract') = oesophageal. Then bilateral lung sliding = both lungs ventilated, one-sided = mainstem; useful in arrest when ETCO2 is low.

DocT: Palpation often misidentifies the cricothyroid membrane in obese or female necks. Mark it with ultrasound BEFORE induction in a predicted difficult airway: linear probe longitudinal in the midline, trace the tracheal rings ('string of pearls') up to the cricoid; the membrane lies just above.

DocT GT: Partial glottic view (Cormack–Lehane 2b/3) on direct or video laryngoscopy → gum-elastic bougie first: it passes under the epiglottis by feel (tracheal clicks, hold-up at the carina) and the tube is railroaded over it. BOUGIE trial (Driver 2018, ED patients with a difficult-airway feature): first-pass success 96% vs 82% with a stylet.

DocT GT: PLAX is the best transthoracic view of the aortic root and proximal ascending aorta (dilatation, intimal flap, AR, pericardial effusion) and shows the descending thoracic aorta in cross-section behind the LA; TTE can still miss a dissection, so CT aortogram or TEE confirms.

DocT: RVSP = 4 × (peak TR velocity)² + RAP: 4 × 3.5² = 49, + 10 = 59 ≈ 60 mmHg. 49 (the commonest wrong pick) is only the RV–RA gradient with RAP forgotten; TR velocity >2.8 m/s suggests pulmonary hypertension.

DocT: In MDMA toxicity hyperthermia is the killer: above 40-41 C it drives rhabdomyolysis, DIC and multi-organ failure, and mortality climbs with peak temperature. Cool first (ice-water immersion, benzodiazepines, paralysis and intubation above 41 C) before treating the blood pressure.

DocT GT: MDMA hyponatraemia is SIADH-type (drug-driven ADH release) plus heavy water drinking - euvolaemic, urine osmolality >100, urine Na >30. Mild symptoms get fluid restriction; seizures or coma get 3% saline 100-150 mL boluses. Demeclocycline is too slow and nephrotoxic.
