Standard SDD (colistin/tobramycin/amphotericin) does not lower MRSA colonisation and may raise it; colistin resistance has been rare in SDD trials.

DocT GT: In active bleeding after cardiac surgery, platelet FUNCTION is tested with viscoelastic assays (TEG MA or ROTEM EXTEM MCF against FIBTEM, platelet mapping if available) - point-of-care, fast, and they separate platelets from fibrinogen from residual heparin. PT, aPTT and thrombin time do not measure platelets, and PFA-100 is unreliable when the haematocrit is <30% or platelets <100.

DocT GT: Portal venous gas with pneumatosis in acute mesenteric ischaemia means transmural infarction (mortality ~75–85%) and is a near-universal indication for urgent laparotomy. It is not specific for venous thrombosis and never means early, reversible ischaemia.

DocT GT: ASV's practical advantage in stable post-operative recovery is automation: it adjusts rate and pressure breath by breath, so it needs fewer clinician changes, alarms and ABGs, and weans automatically as effort returns (passive → P-SIMV → pressure support). It does not fix I:E or force high tidal volumes.

Marrow: ASV self-adjusts for dead space and auto-PEEP (via the expiratory time constant), but in low-FRC/obese patients its small-VT, low-pressure choices can cause derecruitment — set adequate PEEP and check %MinVol.

DocT GT: In ASV the clinician never sets tidal volume. The pressure limit (Pmax, default ~30 cmH2O; ASV works 10 cmH2O below it) is the one safety cap that stops it delivering large VT and causing VILI; %MinVol sets total ventilation, FiO2 oxygenation, and the I:E is chosen from the time constant.

cross: DocT GT keys 'target MAP >75 only if there is ongoing hypoperfusion' for an 80-year-old hypertensive at MAP 65. Truth: SSC 2026 gives 65 (strong) and 60–65 for age ≥65; SEPSISPAM's 80–85 in chronic hypertension cut RRT but not mortality and caused more AF. If 'maintain 65' is offered for an elderly patient, it is the guideline answer; DocT keys the individualised higher target.

lines: DocT GT: Parenteral-nutrition-associated cholestasis: rising conjugated bilirubin after ~1–2 weeks of TPN with near-normal transaminases, no obstruction, no haemolysis; causes are absent enteral stimulation, overfeeding/excess dextrose, soybean lipid >1 g/kg/day (phytosterols) and sepsis. Fix: any enteral feed, cut calories and lipid, consider fish-oil/mixed lipid emulsions.

DocT GT: Accidental/clinical hypothermia grades differ from the surgical DHCA consensus: mild 32–35 °C, moderate 28–32 °C, severe <28 °C (some add profound <24 °C). So 30 °C in the ICU is MODERATE, though on the cardiac-surgery scale it would be 'mild' (28.1–34 °C).

DocT GT: CI-AKI is a diagnosis of exclusion - AKI within 48-72 h of contrast with no other cause. Supporting features: high contrast dose, intra-arterial first-pass renal exposure, pre-existing CKD (eGFR <30), diabetes. Against it: an alternative insult such as septic shock (which makes it CA-AKI) or RBC casts pointing to glomerulonephritis or vasculitis.

DocT GT: CI-AKI runs a set course: creatinine starts rising within 24-48 h, peaks on day 2-3 and usually returns to baseline within 1-2 weeks; a rise that keeps going beyond that suggests another cause such as cholesterol atheroembolism.
Marrow: Smoke-inhalation timeline: immediate upper-airway (laryngeal) oedema → at 4–5 days pneumonia and ARDS → late subglottic stenosis, bronchiectasis and bronchiolitis obliterans.
Marrow: In trauma, an APACHE II ≥16 carries ~2.5× the ARDS risk; the commonest surgical causes are lung contusion, multiple long-bone fractures (fat embolism) and chest-wall trauma.

DocT GT + Marrow: Pulmonary hypertension is now mPAP >20 mmHg at right heart catheter (ESC 2022; this card's >25 is the old cut-off); PAWP ≤15 = pre-capillary and excludes left heart disease (Group 2), PVR >2 WU. Exertional dyspnoea, right heart failure and a loud P2 in a young woman with Raynaud's = Group 1 PAH from connective-tissue disease (systemic sclerosis).

DocT GT: The commonest symptom of pulmonary hypertension is exertional dyspnoea (the RV cannot raise output); then fatigue, exertional angina (RV ischaemia), exertional syncope or near-syncope (fixed output) and late peripheral oedema.
cross: DocT GT keys 'mPAP >25 mmHg' as the true RHC statement for PAH. Truth: ESC/ERS 2022 uses mPAP >20 with PAWP ≤15 and PVR >2 WU. If >20 is offered, pick it; if only >25 appears with PAWP ≤15, pick that.

fix.t: Pulmonary hypertension: mPAP >20 mmHg at rest (PAH: + PAWP ≤15, PVR >2 WU)
fix.why: Defines pulmonary hypertension as mPAP >25. ESC 2022 uses >20.

lines: DocT GT: IABP practicalities: 7–8 Fr femoral sheath (13–14 Fr is Impella/ECMO territory), femoral artery ≥4 mm to avoid limb ischaemia, balloon sized to height, regular rhythm for ECG triggering; support is days, beyond ~1–2 weeks limb ischaemia, infection and thrombocytopenia rise. Absolute contraindications: moderate–severe aortic regurgitation (diastolic inflation drives more regurgitation), aortic dissection, severe aorto-iliac disease.

DocT GT: Blood in the IABP gas line = balloon rupture: stop pumping, clamp the line and remove the IABP at once (helium embolism; clot inside can trap the balloon); never reinsert the same balloon. Tip ~2 cm below the top of the aortic arch, above the renal arteries.

Marrow + DocT GT: Timing: inflate at aortic-valve closure (dicrotic notch) and deflate just before systole. Early inflation inflates against LV ejection (raises afterload and LV work); late inflation loses augmentation; late deflation is the most harmful (balloon still up as the LV ejects). A stationary balloon is thrombogenic, so anticoagulate and never leave it switched off in situ.

DocT GT: A low vancomycin level on CRRT or with augmented renal clearance is a dosing problem: fix it with TDM, AUC-guided dosing (AUC/MIC 400–600, Bayesian software, trough-based if unavailable) after a 25–30 mg/kg load, adjusted for effluent rate.

DocT: Each control variable has its own failure: volume control fixes VT, so falling compliance raises plateau pressure (barotrauma risk); pressure control fixes pressure, so VT swings with compliance and can surge as lungs open up (volutrauma) or collapse as they stiffen (hypoventilation).

DocT GT: In pressure control, delivered VT depends on set pressure, inspiratory time, compliance and airway resistance. A bronchodilator lowers resistance, so more volume enters within the same Ti; a rising VT at unchanged settings means falling resistance (or rising compliance).
cross: DocT keys 'volutrauma from large tidal volumes' as the drawback of volume control. Truth: a large VT is a setting error; the mode-specific drawback of VC is rising Pplat when compliance falls, and of PC is variable VT. If an option says 'airway pressure rises as compliance falls', pick it for VC.

DocT says the ABG (FiO2 0.75, pH 7.295, PaCO2 63, PaO2 58, HCO3 29.8) 'does not match' a respiratory acidosis. Truth: P/F = 58/0.75 = 77 → severe ARDS (key C right), and the gas is ALSO a partly compensated respiratory acidosis. Always compute P/F from the FiO2 shown; if asked for severity, pick severe.

DocT GT keys 'proning improves oxygenation by redistributing ventilation and perfusion', but 'unstable spinal fracture is an absolute contraindication' is also true, so two options are correct. Pick the mechanism statement as keyed.

lines: Marrow: Most patients become symptomatic within 24 h of the insult (hypoxaemia by ~6 h, chest X-ray changes at 12–48 h); the Berlin 1-week window is generous, not typical.

DocT GT: RV dysfunction from ARDS (acute cor pulmonale, D-shaped LV) does not automatically need VA-ECMO. VV-ECMO corrects hypoxaemia and hypercapnic acidosis, relieving hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction and allowing lower plateau pressure and PEEP, so RV afterload falls; VA (or VAV/RVAD) is for persistent cardiogenic shock despite this.

DocT GT: As a bridge to lung transplant, awake (non-intubated) ECMO is preferred to intubation: it allows physiotherapy and ambulation and avoids VAP, barotrauma and deconditioning that worsen transplant outcome. VV for pure hypoxaemia; VA (or PA-LA/oxy-RVAD) when pulmonary hypertension has caused RV failure.

Marrow: The original GOS has 5 points: 5 good recovery, 4 moderate disability, 3 severe disability, 2 persistent vegetative state, 1 dead (higher = better). GOS-E splits each survivor category into upper/lower to give 8.

Marrow: RA collapse is the earliest and most sensitive echo sign of tamponade; LA collapse is late (and can occur with a loculated posterior effusion); electrical alternans means a large effusion with the heart swinging.

Marrow: Mini fluid challenge read by pulse contour: a cardiac-output rise ≥5% after 100 mL predicts responsiveness (vs VTI >10% by echo); don't confuse with the PLR threshold (≥10% CO rise) or PPV/SVV ≥12–15%.

cross: Marrow keys a Group A index (PPV/SVV) as the dynamic index, but IVC distensibility (option A) is also dynamic (Group B). Truth: both are dynamic; only Group A tracks stroke volume. If asked for a stroke-volume-based dynamic index, pick PPV/SVV; if asked 'dynamic vs static', IVC variation counts too.

lines: Marrow: Weil's 2–5 rule for a fluid challenge by CVP: rise <2 mmHg → continue; 2–5 → pause and recheck at 10 min; >5 → stop. (Historical — CVP should not guide fluids today.)

Marrow: Hydroxyethyl starch harms: AKI and more RRT, coagulopathy (vWF/factor VIII), tissue deposition with pruritus, and anaphylactoid reactions — hence strong against; interference with cross-matching is a DEXTRAN effect.

Marrow: Excess chloride from saline in any concentration (including 7.5% hypertonic) causes hyperchloraemic normal-anion-gap acidosis and renal vasoconstriction — the reason balanced crystalloids are preferred.
Marrow: Split the top row: CURB-65 of 3 = severe, admit and consider ICU; 4–5 = ICU. The QBank keys ICU only at >3, so a score of exactly 3 is 'consider ICU', not automatic ICU.
Marrow: Remdesivir needs no renal dose change: FDA (July 2023) removed the eGFR <30 restriction, dialysis included. Check LFTs and stop if ALT rises >10× normal.
cross: Marrow QB04-Q02 key: avoid remdesivir at eGFR <30. Truth: that was the old label; since July 2023 it is given at any eGFR without adjustment. If the question follows current guidance, pick 'no dose change'; the bank's older answer is 'avoid'.

lines: Marrow: Pneumomediastinum or pneumopericardium without haemodynamic compromise → observe with serial chest X-rays and lung-protective settings; no needle decompression or pericardiocentesis.

Marrow: Suspected double-lumen tube malposition → confirm and correct with bedside fibreoptic bronchoscopy before anything else, never transport first; a LEFT-sided DLT is preferred because the left main bronchus is longer, giving a wider safety margin (the right upper-lobe orifice is easily occluded).

Marrow + DocT GT: Open suctioning disconnects the circuit and loses PEEP, causing derecruitment and desaturation in ARDS: use a closed (in-line) system when PEEP >10 cmH2O or FiO2 >0.6 (it preserves PEEP and oxygenation but does not lower VAP), pre-oxygenate with FiO2 1.0, and exclude pneumothorax before any recruitment manoeuvre.

DocT GT: In the decremental PEEP trial after recruitment, PEEP is stepped down ~2 cmH2O at a time while static compliance is tracked; the step where compliance suddenly falls is the derecruitment (closing) point, seen before oxygenation worsens. Re-recruit and set PEEP ~2 cmH2O above it.

cross: Marrow keys PAOP ≤18 mmHg as an ARDS criterion (AECC 1994). Truth: Berlin 2012 removed the wedge criterion — a raised PAOP can coexist with ARDS. If the stem names AECC, pick PAOP ≤18; if Berlin or no definition is named, wedge is not a criterion.

lines: Marrow: In a chronic CO2 retainer, ventilate to the patient's BASELINE PaCO2 (pH-guided), not to normocapnia or a pH of 7.35–7.45 — over-ventilation dumps bicarbonate and the patient fails weaning when his own drive resumes.
Marrow: Move from controlled to assisted modes (e.g. PSV) only with haemodynamic stability, adequate respiratory drive and no major acidaemia; at pH ~7.15 stay on controlled ventilation.

Marrow: Rheumatoid effusion: very low glucose (<30 mg/dL), high LDH (>1000), pH <7.2, low complement, and sometimes cholesterol crystals (pseudochylothorax) — it mimics empyema biochemically, so look for RA history and nodules.

Marrow: An exudate with glucose >60 mg/dL argues against complicated parapneumonic effusion, rheumatoid, malignant and TB effusions; in a patient without pneumonia features, think pulmonary embolism and get a CTPA.
Marrow: TB effusion: lymphocytic exudate, ADA >40 U/L, few mesothelial cells (<5%); fluid AFB culture yields <30%, so pleural biopsy (histology + culture) is the most sensitive confirmation.
cross: Marrow keys rheumatoid effusion for a patient with fever and productive cough. Truth: RA effusion classically has glucose <30 and pH <7.2, but fever with productive cough fits complicated parapneumonic effusion. If the stem gives RA history/nodules without infective features, pick rheumatoid; with infection, pick parapneumonic.

Marrow keys PE for an exudate with glucose >60. Truth: an uncomplicated parapneumonic effusion also has glucose >60. If there are no pneumonia features and VTE risk is present, pick PE; with pneumonia, pick uncomplicated parapneumonic.

lines: Marrow: Bacteria are found in the lower airways in ≥50% of COPD exacerbations (GOLD), but chronic colonisation makes a positive sputum culture hard to interpret.
Marrow: Altered mental status is THE single most important severity sign in AECOPD — prepare to intubate; sputum colour signals bacterial infection, not severity.

Marrow: Peak pressure up with plateau unchanged = rising resistance (plug, kinked tube, biting, bronchospasm) → suction and check the tube; peak AND plateau up = compliance problem (auto-PEEP, pneumothorax, atelectasis, oedema).
Marrow: Pulmonary artery pulsatility index PAPi = (PASP − PADP) / RAP; <0.9 in acute inferior MI predicts RV failure and in-hospital death (<1.85 is the post-LVAD cut-off).
Marrow: Right heart catheterisation is the gold standard to confirm pulmonary hypertension (mPAP, PAWP, PVR) before the aetiological work-up; echo only estimates probability.
Marrow: In inferior STEMI, ST elevation in III > II and ST elevation in V1 point to RV involvement (proximal RCA), alongside ST elevation ≥1 mm in V3R/V4R.

Marrow: Catheter-directed therapy complications: access-site bleeding (commonest), retroperitoneal or pulmonary haemorrhage, PA perforation, tamponade, arrhythmia and contrast nephropathy; overall major bleeding and ICH are lower than with systemic lysis.

Marrow: A PE response team (intensivist, cardiology, radiology, cardiac surgery) speeds reperfusion decisions in high- and intermediate-high-risk PE; for high-risk PE systemic lysis stays first-line, with catheter or surgical options when lysis fails or is contraindicated.
cross: Marrow's key for the commonest CDT complication does not match the evidence. Truth: access-site/minor bleeding is commonest and ICH is rare. If access-site bleeding is offered, pick it.

Marrow keys a PE response team (PERT) as what 'could have prevented' arrest in high-risk PE on heparin, and its explanation calls the PE submassive and favours catheter therapy. Truth: ESC 2019 — high-risk (hypotensive) PE gets systemic thrombolysis first. If systemic lysis is offered, pick it; PERT is a process answer.

lines: Marrow: If an empyema fails to resolve after a drain and intrapleural tPA/DNase, VATS decortication beats open thoracotomy or prolonged tube drainage for morbidity and length of stay.

Marrow: Agitated or delirious at the sedation hold → restart home antipsychotics and switch to dexmedetomidine, which causes no respiratory depression and allows extubation while still on the infusion.

Marrow: Midazolam's active metabolite (α-hydroxymidazolam glucuronide) accumulates in renal failure and delays waking — a common cause of 'difficult' weaning; PADIS favours propofol or dexmedetomidine over benzodiazepines.
Marrow: Refer early to an ECMO centre once P/F stays <80 despite optimisation, while cardiac function is still preserved — extra fluid or inotropes will not fix ARDS hypoxaemia.

Marrow: Oxygenation index = FiO2 × mean airway pressure × 100 / PaO2 (it captures how much pressure buys the PaO2); OI >40 is a classical ECMO trigger. Inhaled NO adds nothing above 20 ppm and does not improve survival.

DocT GT: The Murray Lung Injury Score averages four components scored 0–4: CXR quadrants, P/F, PEEP and static compliance. >2.5 = severe lung injury; ≥3 (or uncompensated pH <7.20) was the CESAR referral threshold. It grades severity; it does not predict 90-day mortality and contains no SOFA items.
Marrow: Currant-jelly sputum with upper-lobe cavitation or a bulging fissure in an alcoholic or diabetic = Klebsiella pneumoniae (the card's 'alcoholism → GNB').

Marrow: Tularaemia (rabbit handling, mowing over carcasses) is treated with streptomycin or gentamicin (doxycycline or ciprofloxacin if mild). Diagnose by serology, because culture is a laboratory-acquired-infection hazard.

Marrow + DocT GT: Legionella = stagnant water (humidifiers, cooling towers, hot tubs, cruise ships) in an elderly or immunosuppressed patient with diarrhoea, confusion, hyponatraemia and raised LFTs. Urinary antigen detects only serogroup 1. Treat with levofloxacin 750 mg/day (preferred if severe or immunocompromised) or azithromycin for 7–14 days, about 21 days if immunosuppressed.

Marrow: Mycoplasma also causes mucositis-predominant SJS (MIRM) and cold-agglutinin (IgM anti-I) haemolysis. Treat with azithromycin for 5 days, or doxycycline or a respiratory fluoroquinolone for 7–14 days; β-lactams fail because it has no cell wall.

Marrow: HIV with CD4 >200 and lobar consolidation = bacterial (pneumococcal) pneumonia, the commonest HIV pneumonia at any CD4. PCP is unlikely above 200 and gives diffuse ground glass, not lobar consolidation.
Marrow: A patient too exhausted to speak with severe hypoxaemia needs the airway secured first; bronchoscopy/BAL, HIV testing and other diagnostics come after intubation, never before.

Marrow: Mycoplasma is diagnosed by PCR on a throat/nasopharyngeal or lower-respiratory sample; IgM serology is the slower, less specific alternative, and cold agglutinins are positive in only about half.

Marrow: Obesity hypoventilation syndrome = BMI ≥30 + awake daytime PaCO2 >45 mmHg with other causes excluded (hypoxaemia not required); screen with serum bicarbonate — a raised HCO3 (≥27) in an obese patient calls for a room-air ABG.

Marrow: CPAP lifts FRC back above closing capacity, re-opening dependent airways and reducing atelectasis and intrinsic PEEP (RV and TLC do not change); if hypoventilation persists, use BiPAP to add tidal volume.

DocT GT: Supine posture drops FRC below closing capacity (abdominal contents push the diaphragm up — worse with obesity), causing dependent atelectasis; sitting up 30–60° (or reverse Trendelenburg) raises FRC by up to ~30% and is the first non-invasive fix. A bigger VT does not restore FRC; prone is for ARDS.

Marrow: Obese patients desaturate fast at induction (low FRC, high O2 consumption): predict difficulty (3-3-2 rule, neck circumference, Mallampati), ramp them, call senior help before RSI and have a front-of-neck plan ready.

DocT Recall25: Persistent vomiting loses gastric HCl, giving metabolic alkalosis with HIGH pH, HIGH HCO3 and a compensatory HIGH PaCO2 (~0.7 mmHg per 1 mmol/L rise in HCO3), plus hypochloraemia and hypokalaemia; volume contraction and low chloride keep the kidney reabsorbing bicarbonate.
cross: Marrow's answer treats a PaCO2 of 30 as appropriate. Truth: with that bicarbonate Winter's predicts 26 plus or minus 2, so 30 is slightly high and indicates an added respiratory acidosis; the keyed option is the best of those offered rather than a correct statement. Always compute Winter's before accepting a compensation label.

lines: DocT GT: For impending herniation (new anisocoria, posturing) 23.4% saline 30 mL over 10–15 min via a central line gives the fastest, largest osmotic gradient: ICP falls within minutes and transtentorial herniation can reverse. Mannitol 0.25 g/kg is a low dose; acetazolamide and furosemide are slow and weak.

Marrow: Obstructive shock also includes tension pneumothorax and obstruction to forward flow — critical AS, dynamic LVOT obstruction (HCM), MS, LA myxoma; adrenal crisis is DISTRIBUTIVE (endocrine), and myocardial contusion is a contractility (cardiogenic) cause.

Marrow: Read sepsis markers for their confounders: the PCT trend tracks response to antibiotics; adrenaline raises lactate (β2-driven aerobic glycolysis, type B) without hypoperfusion; acidosis may be hyperchloraemic from saline; steroids raise the neutrophil count by demargination.

Marrow: Match monitor to principle: NIBP → oscillometry (Riva-Rocci cuff for the auscultatory method); invasive BP → Fourier analysis of the waveform; SpO2 → Beer–Lambert law (red/infrared absorption); EtCO2 → infrared absorption spectroscopy.

Marrow: Septal shift explains a high LA pressure with a LOW LV end-diastolic volume in pulmonary hypertension, high PEEP and severe acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure — the LV is compressed, not overfilled; aortic regurgitation, by contrast, raises LVEDV.

Marrow: Arterial compliance C = ΔV/ΔP, so stiffer arteries give a bigger pressure change for the same stroke volume (wider pulse pressure); the aortic Windkessel stores part of each stroke volume in systole and releases it in diastole, turning intermittent ejection into continuous flow.

Marrow: AMI cardiogenic-shock risk: older age, anterior MI, multivessel disease, prior MI, diabetes, prior HF (a first posterior infarct with shock → look for a mechanical complication or RV involvement). Lactate >2 mmol/L (the higher the worse) and admission glucose independently predict death; transaminases rise from hypoperfusion; cystatin C/NGAL add little over creatinine.
Marrow: Most early STEMI deaths (within 24 h, mostly in the first hour) are from VF — hence continuous monitoring and defibrillator-capable transport from first medical contact.

Marrow: IV β-blocker contraindications in ACS: signs of HF or low output, LVEF ≤40% with shock risk, PR >240 ms or 2nd/3rd-degree block, hypotension (SBP <120 with risk factors), active asthma/bronchospasm, and age >70 with tachycardia >110 (COMMIT: more cardiogenic shock).
Marrow: A troponin rise after acute stroke is usually myocardial injury (neurogenic catecholamine surge), not NSTEMI — no ACS antithrombotics, and after alteplase antiplatelets are held for 24 h.
cross: Marrow keys 21-day DAPT for a patient who woke with a stroke and received alteplase. Truth: 21-day DAPT is for minor stroke (NIHSS ≤3) or high-risk TIA without lysis; after alteplase no antiplatelet for 24 h, and wake-up stroke needs MRI mismatch before lysis. If the stroke is minor and not lysed, pick DAPT; after alteplase, pick 'no antiplatelet for 24 h'.

lines: Marrow: NSTEMI is a subendocardial (non-transmural) infarct; STEMI is transmural — the wavefront spreads from endocardium to epicardium, so ST elevation marks full-thickness injury.
cross: Marrow keys NSTEMI (subendocardial) for ST depression in V1–V3 with a troponin rise. Truth: ST depression confined to V1–V3 may be a posterior STEMI (transmural; check V7–V9 ≥0.5 mm). If the stem gives posterior leads or tall R in V1–V2, pick posterior STEMI; otherwise NSTEMI.

lines: Marrow: CHA2DS2-VASc: CHF 1, hypertension 1, age ≥75 = 2, diabetes 1, stroke/TIA/thromboembolism = 2, vascular disease 1, age 65–74 = 1, female sex 1. Anticoagulate at ≥2 in men or ≥3 in women (consider at 1/2); female sex alone adds risk only with another factor.

Marrow: Class Ib drugs (lidocaine, mexiletine) work only on ventricular arrhythmias — they bind Na channels in the long ventricular action potential, and the short atrial one gives them no time — and they SHORTEN the QT. ECG by class: Ia widens QRS and lengthens QT, Ib shortens QT, Ic lengthens PR and QRS, III lengthens QT.
Marrow: In Brugada the ICD is also indicated after arrhythmic syncope, not only after arrest; quinidine is used if an ICD is refused or for recurrent shocks/electrical storm (isoprenaline acutely).
Marrow: Polymorphic VT from a reversible cause (drug-induced long QT, electrolytes) is treated by removing the cause — no ICD; an ICD is for polymorphic VT/VF without a reversible cause.

cross: Marrow keys atropine 0.5 mg. Truth: 0.5 mg (max 3 mg) is the pre-2020 AHA dose; AHA 2020/2025 give 1 mg every 3–5 min, max 3 mg. If 1 mg is offered, pick it; pick 0.5 mg only when it is the only atropine option.

Recall25 keys dopamine when transcutaneous pacing fails in symptomatic bradycardia. Truth: AHA lists dopamine OR adrenaline infusion as equals (ERC prefers adrenaline/isoprenaline). Pick dopamine for this recall; pick adrenaline if dopamine is not offered.

lines: Marrow: Start adenosine at 3 mg (not 6) when given via a central line, after heart transplant (denervated, supersensitive) or with dipyridamole or carbamazepine (which potentiate it); theophylline and caffeine antagonise it, so larger doses may be needed.

Marrow: Takotsubo mimics STEMI (ST elevation + troponin) but the wall-motion abnormality extends beyond one coronary territory with unobstructed coronaries; contraction-band necrosis on histology, recovery within weeks. Variants: apical ballooning (typical), mid-ventricular, basal/reverse (basal akinesis with hyperkinetic apex — post-operative or catecholamine-driven), focal and RV; men are fewer but do worse.
Marrow: Apical HCM (Yamaguchi): giant precordial T-wave inversion (>10 mm) with a spade-shaped LV cavity on ventriculography or echo; lower sudden-death risk than septal HCM.

Marrow: ARVC = desmosomal gene mutation (commonly plakophilin-2) with fibrofatty replacement of the RV; Naxos disease = ARVC + woolly hair + palmoplantar keratoderma; Carvajal syndrome = the same skin/hair with a dilated LV.

Marrow: The ECG in myocarditis is INSENSITIVE and non-specific (sinus tachycardia, non-specific ST-T changes) — it screens but cannot exclude; troponin I is more specific than sensitive, so CMR or biopsy confirms.

Marrow: AHA/Fink indications for endomyocardial biopsy: refractory HF or worsening EF despite therapy, new heart block or VT, HF with rash/fever/eosinophilia, connective-tissue disease, suspected amyloid/sarcoid/haemochromatosis, and suspected giant-cell myocarditis.

DocT GT: Giant cell myocarditis (giant cells + extensive myocyte necrosis on biopsy) is the one myocarditis where combined immunosuppression (steroid + cyclosporine ± azathioprine) is life-saving; refractory VT and shock are typical, so plan early mechanical support or transplant. Lymphocytic viral myocarditis gets supportive care.
cross: Marrow treats persistent LV dysfunction after 3 months as NOT an EMB indication (Fink/AHA table). Truth: ESC (CVS-45) sends persistent LV dysfunction after 3 months to EMB. If the question follows AHA, exclude it; if ESC, it is an indication.

lines: Marrow: If neither IV nor IO is possible, endotracheal adrenaline needs 2–2.5× the IV dose (diluted in 5–10 mL); the intracardiac route is abandoned. 1 mg adrenaline = 10 mL of 1:10,000.

DocT GT: In haemorrhagic shock, if peripheral IV access fails after 2 attempts or 90 s, place an intraosseous needle (proximal humerus is fastest, or tibia): blood, drugs and pressure infusion within a minute. Central lines take longer and risk pneumothorax in a collapsed patient.

DocT GT: IO infusion is painful in a conscious patient (periosteal and marrow stretch): inject 40 mg preservative-free 2% lidocaine slowly into the marrow over 2 min, let it dwell ~1 min, flush 5–10 mL saline, then 20 mg more if needed. Contraindications: fracture or prior IO in that bone, site infection, osteogenesis imperfecta.

Marrow: Adult BLS order is C-A-B: compressions (30:2) start before airway opening and breaths, because in primary cardiac arrest the blood is still oxygenated and any delay to compressions cuts coronary perfusion.
Marrow: Traumatic arrest — resuscitative thoracotomy is for penetrating trauma with downtime <15 min (blunt <10 min); beyond ~20 min of CPR with no cardiac activity on echo, stop.
Marrow: Aortic dissection or rupture is the leading cause of death in Marfan syndrome; mitral valve prolapse is commoner but far less lethal.
Marrow: The IABP-SHOCK II risk score uses six variables: age >73, prior stroke, glucose >191 mg/dL, creatinine >1.5 mg/dL, TIMI flow <3 after PCI and lactate >5 mmol/L.

Marrow + DocT Recall25: Sympathetic crashing acute pulmonary oedema (SCAPE, hypertensive AHF, e.g. SBP 180): high-dose IV nitrates are first-line to unload the LV, with NIV; IV furosemide second; avoid nitrates if hypotensive. Morphine is no longer routine (more ventilation and mortality).
Marrow: Other chest X-ray signs of dissection: double or irregular aortic contour and inward displacement of intimal calcification >5 mm from the outer aortic wall (calcium sign).

Marrow: On an arterial line, tamponade's pulsus paradoxus shows as an inspiratory fall in systolic pressure (>10 mmHg) and pulse pressure while the diastolic barely changes — inspiration fills the RV, the septum shifts left and LV stroke volume falls.

Marrow: Retroperitoneal haematoma after PCI follows a femoral puncture ABOVE the inguinal ligament: back/flank pain and hypotension with little groin swelling — diagnose by non-contrast CT; radial access avoids it.

DocT GT: Hypotension hours after an uncomplicated RADIAL PCI with no new ECG change → urgent bedside echo for tamponade from coronary or wire perforation (or a new mechanical complication); retroperitoneal bleeding belongs to femoral access, stent thrombosis to new ST elevation.

Marrow: Blunt cardiac injury: screen every significant chest trauma with ECG and troponin; if either is abnormal, monitor for 24–48 h (arrhythmias) and get an echo if haemodynamically unstable; normal ECG + normal troponin excludes significant injury.

DocT GT: Cold, clammy, confused and oliguric 6–12 h after on-pump CABG = low cardiac output syndrome (the commonest early complication: stunning after bypass). Optimise preload and afterload, correct K/Mg/Ca, rate and rhythm (pacing), then inotropes (dobutamine/milrinone), IABP/MCS if refractory, and exclude tamponade and graft ischaemia; high-dose vasoconstrictors alone worsen output.

Marrow: AKI with myocardial depression in septic shock is cardiorenal syndrome type 5 (a systemic disease hitting heart and kidney together): treat the sepsis and perfusion, not the kidney in isolation. Fluid is 30 mL/kg in 3 h, not per hour.
Marrow: Ectopics as the guidewire is passed = wire tip in the right atrium/ventricle; withdraw it into the SVC (keep ECG monitoring during insertion).

Marrow (×2): Air in the syringe during subclavian access = lung apex puncture; dynamic ultrasound cuts complications. A CVC-related haemothorax needs drainage (standard = tube thoracostomy; Marrow keys CT-guided drainage); removing the line does not fix it.

Marrow + DocT GT: Venous air embolism on line removal (dyspnoea, desaturation, RV strain) → left lateral head-down (Durant) + 100% O2, aspirate through a catheter; prevent by removing supine/Trendelenburg with Valsalva. Arterial (paradoxical) air needs a right-to-left shunt (Eisenmenger, Fallot, PFO with high right pressure, or massive air); left-to-right PDA/ASD/VSD carry the lowest risk.
cross: Marrow keys CT-guided drainage for haemothorax 6 h after subclavian cannulation. Truth: tube thoracostomy is the standard first step. If tube thoracostomy is offered, pick it.

lines: DocT GT: Metronidazole is the anaerobic drug in brain abscess, especially for Bacteroides fragilis: bactericidal, excellent brain and pus penetration, resistance rare. Clindamycin penetrates the CNS poorly and B. fragilis resistance exceeds 20%; oral vancomycin is not absorbed.

Marrow: Penicillin (or doxycycline) for leptospirosis can trigger a Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction within hours (fever, rigors, hypotension from cytokine release as spirochaetes lyse); treat supportively and do not stop the antibiotic.

Marrow: Ixodes ticks carry Lyme (Borrelia), anaplasmosis and babesiosis in the same areas, so co-infection is common. New haemolysis or shock on doxycycline for anaplasmosis = blood smear for Babesia (doxycycline does not cover it) → atovaquone + azithromycin (IDSA 2020), with clindamycin + quinine as the alternative.
Marrow: Lyme carditis with high-grade AV block → admit, IV ceftriaxone and temporary pacing; the block usually resolves within 1–2 weeks, so a permanent pacemaker is rarely needed.
Marrow: Severe Indian tick typhus (R. conorii) is predicted by older age, alcoholism, diabetes, G6PD deficiency, immunosuppression and delayed or wrong (non-doxycycline) antibiotics.

fix.t: Q fever | C. burnetii | No vector — inhaled aerosol (birth products, dust) | Cattle, sheep, goats. Epidemic typhus | R. prowazekii | Louse | Humans. Watch: louse-borne diseases (epidemic typhus, trench fever — Bartonella quintana) have HUMAN reservoirs.
fix.why: Q fever is spread by inhaled aerosols from animals, not lice or mites; epidemic typhus also has a human reservoir.

lines: Marrow: A catheter-related thrombus can embolise and cause PE; massive (shocked) or peri-arrest PE needs systemic thrombolysis, because heparin alone only stops propagation and does not clear the clot.

Marrow + DocT GT: Burkholderia pair: glanders (B. mallei; horses, non-motile, lung abscesses) and melioidosis (B. pseudomallei; soil/water in SE Asia and northern Australia, rice farmers, diabetics, abscesses) are both treated with IV imipenem/meropenem or ceftazidime (+ doxycycline in glanders), then months of oral eradication therapy. A cruise-ship or hotel stay points to Legionella, not melioidosis.

Marrow: A recent course of one antipseudomonal class (e.g. cefepime) means switching to a different class (piperacillin-tazobactam or a carbapenem) for the next empirical choice; bronchiectasis always needs Pseudomonas cover.

DocT GT: The card's 'P. cepacia' is Burkholderia cepacia complex (CF, CGD, haemodialysis or contaminated solutions, prosthetic valves): intrinsically resistant to aminoglycosides and colistin, so treat with TMP-SMX, or meropenem, ceftazidime or minocycline, often combined for endovascular infection.

Marrow: Iron overload (haemochromatosis, transfusion dependence, deferoxamine) favours siderophilic organisms (Listeria, Yersinia, Vibrio vulnificus), so meningitis in these patients needs ampicillin added for Listeria.

DocT GT: Listeria rhombencephalitis: prodrome, then asymmetric cranial-nerve palsies, cerebellar signs and vomiting with brainstem lesions on MRI in an older or immunocompromised adult; CSF can be near-normal and blood cultures are often positive. Treat with high-dose ampicillin ± gentamicin (co-trimoxazole if allergic), since cephalosporins miss Listeria.
Marrow: No anti-Pseudomonal activity: ertapenem (unlike meropenem/imipenem), ceftriaxone/cefotaxime, ampicillin-sulbactam and tigecycline, so never choose them when Pseudomonas must be covered.

cross: Marrow QB30-Q09 key: metronidazole first-line. Truth: IDSA/SHEA 2021 first-line for an initial episode is fidaxomicin (preferred) or oral vancomycin; metronidazole only for non-severe disease when both are unavailable, and GDH alone never diagnoses CDI (needs toxin or PCR, CDI-18). If vancomycin or fidaxomicin is offered, pick it.

lines: Marrow: Sheehan's syndrome is an anterior pituitary loss, so it gives chronic central hypothyroidism, failed lactation and amenorrhoea; DI is rare because the posterior pituitary is spared. That is the discriminator from pituitary apoplexy with stalk involvement.

DocT GT: Diabetes mellitus, sickle cell disease and hypertension predispose to pituitary apoplexy (microvascular ischaemia or BP surges inside an adenoma) and belong beside the card's triggers; hyperthyroidism does not.

Marrow: For hypoglycaemia on an insulin infusion: stop the infusion, give IV dextrose (D50 25 g or D10), recheck every 15 min and flush the carrier line, which can hold residual insulin. Note the threshold difference - the QBank uses <70 mg/dL while this card uses <60 mg/dL.
cross: Crossfire · Marrow/ICU texts: ICU hypoglycaemia CBG <60 mg/dL; ADA Standards 2025 & SCCM 2024: level 1 <70, level 2 (clinically significant) <54, level 3 = severe with altered mentation. In exam: <70 if ADA framing/levels in options, else <60 (Marrow key). [Claim is wrong that GLY-01 says <70 — it also says <60.]

lines: Marrow: In an overloaded AKI patient use the IV not the oral loop diuretic (gut oedema blocks absorption), at least double the home dose, and expect a response within 2 h; no response means escalate to kidney replacement therapy rather than repeating the dose.

Marrow: Type 1 cardiorenal syndrome with venous congestion gets the loop diuretic first; ultrafiltration is only for diuretic resistance (CARRESS-HF showed worse renal outcomes with routine ultrafiltration).
cross: Marrow keys a loop diuretic for a congested cardiorenal patient whose BP is 82/64 with confusion. Truth: those numbers describe a low-output state, where an inotrope (and perfusion pressure) comes before diuresis. Pick the diuretic when perfusion is adequate; pick inotropic support when the BP and mentation say output is the problem.

lines: Marrow: Add obstruction to step 1: obstructive AKI with anuria or hyperkalaemia needs immediate decompression, and in an unstable patient bedside percutaneous nephrostomy under local anaesthesia is the fastest route, with CT afterwards.

Marrow: Add a non-renal START NOW threshold: a urea-cycle disorder or other hyperammonaemia with NH3 >500 micromol/L (or rising, or with encephalopathy) needs emergent haemodialysis, with arginine and sodium benzoate or phenylbutyrate alongside.

Marrow: Hold the mirror list of NON-dialysable drugs: calcium-channel blockers such as verapamil, beta-blockers other than atenolol and sotalol, tricyclics and digoxin - all with high protein binding or a large volume of distribution, which is why their overdoses are managed pharmacologically, not by dialysis.

Marrow: Add a fifth step to the ECG sequence: in severe hypokalaemia the fused T-U wave with a long QU interval can progress to torsades de pointes as well as VT or VF, which is why magnesium is replaced alongside potassium.

Marrow: Fix magnesium first (low Mg causes renal K wasting and makes hypokalaemia refractory); give IV K for arrhythmia, digoxin, ischaemia or paralysis, oral if stable; add a K-sparing diuretic for ongoing renal loss.
cross: CGT2 Q108 keys 'K 3.0 mEq/L in a 70 kg patient corresponds to a deficit of about 175 mEq' as true. Truth: a 1 mEq/L fall from 4 to 3 reflects ~200-400 mEq (DocT's own 10% of 3,500 gives 350), and the other options (IV rate, magnesium) are also false, so the key is only the least wrong. If every option has an error, pick the deficit statement; learn 200-400 mEq per 1 mEq/L.

Marrow keys oral KCl 40 mEq for K 2.7 with U waves and long QT on diuretics (explanation equivocal). Truth: ECG changes push toward IV replacement with monitoring. If the stem stresses arrhythmia or ECG change, pick IV; if stable, oral.

Marrow's explanation says magnesium causes SA and AV block yet denies bradycardia. Truth: at a magnesium of 16 mEq/L bradycardia and heart block are both expected, since magnesium is a calcium antagonist that slows conduction. Treat the explanation as self-contradictory and keep the card's level-by-level table.

lines: Marrow: Stopping PN abruptly → rebound hypoglycaemia (circulating insulin outlasts the dextrose); taper or run 10% dextrose and check glucose.
Marrow: New hyperglycaemia on previously stable PN heralds catheter-related sepsis; other PN complications are hepatic steatosis, cholestasis and gallbladder sludge.
cross: Marrow keys hyponatraemia as the PN metabolic complication. Truth: hyperglycaemia is the commonest TPN metabolic complication (plus refeeding hypophosphataemia/hypokalaemia). If hyperglycaemia is offered, pick it.

lines: Marrow: Transition off the DKA infusion by overlap: give the basal SC insulin 1-2 h BEFORE stopping the drip, with prandial rapid-acting insulin when eating, since the infusion's effect ends within minutes and ketosis can rebound. Diabetes-specific enteral formulas give no benefit.
cross: Marrow's option text for the transition omits the basal overlap. Truth: resolution criteria plus the ability to eat allow the switch, but only with SC basal insulin given 1-2 h before the infusion stops. Pick the option that includes an overlap; if none does, pick the one that continues the infusion.

lines: Marrow: Fix dynamic hyperinflation by lengthening expiration: lower RR (the strongest lever), raise inspiratory flow and shorten Ti, reduce VT, and accept permissive hypercapnia; in a disconnect-worthy crisis, briefly disconnect to let the trapped gas out.
cross: Marrow's keyed option (B) describes 'metabolic compensation' with HCO3 25. Truth: HCO3 25 with a high PaCO2 is an acute, UNcompensated respiratory acidosis from dynamic hyperinflation. If an option says acute uncompensated respiratory acidosis, pick it; otherwise B is the keyed answer despite the wording.

lines: Marrow: Child-Pugh predicts overall survival, variceal bleeding and operative risk: 1-year survival A ~100%, B ~80%, C ~45%. Older versions score prothrombin-time prolongation (1–3 s / 4–6 s / >6 s) in place of INR.

DocT PYQ: The best single marker of severity in chronic liver disease is PT/INR, since factor VII's short half-life makes it move first; albumin and bilirubin add to it (MELD = bilirubin, INR, creatinine ± Na). Transaminases measure ongoing injury, not hepatic reserve, and can be normal in end-stage cirrhosis.

Marrow: Add the mimic: extramedullary haematopoiesis in thalassaemia or chronic haemolysis can compress the cord or cauda equina and is relieved by laminectomy (with transfusion or radiotherapy), so a cord syndrome in a chronically haemolysing patient is not automatically malignant.

Marrow: Suspected pseudoaneurysm bleed (shock, falling Hb, a collection that suddenly enlarges, blood in a drain) → CT angiography first to find it, then angio-embolisation; surgery only if embolisation fails or the patient cannot be stabilised.

Marrow + DocT GT: Angiotensin II (Giapreza; ATHOS-3) for catecholamine-refractory vasodilatory shock: start 20 ng/kg/min, max 80 in the first 3 h then ≤40, for up to 7 days; give VTE prophylaxis (thrombosis). Rationale: endothelial injury lowers pulmonary ACE activity, so angiotensin I accumulates and Ang II is relatively low (IL-6 drives hepatic angiotensinogen).
Marrow: HEV IgM can be falsely negative (early, or immunosuppressed), so send HEV RNA PCR when suspicion is high: pregnancy, travel to an endemic area, or acute-on-chronic liver failure in India.

DocT GT: Factor V is the liver-made factor that is NOT vitamin K-dependent: low II/VII with normal V = vitamin K deficiency (cholestasis, antibiotics, poor intake) → IV vitamin K 10 mg; low II, VII and V = synthetic failure; low V with low VIII = DIC.

Marrow: Halothane hepatitis is immune-mediated (trifluoroacetylated protein adducts), typically after repeated exposure within weeks; fulminant cases have high mortality and count as a non-paracetamol cause under King's criteria (ALF-33).

Marrow: Diarrhoea on enteral feeding is not a reason to stop or slow the feed: keep the same rate, review drugs and test for C. difficile. Do not raise density or rate, give fluid boluses, or add supplemental PN before day 7.

Marrow: Suspected intra-abdominal abscess → contrast CT is the definitive test and guides percutaneous drainage; plain films and bedside ultrasound are insensitive in the gassy, post-operative abdomen.

DocT Recall25: Desaturation and rising airway pressures right after NG insertion, with the tube in a bronchus on X-ray → stop feeds, remove the tube, re-insert under direct (video-laryngoscope) vision and confirm by X-ray or aspirate pH ≤5.5 before any feed. Never advance it further; a cuffed ETT does not prevent tracheobronchial placement.

Marrow: Worsening toxic megacolon or suspected perforation in CDI → resuscitate, then subtotal colectomy with end ileostomy (diverting loop ileostomy with colonic vancomycin lavage is the colon-sparing alternative). Involve surgeons at diagnosis: operating before lactate reaches 5 mmol/L improves survival.
Marrow: Continue home baclofen, antipsychotics and anxiolytics in ICU: abrupt withdrawal mimics a failed SAT or delirium (baclofen withdrawal can also cause seizures and hyperthermia).

Marrow: Poor-prognosis signs after arrest (multimodal, ≥72 h): status epilepticus or myoclonic status during temperature control, bilaterally absent pupillary and corneal reflexes, high NSE, burst suppression on EEG, sustained upgaze. Absent arm movement with preserved legs may be man-in-a-barrel (watershed infarct) and is not always poor; a brief 3–5 min arrest can recover fully.

Marrow: Rewarm after temperature control at ~0.25 °C/h on an automated device (about 16 h for 4 °C) and never faster than 0.5 °C/h; rapid rewarming causes vasodilatory hypotension, potassium shifts and rebound fever.

fix.t: b: SpO2 90–98% (PaO2 60–105); PaCO2 35–45. a: MAP ≥ 65 (2025 dropped the SBP target). [ACLS-42 watch is correct.]
fix.why: Post-ROSC SpO2 target: 92–98% vs 90–98% (AHA 2025). Check against the AHA 2025 text.

lines: Marrow: Modified Fisher (CT) predicts VASOSPASM risk; Hunt & Hess (clinical) predicts MORTALITY. Match the scale to the outcome the stem asks about.
Marrow: Hunt & Hess mortality rises with grade: about I 30%, II 40%, III 50%, IV 80%, V 90% (figures vary by series; the 1968 original was lower for grades I–III).

Marrow: Cerebral salt wasting = HYPOvolaemic (poor turgor, rising Hct, low CVP) → fluids + salt (fludrocortisone); SIADH = eu/hypervolaemic → fluid restriction. In SAH never fluid-restrict (vasospasm risk), so treat as CSW.

DocT GT: Neurogenic pulmonary oedema follows any sudden CNS insult (status epilepticus, SAH, TBI): a hypothalamic/medullary catecholamine surge raises pulmonary capillary pressure and damages endothelium → protein-rich oedema within minutes–hours, pink frothy sputum, bilateral infiltrates, normal LV filling pressure. Treat the brain cause plus PEEP and lung-protective ventilation; it usually clears in 48–72 h.

DocT GT: Post-SAH ECG: the catecholamine surge gives 'cerebral T waves' (deep symmetric T inversion, sometimes tall peaked T), QT prolongation, U waves and ST depression or elevation, with troponin rise and wall-motion loss that fits no coronary territory (neurogenic stunning, reversible). Correct K and Mg: long QT predisposes to torsades.
cross: DocT GT keys 'peaked T waves' as the typical post-SAH ECG change (40% chose it). Truth: the classic cerebral T wave is deep symmetric T INVERSION with QT prolongation, and ST elevation also occurs. If T inversion/long QT is offered pick it; between peaked T and ST elevation, DocT picks peaked T.

fix.t: Hyponatraemia (CSW/natriuresis): fludrocortisone and hypertonic saline for prevention and correction
fix.why: Says "Hypernatraemia: fludrocortisone and hypertonic saline". Should read hyponatraemia (cerebral salt wasting).

fix.t: Glucose target "80–120 mg/dL" in aSAH is doubtful; current guidance is to avoid both hyper- and hypoglycaemia rather than a tight band.

lines: Marrow: Diffuse hypoattenuation with lost grey–white differentiation after arrest = global anoxic injury: there is no surgical role, so the step is multimodal prognostication and counselling the family, not a neurosurgical referral.

DocT GT: Cushing's TRIAD = hypertension (wide pulse pressure) + bradycardia + irregular respiration, from brainstem ischaemia as ICP rises: a late sign of impending herniation. Tachycardia is not part of it; it belongs to the later autonomic storm when the vagal nucleus dies.

Marrow: Donation after circulatory death: the treating team decides and performs withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment (can be in theatre) → circulatory death → mandatory no-touch period (2–5 min) → procurement; comfort care continues, and the donation team is contacted but never leads WLST.
cross: Marrow keys delaying temperature control because of residual sedation. Truth: AHA/ERC give temperature control to ALL comatose post-arrest patients; residual sedation delays brain-death testing and neuroprognostication, not temperature control. If the question asks about starting temperature control, pick 'start it'; if about prognosis/brain death, pick 'wait for sedation to clear'.

lines: Marrow: Ramsay scale (older alternative to RASS): 1 anxious/agitated, 2 cooperative and tranquil, 3 responds to commands only, 4 asleep with brisk response to glabellar tap or loud noise, 5 sluggish response, 6 no response.

Marrow: Babinski sign = corticospinal (UMN) lesion; areflexia right after cord injury may be spinal shock rather than a peripheral lesion; pain on moving a joint points to a musculoskeletal cause, not weakness.

Marrow: Mannitol contraindications = progressive heart failure or pulmonary congestion, anuria, severe dehydration and severe electrolyte derangement, because the initial volume expansion and later diuresis worsen each.
cross: Marrow attributes a new EF of 20% to mannitol. Truth: mannitol worsens existing heart failure but does not cause cardiomyopathy; new LV failure after >24 h of sedation also fits propofol infusion syndrome. If PRIS is offered with propofol in the stem, consider it.

lines: Marrow: 4-factor PCC contains heparin, so avoid it in HIT; reverse warfarin there with FFP 15–20 mL/kg + IV vitamin K.

fix.t: CRASH-3 (n=12,737): mild-to-moderate TBI (GCS 9–15) → lower head-injury death, best if given ≤3 h; severe (GCS 3–8): no benefit. CRASH-2 row = IBS substudy (270 TBI pts): non-significant trend to less haemorrhage growth, fewer new ischaemic lesions. Watch: "benefit in mild-to-moderate (GCS 9–15), not severe".
fix.why: CRASH-3 benefit was in mild-to-moderate TBI (GCS 9–15), not mild only; the CRASH-2 row describes the intracranial-bleeding substudy.

lines: Marrow: Cerebral blood flow falls with hypocapnia/alkalosis and hypothermia, and rises with hypercapnia/acidosis, hypoxia (PaO2 <50 mmHg), hyperthermia, volatile agents and pain. This is why hyperventilation lowers ICP but risks ischaemia.

Marrow: A small craniectomy flap lets swollen brain herniate through the bone edge (extracalvarial herniation), causing venous and cortical infarcts at the edge; that is the reason for a large (≥12 × 15 cm) flap.

Marrow: Meningococcus takes the haematogenous route: nasopharyngeal colonisation → mucosal invasion → bacteraemia → crossing into the CSF, which is why meningococcaemia can precede or occur without meningitis.
Marrow: In suspected TTP, send ADAMTS13 and then start plasma exchange immediately - never wait for the result; steroids go with it, with caplacizumab and rituximab as add-ons.
Marrow: Early onset (<34 weeks) marks severe pre-eclampsia; SBP 140 alone is not a severe feature (severe = ≥160/110).

DocT GT: Hypertension found before 20 weeks is chronic; calling it ESSENTIAL rests on primary-hypertension risk factors (family history, obesity, diabetes) and no clue to a secondary cause (renal disease, phaeochromocytoma, coarctation). Absent proteinuria only says it is not pre-eclampsia.

Marrow: Overwhelming post-splenectomy infection is the main long-term lethal risk of asplenia: encapsulated organisms (pneumococcus, Hib, meningococcus) cause fulminant sepsis with DIC and purpura (mortality ~50%). Prevent with vaccination ≥2 weeks before elective splenectomy, antibiotic prophylaxis and a standby course.

Marrow: ASPEN limits: glucose ≤5 mg/kg/min (start ~100–150 g/day) and lipid 20–30% of calories. Worked check: 12.5% dextrose at 100 mL/h = 300 g/day; 20% lipid at 50 mL/h = 2,400 kcal/day (Marrow's explanation gets this arithmetic wrong).

cross: Marrow keys the IV route for a moderately low phosphate on the grounds that oral phosphate absorbs poorly in critical illness. Truth: the card's thresholds (oral for 1.5-2.5 mg/dL, IV below 1.0 or with cardiac or respiratory dysfunction) are the standard. Pick IV when the level is below 1.0, there is diaphragm or myocardial dysfunction, or the gut is not working; otherwise oral.

lines: Marrow: Low plasma zinc is common in ICU (inflammation redistributes it); monitor and supplement only with deficiency signs or ongoing losses (burns, fistulae, CRRT), giving it IV because oral absorption is poor.
cross: Marrow keys 'monitor only' while its explanation says treat if severely low (0.2 is low). Truth: low zinc in acute inflammation is mostly redistribution; replace when deficiency is clinically likely or losses are high. If the stem gives signs or high losses, pick replacement.

lines: Marrow: High aspiration risk (prior aspiration, supine positioning, ventilated) is itself an indication for post-pyloric feeding.

Marrow: Split the raised osmolal gap by anion gap: normal anion gap with a raised osmolal gap means isopropanol, acetone, mannitol or diethyl ether; a high anion gap with it means methanol, ethylene glycol, formaldehyde or paraldehyde.

Marrow: In carbon monoxide poisoning pulse oximetry reads falsely normal and the PaO2 is unchanged, because both measure dissolved oxygen and oxyhaemoglobin rather than COHb; late damage targets the globus pallidus. Hyperbaric oxygen is considered for COHb >25% (>15% in pregnancy), loss of consciousness, ischaemia or neurological signs.

DocT GT: Methaemoglobin absorbs equally at 660 and 940 nm, so SpO2 drifts to about 85% whatever the true saturation, while the ABG-calculated SaO2 reads falsely normal (the saturation gap); PaO2 is normal, blood is chocolate-brown and cyanosis ignores oxygen. Commonest drug causes are topical benzocaine or prilocaine before endoscopy, dapsone, nitrites/nitrates, primaquine, rasburicase and sulfonamides (not paracetamol, atropine or digoxin); confirm by co-oximetry and give methylene blue 1-2 mg/kg if symptomatic or MetHb >20-30%, never in G6PD deficiency.
Marrow: Salicylate haemodialysis indications belong on this card: level >100 mg/dL, deteriorating CNS, renal failure, acute lung injury, or severe acidosis despite treatment.

Marrow: Carbamazepine is toxic above 40 microgram/mL, and CYP3A4 inhibitors (diltiazem, valproate, isoniazid, macrolides) push a stable patient into toxicity - the reason it is on both the multi-dose charcoal and the haemoperfusion list.

Marrow: Staff decontamination belongs with the patient's: organophosphates are absorbed through skin and inhaled from vomit and soaked clothing, so gloves, gown, eye protection and a ventilated space protect the team while clothes are removed and the skin washed.

Marrow: Add dextromethorphan to the dissociative list - it is an NMDA antagonist available over the counter and often co-formulated with paracetamol, so check a paracetamol level; agitation is treated with benzodiazepines.

Marrow: Budd–Chiari presenting as ALF: anticoagulate, decompress with TIPS (or angioplasty/stent), and list for transplant if that fails. Doppler/MRI confirms the hepatic-vein block; ursodiol and open shunt surgery have no role.
cross: Marrow QB58-Q02 key: transplant evaluation for fulminant Budd–Chiari despite colon cancer 2 months earlier. Truth: fulminant Budd–Chiari is a transplant indication, but a recent extrahepatic malignancy is a contraindication (ALF-32c). If the stem has active or recent cancer, pick TIPS + anticoagulation; if not, pick transplant evaluation.

lines: Marrow: Any bowel obstruction (including adult intussusception) with signs of sepsis or ischaemia (peritonism, rising lactate, shock) goes straight to emergency laparotomy; CT angiography only delays it.

Marrow + DocT GT: Penetrating injury in the 'box' (clavicles, nipples, costal margins) with shock → pericardial ultrasound first; tamponade or arrest after penetrating trauma → resuscitative thoracotomy (stable with effusion → pericardial window/sternotomy). Blunt arrest with >10 min of CPR or asystole and no cardiac motion on POCUS → stop; thoracotomy only within 10 min of CPR with signs of life.

Recall25: Airway with C-spine control escalates stepwise: suction → jaw thrust (moves the neck least; preferred to chin lift) → OPA/NPA → cuffed tube by RSI with manual in-line stabilisation → surgical airway if intubation fails.

Recall25: Flail chest (≥2 ribs broken in ≥2 places) = paradoxical movement and abnormal chest-wall mechanics; the treatment that works is analgesia, ideally thoracic epidural, plus O2/NIV, ventilating only for failure. The underlying contusion drives most hypoxia, but a chest tube does not treat a contusion.

Marrow: Muir-Barclay albumin (colloid) formula: one portion = 0.5 mL × %TBSA × kg, six portions over 36 h in periods of 4, 4, 4, 6, 6 and 12 h. Used where colloid-based resuscitation is asked; Parkland remains the crystalloid standard.

Marrow: Clinical brain-death criteria: coma of known irreversible cause, absent brainstem reflexes, positive apnoea test (no breathing at PaCO2 ≥60 or ≥20 above baseline in CO2 retainers, pH <7.30); spinal reflexes may persist. Prerequisites: core temperature ≥36 °C, SBP ≥100 (vasopressors allowed), eucapnia at start, no confounding drugs; locked-in syndrome is a mimic.

Marrow + DocT GT: Three oedema types: vasogenic (BBB broken, extracellular fluid in white matter; tumour, abscess, meningitis; steroid-responsive), cytotoxic (cell swelling with BBB intact, grey and white matter; ischaemia, hypo-osmolality), hydrostatic (high pressure through an intact BBB; PRES).

Marrow: In a sedated resting patient (low cerebral VO2) ScvO2 can run 2–3% HIGHER than SvO2 even without shock; a 'normal' ScvO2 >70% has no prognostic value — the threshold matters only when it is low.
cross: Marrow's explanation says ScvO2 is 2–3% higher than SvO2, the reverse of this card. Truth: in awake healthy people ScvO2 is 2–3% LOWER (brain extracts more); in shock or sedation it becomes higher. If the stem is a healthy awake subject, pick lower; if shock/sedated, pick higher.

lines: Marrow: Coronary perfusion pressure: LV CPP = diastolic BP − PAOP (LVEDP), since the LV is perfused in diastole; RV CPP = MAP − mean RV pressure, since the RV is perfused through the whole cycle — a rising RV pressure starves the RV.
Marrow: Measured vs derived: BP, RAP, PAP, PAOP and thermodilution CO are measured; SV (CO ÷ HR), CI, SVI, SVR and PVR are derived (MAP is integrated from the waveform).
Marrow: More thermodilution errors: slow injection (>4 s), injectate volume smaller or warmer than programmed (both OVERestimate CO), abnormal haematocrit, arrhythmias and extremes of cardiac output.
Marrow: COPD/asthma sits in the resistance pattern (peak up, plateau unchanged); lung resection (smaller lung) and abdominal distension raise elastic pressure, so peak and plateau rise together.

Marrow: Other ventilator signs of airway obstruction: a large peak–plateau gap (resistive pressure) on an inspiratory pause, and a biphasic expiratory flow curve — a high early spike then an abrupt fall to a low tail — from early airway collapse (emphysema).
cross: DocT PYQ keys auto-PEEP as what flow-time and pressure-time waveforms identify. Truth: asynchrony, flow starvation and breath stacking are all read from the same waveforms, so every option is true. Pick auto-PEEP (expiratory flow not returning to zero) as the classic answer.

lines: DocT GT: The same 20% lipid regimen (1.5 mL/kg bolus, then 0.25 mL/kg/min) is a rescue for lipophilic cardiotoxins - propranolol, verapamil/diltiazem, TCAs - once glucagon, high-dose insulin, pressors and bicarbonate have failed; VA-ECMO is the step after that.

cross: GT6 Q135 keys elevated BUN as 'the hallmark of AKI'. Truth: KDIGO defines and stages AKI by serum creatinine and urine output; BUN rises with GI bleeding, steroids and catabolism, and 'azotaemia' is only Harrison's older wording. If creatinine/urine output is offered pick it; pick BUN only when it is the sole kidney-function option.

lines: DocT GT: On TEG, LY30 >3% defines hyperfibrinolysis in trauma and carries about a 10-fold mortality, so an LY30 of 5% is NOT normal → tranexamic acid (CRASH-2: 1 g within 3 h of injury, then 1 g over 8 h). A very low LY30 (<0.9%, 'shutdown') also predicts a worse outcome.

DocT GT: Shock-activated protein C cleaves factors Va and VIIIa, so factor V is the factor most consistently depleted in haemorrhagic shock, falling with shock severity before any dilution (alongside early fibrinogen loss). Factors IX, XI and XIII are not the typical deficits.

DocT GT (×3): Endotheliopathy of trauma (SHINE): shock and the catecholamine surge shed the endothelial glycocalyx (syndecan-1 rises and predicts death) and neutrophil reactive oxygen species and proteases damage it → capillary leak, ARDS, MODS, autoheparinisation, hyperfibrinolysis. The glycocalyx is the main regulator of permeability; plasma restores it while crystalloid worsens shedding, one reason for plasma-first resuscitation.

DocT PYQ: On M-mode a pleural effusion gives the sinusoid sign: the lung line (visceral pleura) moves toward the pleural line in inspiration, tracing a sine wave; with the quad sign it confirms free fluid. Pneumothorax gives the barcode (stratosphere) sign and a lung point.

DocT GT: Liver or spleen 'mirrored' above the diaphragm is a normal artefact that needs air-filled lung, so it means NO effusion at that spot (do not needle there). With an effusion the mirror image disappears and the spine becomes visible above the diaphragm (spine sign); hepatisation is real consolidated lung, not an artefact.

DocT GT: Prone positioning LOWERS chest-wall compliance (the anterior wall is fixed against the bed), so 'improved chest wall compliance' is the false mechanism. Oxygenation improves through more homogeneous transpulmonary pressure and ventilation, dorsal recruitment with better V/Q, and less compression of the left lower lobe by heart and abdomen.

DocT PYQ: Hypovolaemia on echo: small hyperdynamic LV with end-systolic cavity obliteration ('kissing' papillary muscles) and a small collapsing IVC. A dilated, poorly contracting LV is cardiogenic; a dilated RV with septal flattening points to PE or RV failure.

DocT GT: In PLAX, fluid ANTERIOR to the descending thoracic aorta (between aorta and LA) is pericardial; fluid posterior or lateral to it is pleural, because the pericardial reflection stops at the aorta.

DocT Recall25: Giant v wave on the wedge trace = acute mitral regurgitation (systolic backflow into a non-compliant LA; also VSD). Large a wave = mitral stenosis, LA myxoma or a stiff LV (atrium contracting against resistance); no a wave = AF.
cross: Recall25 keys left atrial myxoma for PCWP < LVEDP. Truth: myxoma, like mitral stenosis, obstructs LA→LV flow and makes PCWP HIGHER than LVEDP; PCWP < LVEDP occurs in aortic regurgitation (premature mitral closure), a stiff LV and LVEDP >25. Pick aortic regurgitation if offered; the card is right.

lines: DocT PYQ: qSOFA (≥2 of RR ≥22, SBP ≤100, altered mentation) is a PROGNOSTIC marker that flags infected patients at risk of death or prolonged ICU stay. It is not a screening tool (too insensitive) and not diagnostic; sepsis is diagnosed by an acute SOFA rise ≥2.

DocT PYQ: FAST has four windows for free fluid: pericardial (subxiphoid), RUQ (Morison's pouch), LUQ (splenorenal) and pelvis (pouch of Douglas/rectovesical); eFAST adds both anterior chests for pneumothorax. It does not image the brain or the retroperitoneum.

DocT GT: Pregnant with high suspicion of PE: start heparin before imaging (LMWH by weight, UFH if unstable or if lysis or delivery is likely); warfarin is teratogenic and DOACs are contraindicated. Then compression ultrasound (if leg symptoms), CTPA or V/Q; imaging must not delay anticoagulation.

DocT GT: D-dimer is raised in most ICU patients (sepsis, surgery, trauma, age, malignancy), so a positive ICU result means almost nothing (PPV ~27%). Only a normal D-dimer has value, to exclude VTE at low or intermediate pre-test probability; it never confirms PE or triggers lysis.

DocT GT: Vasopressor-refractory shock in ALF (vasodilatory, with frequent relative adrenal insufficiency) → low-dose hydrocortisone 200 mg/day on top of noradrenaline; it cuts the vasopressor dose without proven survival benefit (AASLD/EASL). High-dose steroids and adrenaline boluses are wrong.

fix.t: c None absolute: noradrenaline first; low-dose vasopressin may be added (SCCM 2020); use terlipressin cautiously if ICP high.
fix.why: Says vasopressin is "better avoided". AASLD/EASL allow vasopressin or terlipressin as an add-on to noradrenaline.
fix.src: SCCM ALF/ACLF Guidelines 2020; EASL ALF CPG 2017

lines: DocT GT: In HHS depressed consciousness tracks effective osmolality: stupor, coma and seizures appear once it passes ~320-330 and are typical above 350 mOsm/kg. Coma at a lower osmolality should send you looking for another cause (stroke, sepsis, drugs).

Marrow: Work out the subcutaneous dose from the infusion: average rate over the last 6-8 h x 24 x 70-80% = total daily dose; if the patient is nil by mouth give 100% of it as basal, and give that basal dose 2-3 h BEFORE stopping the drip so the two overlap.

DocT GT: Suspected infection in ALF (fever, rising WBC, new infiltrate; pneumonia commonest) → immediate empirical extended-spectrum β-lactam (piperacillin-tazobactam or a carbapenem by local Gram-negative ecology) after cultures, without waiting for results. Add antifungals only for deterioration despite antibiotics or a prolonged course.

DocT GT: The same idea outside brain injury: after emergency intubation for coma (alcohol, arrest) a short beta-lactam course (cefuroxime 2 doses in 24 h, Sirvent 1997; ceftriaxone single dose, PROPHY-VAP) cuts early VAP from aspirated flora without raising resistance. A 7-day carbapenem or vancomycin + aminoglycoside is wrong.

DocT GT: Pre-eclampsia with SEVERE features = SBP ≥160 or DBP ≥110, or any end-organ sign: platelets <100,000, creatinine >1.1 mg/dL or doubled, transaminases twice normal or RUQ pain, pulmonary oedema, new headache or visual change. The amount of proteinuria (e.g. 6 g/day) no longer grades severity; a seizure makes it eclampsia.

DocT GT: Stable monomorphic VT with heart failure or poor LV function → amiodarone. Procainamide and sotalol are negatively inotropic and hypotensive, so avoided in HFrEF; procainamide is first choice only with preserved LV function (PROCAMIO). Adenosine and verapamil are wrong in VT; DC cardioversion is for instability.

DocT GT: Early fluids in severe pancreatitis = goal-directed Ringer's lactate at a moderate rate (DocT keys ~3 mL/kg/h; WATERFALL 2022 used 1.5 mL/kg/h plus a 10 mL/kg bolus only if hypovolaemic, and stopped early for overload in the aggressive arm). Reassess at 3, 12 and 24 h against urine output >0.5 mL/kg/h and falling haematocrit and BUN.
Marrow: Killip class: I no heart failure; II S3 and/or rales in <50% of lung fields; III frank pulmonary oedema (rales >50%); IV cardiogenic shock — mortality rises steeply with each class.

DocT GT: Hypertensive acute pulmonary oedema (SCAPE): high-dose IV nitroglycerin (titratable preload and afterload reduction) plus NIV/CPAP first; most patients are redistributed, not overloaded, so 'loop diuretic and wait' is too slow. Hydralazine is unpredictable with reflex tachycardia, labetalol's β-blockade depresses a failing LV, oral ACEi is too slow; intubate only for NIV failure or falling GCS.

DocT GT: Chronic calcific constrictive pericarditis is cured only by pericardiectomy. Diuretics only palliate congestion, and anti-inflammatory therapy helps only transient (inflammatory, CMR late-gadolinium-positive) constriction. Calcification on CT after cardiac surgery or TB is the classic clue.

DocT GT: Constriction vs restrictive cardiomyopathy on echo: constriction shows >25% respiratory variation of mitral inflow, septal bounce, a preserved or high septal e' (annulus paradoxus/reversus: septal e' ≥ lateral) and a thick or calcified pericardium. Restriction (amyloid) has little respiratory variation, a low e' (<8 cm/s), thick myocardium and biatrial enlargement. TB is the classic cause of constriction in India.

DocT GT: At catheterisation the discriminator is DISCORDANT RV and LV systolic pressures with breathing in constriction (inspiration: RV up, LV down, from ventricular interdependence inside a fixed pericardium) vs CONCORDANT changes in restriction. Dip-and-plateau and equalised end-diastolic pressures occur in both, so they do not separate them; BNP is high in restriction and near-normal in constriction.

DocT GT: Ventilate ARDS in pregnancy at 6 mL/kg predicted body weight with Pplat <30 (a stiff chest wall may tolerate slightly more); no guideline supports larger breaths. The real adaptation is avoiding permissive hypercapnia: keep PaCO2 about 30–45 mmHg so the fetus can offload CO2.

DocT GT (×2): Pregnant woman with ARDS (P/F <200) who is DROWSY → intubate, not CPAP/NIV: she cannot protect the airway, and pregnancy adds aspiration risk (relaxed LOS, raised intragastric pressure) and fast desaturation (FRC −20%, high O2 use). Delivery and tocolysis are decided after maternal stabilisation.
cross: DocT GT keys 8–9 mL/kg as the 'safe' tidal volume in pregnant ARDS (cohort 3%). Truth: 6 mL/kg PBW applies in pregnancy (SMFM, ARDSNet); the physiological rise in maternal tidal volume is no reason to ventilate at 8–9. Pick 6 mL/kg if offered; for DocT, 8–9 is the keyed answer.

GT5 Q116 key: hepatic + coagulation dysfunction as most predictive of death in post-pancreatitis MODS. Truth: Revised Atlanta and modified Marshall score respiratory, cardiovascular and renal failure, and mortality tracks PERSISTENT (>48 h) and MULTIPLE organ failure (~30–50%); no guideline ranks liver + coagulation highest. If a respiratory/cardiovascular/renal combination or 'persistent multi-organ failure' is offered, pick it; otherwise accept the bank key.

lines: DocT GT: Current DKA criteria (ADA/EASD/JBDS 2024 consensus): glucose >=200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) OR known diabetes, ketones >=3.0 mmol/L, and pH <7.3 and/or bicarbonate <18 mmol/L - the card's 250 mg/dL is the older ADA cut-off, and euglycaemic DKA meets the new definition. pH <7.1 and bicarbonate <10 mark severity, not diagnosis.

fix.t: DKA-05: Glucose ≥200 mg/dL OR known diabetes; ketones (BHB) ≥3.0 mmol/L or urine ≥2+; pH <7.3 and/or HCO3 <18. DKA-06: glucose ≥200; grade by pH/HCO3 (7.25–7.30/15–18; 7.0–<7.25/10–<15; <7.0/<10); HHS glucose ≥600, effective osm >300 (total >320), pH ≥7.3, HCO3 ≥15, BHB <3.
fix.why: Define DKA by glucose >250 mg/dL. 2024 consensus: glucose ≥200 mg/dL or known diabetes, ketones ≥3.0 mmol/L, pH <7.3 and/or bicarbonate <18.

lines: DocT GT: Typical (slow–fast) AVNRT is re-entry within the AV node through dual pathways: atria and ventricles fire together, so retrograde P waves hide in or just after the QRS (pseudo-S in II, III, aVF; pseudo-r' in V1). AVRT needs an accessory pathway (delta wave in sinus rhythm, longer RP); focal atrial tachycardia shows a distinct P before each QRS.

DocT GT: After 4 days of vomiting a chloride of 87 (gastric HCl loss) with a high anion gap (130 - 87 - 18 = 25) from lactate means a hidden metabolic alkalosis alongside lactic acidosis; 0.9% saline replaces both volume and chloride. HES is contraindicated (AKI, mortality) and albumin is not first-line.

DocT GT: NSE is also present in red cells and platelets, so a HAEMOLYSED sample (or haemolysis on ECMO) gives a falsely high NSE; check free Hb before prognosticating. S-100B (glia) and NfL are not raised by haemolysis in the same way.

DocT GT: Neurofilament light chain is a structural protein of large myelinated AXONS, so raised CSF/serum NfL means axonal injury; it rises even after repetitive mild TBI (boxers). Contrast: NSE = neuronal cell body, S-100B/GFAP = glia/astrocytes.

DocT GT: A malignant effusion is an exudate because tumour on the pleura raises capillary permeability AND blocks parietal-pleural lymphatic drainage (stomata, mediastinal nodes); the lymphatic block is why it recurs. Raised hydrostatic or low oncotic pressure gives a transudate; thoracic-duct disruption gives chyle (TG >110 mg/dL).

DocT GT: Adrenal insufficiency on a checkpoint inhibitor is usually HYPOPHYSITIS (classically anti-CTLA-4 ipilimumab): low ACTH, secondary AI, often with headache and low TSH and gonadotrophins; primary adrenalitis is rare. Give hydrocortisone first and replace cortisol before thyroxine; the replacement is usually lifelong.

DocT GT: Coronary perfusion pressure (aortic DIASTOLIC minus right-atrial diastolic pressure during the release phase) is the best predictor of ROSC; ≥15–20 mmHg is usually needed. That is why the arterial-line target is diastolic >20 mmHg; systolic peaks and a palpable femoral pulse (may be venous) do not reflect myocardial perfusion.

Marrow: Opioid hypoventilation (RR 8, PaCO2 78, PaO2 45 on air): PAO2 = 150 − 78/0.8 ≈ 52, A–a ≈ 7 = NORMAL, so hypoxaemia is from hypoventilation alone (corrects with ventilation, not by searching for lung disease).

DocT GT: A low PbtO2 (<20 mmHg) with a normal ICP and CPP still means hypoxic brain tissue: microcirculatory dysfunction, a diffusion barrier (oedema) or low O2 delivery (anaemia, hypoxaemia). A normal ICP does not prove adequate oxygenation.

DocT GT: PbtO2 <20 mmHg for >10 min in TBI with a normal ICP: raise O2 delivery first by raising CPP (MAP up with fluid or vasopressor), then FiO2/PaO2, transfuse if Hb <7, treat fever, seizures and shivering. Steroids harm in TBI (CRASH) and craniectomy is for refractory ICP, not isolated low PbtO2.

DocT GT: Triggered palliative-care involvement for ventilated patients with a poor prognosis shortens ICU and hospital stay, cuts non-beneficial procedures and ICU readmission and lowers cost, with equal or better family satisfaction and no rise in mortality. SSC still advises against routine formal consultation for every septic patient.

DocT GT: Tocilizumab binds the IL-6 RECEPTOR (membrane and soluble), blocking classic and trans-signalling; it does not bind IL-6 itself (siltuximab does), gp130, or IL-1 (anakinra). Because the receptor is blocked, serum IL-6 rises after a dose.

DocT GT: Carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter (CRAB, OXA-23/24-type) is NOT reliably covered by ceftazidime-avibactam, meropenem-vaborbactam or ceftolozane-tazobactam, so among those options cefiderocol is the active drug. IDSA 2024 prefers sulbactam-durlobactam + a carbapenem (or high-dose ampicillin-sulbactam combination) and keeps cefiderocol for combination use when others fail, because CREDIBLE-CR showed higher mortality with cefiderocol in Acinetobacter.

fix.t: OXA-48 | Enterobacterales (esp. K. pneumoniae) | ... | Ceftazidime-avibactam (preferred); cefiderocol. Add: CRAB = OXA-23/24/58 (+ intrinsic OXA-51) → sulbactam-durlobactam + carbapenem; CZA inactive.
fix.why: Lists OXA-48 for Acinetobacter and treats it with ceftazidime-avibactam. OXA-48 is an Enterobacterales enzyme; CRAB carries OXA-23/24/58, and ceftazidime-avibactam is not reliably active.

lines: Marrow: When withdrawing life support, stop tube feeds early (aspiration and bloating, no comfort) while keeping comfort measures — oxygen if it eases dyspnoea, opioids, anxiolytics, glycopyrrolate for secretions, eye and mouth care.

DocT GT: In PD, small-solute clearance depends on how often fresh dialysate restores the gradient, so with a tense abdomen (fill volume cannot rise) use more frequent, shorter exchanges. Longer dwells favour larger molecules and lose ultrafiltration through glucose absorption; higher dextrose raises ultrafiltration, not urea clearance.

DocT GT: In drowning the arrest is hypoxic, so CPR starts with rescue breaths (ERC: 5 initial breaths, then 30:2), care-first even for a lone rescuer. Abdominal thrusts to 'drain water' are not recommended: little water is aspirated, and they delay ventilation and cause regurgitation.

DocT GT: Upright, ventilation and perfusion are both greater at the bases, but perfusion rises more steeply, so V/Q is highest at the apex (~3) and lowest at the base (~0.6); 'V/Q greater at the bases' is false. Supine, the same gradient runs posterior (low V/Q) to anterior (high V/Q).

cross: DocT GT keys 'all secondary pneumothoraces don't need a tube' as the false statement. Truth: BTS (and this card) observe a secondary pneumothorax <1 cm, so 'not all need a tube' is true; 'most should have thoracotomy/stapling' (Harrison wording) is not current BTS 2023 practice and is the more defensible false statement. For DocT, pick its key.

lines: DocT GT: On CT a main pulmonary artery diameter >3 cm (≥29 mm, measured before the bifurcation) or a PA:aorta ratio >1 suggests pulmonary hypertension; the PA:A ratio >1 also predicts COPD exacerbations and mortality. Confirm with echo (TR velocity >2.8 m/s) and right-heart catheter.

DocT GT: Pericarditis by time course: acute = fibrinous or effusive (serous, purulent, haemorrhagic); subacute = effusive-constrictive or constrictive; chronic (>3 months) = constrictive, adhesive or effusive. So 'fibrinous' is the acute form.

DocT GT: Tracheostomy indications in ICU: expected prolonged ventilation or failure to wean; inability to protect the airway or clear secretions; airway oedema or high-risk airway after maxillofacial surgery or trauma; and cervical immobilisation making re-intubation hazardous. Early tracheostomy (≤7–10 days) does not lower mortality (TracMan).

DocT GT: In an alcoholic with low K, Ca and Mg, perioral tingling from hypocalcaemia is fixed by IV magnesium: low Mg suppresses PTH release and causes PTH resistance, and it wastes K through renal ROMK channels, so Ca and K stay low until Mg is replaced - calcium or KCl alone fail.

DocT GT: Infuse IV phenytoin no faster than 50 mg/min (25 mg/min in the elderly or cardiac patients; fosphenytoin ≤150 mg PE/min) with continuous ECG and BP monitoring: Na-channel block plus the propylene glycol vehicle cause hypotension, bradycardia, AV block and VF. Extravasation causes purple glove syndrome.

DocT GT: Absence (and myoclonic) status responds to a benzodiazepine, then IV valproate (25–40 mg/kg) or levetiracetam. Phenytoin and carbamazepine are ineffective and can worsen generalised absence seizures, which are thalamocortical T-type Ca2+-driven, not Na-channel driven.

DocT GT (×2): Only the anaesthetic infusions (midazolam, propofol, pentobarbital/thiopentone 5–15 mg/kg then 0.5–5 mg/kg/h) are titrated on continuous EEG to seizure suppression or burst suppression for 24–48 h. Second-line drugs (fosphenytoin, levetiracetam, valproate) are fixed loading doses, not EEG-titrated.

DocT GT: Piperacillin-tazobactam covers Gram-positives, Gram-negatives including Pseudomonas, and anaerobes, but never MRSA: PBP2a resists every β-lactam except ceftaroline/ceftobiprole, so add vancomycin or linezolid.

DocT GT: Respiratory chest pain comes from the parietal pleura (intercostal nerves; central diaphragmatic pleura via the phrenic nerve refers to the shoulder tip). Visceral pleura, lung parenchyma and small airways have no pain fibres, so parenchymal disease hurts only when it reaches the parietal pleura.
