DocT GT: Both pulsus paradoxus and pulsus alternans can be measured with a BP cuff: paradoxus = gap between the cuff pressure where Korotkoff sounds appear only in expiration and where they are heard throughout (>10 mmHg); alternans = only alternate phase I sounds heard as the cuff is lowered.

DocT GT: For AF >48 h or of unknown duration, anticoagulate 3 weeks before cardioversion (or TEE to exclude LA thrombus) and at least 4 weeks after, whatever the CHA2DS2-VASc, because atrial stunning keeps clot risk high after sinus rhythm returns; long-term need then follows the stroke-risk score.

DocT Recall25: Any tachyarrhythmia with instability (hypotension, shock, chest pain, acute heart failure) gets immediate synchronised cardioversion, AF included (AHA 2025: ≥200 J biphasic for AF). Rate-control drugs (diltiazem, metoprolol) are for stable patients; digoxin is too slow.
DocT GT: Overall, trauma is the commonest cause of subarachnoid blood; a ruptured saccular aneurysm causes ~80% of NON-traumatic SAH and so is the second commonest overall.

DocT GT: Endoscopy in the fulminant colitis behind toxic megacolon shows extensive, deep, friable, bleeding ulceration. Full colonoscopy is relatively contraindicated (perforation risk): at most a limited unprepped flexible sigmoidoscopy with minimal insufflation; diagnose on plain film or CT (colon >6 cm).

DocT GT: In ulcerative colitis, toxic megacolon (transverse colon >6 cm with lost haustra) complicates ~5% of severe attacks, triggered by hypokalaemia, opioids and anticholinergics; about half settle medically, the rest need urgent colectomy. Free perforation carries ~15% mortality (DocT key), and steroids can mask peritoneal signs.

DocT GT: Level and zero the EVD transducer at the tragus (external auditory meatus), the surface marker for the foramen of Monro: this is the card's 'midbrain' level. Mentum, mastoid or angle of mandible give false ICP readings; a drip chamber set too low over-drains CSF (subdural haematoma, slit ventricles).

cross: DocT GT keys PESI class IV for a 70-year-old man with chronic lung disease, HR 118 and SpO2 <90%. Truth: 70 + male 10 + lung disease 10 + pulse 20 + SpO2 20 = 130 = class V (>125); class IV is reached only by omitting the male +10. If class V is offered, pick it; otherwise pick IV.

lines: DocT GT: Acoustic impedance (Z = tissue density × speed of sound) is a medium's resistance to sound propagation; reflection at an interface depends on the impedance mismatch (air–tissue is huge, hence gel, and lung and bowel gas block the beam). Attenuation is energy lost with depth; higher frequency means more attenuation and less penetration.

DocT GT: Bleeding is the commonest ECMO complication (cannula and surgical sites; ICH the most feared), from heparin, acquired von Willebrand loss from pump shear, and platelet consumption and dysfunction. Haemolysis, circuit thrombosis and limb ischaemia are less common; air embolism and oxygenator rupture are rare.

DocT GT: Pregnancy is hypercoagulable: fibrinogen RISES (to about 4–6 g/L), as do factors VII, VIII, X and vWF, while protein S falls. That is why a 'normal' fibrinogen of 2 g/L in PPH predicts severe bleeding.

DocT GT: The INICC multidimensional VAP bundle adds daily readiness-to-extubate assessment, cuff pressure kept at about 20–30 cmH2O, head-up 30–45°, oral care, hand hygiene and surveillance feedback. Routine prophylactic systemic broad-spectrum antibiotics are NOT part of any VAP bundle: they select resistance and have no mortality benefit.

cross: DocT GT keys 'oral voriconazole is preferred in renal dysfunction' as the INCORRECT statement. Truth: it is correct (the IV SBECD cyclodextrin vehicle accumulates, as the card says); the false statements are voriconazole as first line for mucormycosis (amphotericin B is; voriconazole has no mucor activity) and voriconazole as fungicidal for Candida (it is fungistatic). If asked, pick the mucor option as the incorrect one.

DocT GT keys PAR as '30 per 1,000 per year' (incidence total − incidence non-exposed, an absolute difference). Truth: Park (the card) defines PAR as that difference ÷ incidence total = 30/50 = 60%. If the options are rates pick 30/1,000; if percentages pick 60%.

lines: DocT GT: Amniotic fluid embolism runs in two phases: pulmonary vasospasm with acute RV failure (collapse, hypoxia), then LV failure with consumptive DIC. Care is supportive; A-OK (atropine, ondansetron, ketorolac) is an unproven adjunct, fetal squames in pulmonary blood are not diagnostic, and thrombolysis is not indicated.

DocT GT: LOW clinical probability (<15% by gestalt) plus all 8 PERC criteria negative (age <50, HR <100, SpO2 ≥95%, no haemoptysis, no oestrogen, no prior VTE, no unilateral leg swelling, no surgery or trauma within 4 weeks) rules PE out with no D-dimer and no imaging. PERC is not for intermediate/high probability or inpatients.

DocT GT: Early AIDP can look almost normal on distal conduction: the first signs are proximal (absent or prolonged F-waves = root involvement) and 'sural sparing' (abnormal median/ulnar sensory responses with a normal sural SNAP). That pattern is typical of acquired demyelination and the opposite of length-dependent axonal neuropathy such as CIP.

DocT GT: Before URGENT CABG stop clopidogrel or ticagrelor ≥24 h (ACC/AHA class I) to cut bleeding; for elective CABG ≥3 days ticagrelor, ≥5 days clopidogrel, ≥7 days prasugrel. Aspirin is continued; the irreversible/long-acting P2Y12 blocker is the drug to stop first.

DocT GT: The short-acting GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors eptifibatide and tirofiban (reversible, renally cleared) need stopping only 2–4 h before urgent CABG because platelet function recovers within hours; abciximab binds irreversibly and needs ≥12 h.

DocT GT: ELSO (Maastricht) nomenclature: drainage cannula letter before the dash, return after (V-V, V-A, V-P, V-AV), with lowercase cannula prefixes: (dl) dual-lumen, (ca) cavo-atrial. A single bicaval dual-lumen VV cannula is written (dl)V-V(ca).

DocT GT: A double-lumen VV cannula normally goes in the right internal jugular; when vessels are large enough the LEFT SUBCLAVIAN is the alternative, giving comfortable fixation for ambulation in long bridge-to-transplant runs. Femoral sites stop mobilisation, and an artery is never used for VV.

DocT GT: Medium-chain triglycerides go straight into portal blood with little need for lipase, bile salts, micelles or chylomicrons: the fat of choice in pancreatic insufficiency, cholestatic/cirrhotic malabsorption, short bowel and chylous leaks. Long-chain and omega-6-rich emulsions all need lipase and bile.

DocT GT: In shock too little O2 reaches the mitochondria, the electron transport chain stalls and NADH builds up; lactate dehydrogenase then reduces pyruvate to lactate to regenerate NAD+ so glycolysis can keep making ATP. Lactate is the price of keeping anaerobic glycolysis running, not a product of gluconeogenesis.

DocT GT: Organophosphate severity follows RBC acetylcholinesterase activity: mild 20-50% of normal, moderate 10-20%, severe <10%. Severe poisoning shows coma, flaccid paralysis, pulmonary oedema or bronchorrhoea and pinpoint pupils; plasma butyrylcholinesterase does not track severity.

DocT GT: Leukostasis is a clinical diagnosis - hyperleukocytosis plus hypoxaemia, infiltrates or confusion. It can occur below 50,000/microL in AML, especially monocytic M4/M5 with large sticky blasts, so do not wait for 100,000 to start cytoreduction.

DocT GT: APL blasts over-express annexin II, which binds plasminogen and tPA and drives plasmin generation (hyperfibrinolysis) on top of tissue-factor DIC. ATRA differentiates the promyelocytes and rapidly down-regulates annexin II and tissue factor, so the coagulopathy improves within days - hence ATRA on suspicion.

DocT GT: Survival of ventilated HSCT recipients has improved from near zero to ~40-50% in some cohorts, through earlier ICU admission, HFNO or NIV to avoid intubation, and better treatment of SOS/VOD, GvHD and infection; HSCT status alone, even pre-engraftment, is no reason to refuse ICU care.

DocT GT: Idiopathic pneumonia syndrome is a diagnosis of exclusion: widespread alveolar injury (multilobar infiltrates, symptoms, raised A-a gradient) AND no active lower respiratory infection AND no cardiac, renal or iatrogenic fluid overload - so fluid overload is an exclusion, not a criterion.

DocT GT + DocT Recall25: Heparin resistance on ECMO (ACT or anti-Xa not rising despite escalating heparin, circuit clotting) means low antithrombin: heparin works only through AT, which the circuit consumes. Replace AT (concentrate or FFP) or switch to a direct thrombin inhibitor (bivalirudin preferred on ECMO), which needs no AT; LMWH and rivaroxaban are not circuit anticoagulants.

DocT GT: Haemodynamic criteria for cardiogenic shock (SHOCK trial): SBP <90 mmHg for ≥30 min (or vasopressors needed), cardiac index <2.2 L/min/m² on support (<1.8 without), and PCWP >15 mmHg. The raised wedge separates a pump problem from hypovolaemia; cold extremities and a narrow pulse pressure are supportive, not defining.

cross: DocT GT keys Impella CP as the device that works despite recurrent arrhythmias. Truth: only the IABP needs cardiac synchrony; TandemHeart and VA-ECMO are continuous-flow and equally rhythm-independent (VA-ECMO even supports VF). If only one non-IABP device is offered pick it; here pick Impella as keyed.

lines: DocT GT: Intubating a patient in tamponade can precipitate arrest: positive intrathoracic pressure cuts the venous return that keeps the compressed right heart filling, and induction removes compensating sympathetic tone. Drain first (pericardiocentesis under local anaesthesia, sitting up); if intubation is unavoidable keep spontaneous breathing, use ketamine, low PEEP and VT, with the needle ready.

DocT GT: The card's 'no recommendation for CHG sponge dressing' is the 2011 CDC grade. The 2017 CDC update recommends chlorhexidine-impregnated dressings (sponge or gel, e.g. Biopatch) for short-term non-tunnelled CVCs in adults (category IA), the site intervention with the strongest evidence; povidone-iodine ointment and guidewire exchange do not reduce CRBSI.

fix.t: Use CHG-impregnated dressings for short-term non-tunnelled CVCs in adults | IA (CDC 2017 update); neonates: no recommendation
fix.why: "No recommendation" for chlorhexidine sponge dressings (2011). CDC 2017 recommends them for short-term central lines in adults (category IA).

fix.t: Card says both ">5 days" and ">10 days" for antimicrobial-coated catheters; CDC: consider when expected dwell >5 days.

lines: DocT GT: Pseudomonas VAP with only partial improvement at day 7 → extend beyond 7 days (DocT key). IDSA/ATS 2016 gives 7 days whatever the organism, non-fermenters included (PneumA's extra relapses after 8 days did not change mortality), so prolong only for a slow or incomplete response or a complication (empyema, abscess, bacteraemia). Tigecycline and ceftriaxone do not cover Pseudomonas.
cross: GT4 Q80; GT5 Q35 key: extend beyond 7 days for Pseudomonas VAP. Truth: 7 days is standard for every organism; the extension is justified only by the partial response in the stem. If the stem says partial or slow response, pick extend; if it says good response, pick 7 days.

lines: DocT GT: In pressure support with a large leak (cuff leak, bronchopleural fistula), inspiratory flow never falls to the flow-cycling threshold (e.g. 25% of peak), so the breath ends only on the backup maximum inspiratory time (~1–3 s). Fix the leak, raise the expiratory trigger %, or switch to time-cycled pressure control.

DocT GT: SSC likelihood labels: definite/probable = sepsis is the most likely explanation; POSSIBLE = sepsis is plausible but an alternative diagnosis is at least as likely (e.g. pyelonephritis vs pancreatitis); unlikely = another diagnosis clearly explains the picture.

DocT GT: The classic transplant cause of PRES is a calcineurin inhibitor (cyclosporine or tacrolimus): seizures, hypertension, cortical blindness and parieto-occipital vasogenic oedema on MRI. Withdraw or reduce the CNI (switch agent) and control BP aggressively; it is usually reversible.

DocT GT: In an EMS system with low intubation success or little training, a supraglottic airway is the preferred advanced airway in OHCA: faster placement with fewer compression pauses. Endotracheal intubation is for systems with high success rates or frequent practice.

DocT GT: The main limitation of bag-valve-mask ventilation is gastric insufflation: pharyngeal pressure above ~20 cmH2O opens the lower oesophageal sphincter, risking regurgitation, aspiration and a splinted diaphragm. Give each breath over 1 s with just visible chest rise (~500–600 mL), two-person technique, adjuncts, early SGA.

cross: DocT GT keys immediate unsynchronised shock for polymorphic VT 'with a pulse'. Truth: defibrillation is for UNSTABLE or pulseless polymorphic VT; stable polymorphic VT is treated by cause (IV magnesium if long QT, ischaemia work-up, amiodarone if QT normal). If instability is stated or implied, pick defibrillation; if stable with long QT, pick magnesium.

lines: DocT GT: Extreme obesity (e.g. 160 kg) and CrCl <30 both make LMWH dosing unpredictable - it accumulates and weight-based doses misfire - so monitor a PEAK anti-Xa ~4 h after a dose (after the 3rd-4th dose; target ~0.6-1.0 IU/mL for 12-hourly dosing). The aPTT does not measure LMWH.

DocT GT: Supine → upright or semi-recumbent (30–60°) raises FRC by up to ~30% as the abdominal contents stop pushing the diaphragm up, reopening dependent atelectasis: the first, least invasive move in an obese post-op patient. PEEP 10 also raises FRC but is the escalation step (and can drop venous return); a larger VT adds volutrauma, and proning is an ARDS tool.

Marrow: High PEEP (or inverse-ratio ventilation, which raises mean airway pressure) raises intrathoracic pressure, cuts venous return and RV preload, and can cause obstructive-type hypotension in a septic or hypovolaemic patient — lowering PEEP (e.g. 15 → 5) restores BP quickly.

DocT: PEEP causes oliguria even after CO is restored: higher renal venous pressure, sympathetic and RAAS activation, more ADH and LESS ANP (atrial stretch falls), and intrarenal redistribution of flow to juxtamedullary nephrons that reabsorb more sodium (options with ADH down/ANP up are backwards).

DocT GT: In a failing, overfilled LV, PEEP/CPAP RAISES stroke volume: lower venous return moves the dilated LV back from the flat part of its Starling curve, and higher pleural pressure lowers LV transmural pressure (afterload falls, not rises). In a normal, preload-dependent heart the same PEEP drops output.

DocT GT: In obesity or abdominal distension a plateau of 38 cmH2O can still be a safe distending pressure: the stiff chest wall raises pleural (oesophageal) pressure, so transpulmonary pressure (Pplat − Ppl) may be below the ~20–25 cmH2O overdistension limit. VILI follows transpulmonary, not airway, pressure.

DocT GT: Arrest adrenaline 1 mg = 10 mL of 1:10,000 (0.1 mg/mL) IV/IO, then flush. 1 mL of 1:1,000 is the same dose but is the concentrated IM anaphylaxis strength (0.5 mL IM); 10 mL of 1:1,000 would be a 10 mg overdose.

DocT GT: Nitric oxide is the main mediator of septic vasodilation: TNF-α and IL-1 induce iNOS → excess NO → guanylate cyclase → cGMP → smooth-muscle relaxation and catecholamine resistance (why methylene blue works). Endothelin-1 and thromboxane A2 are vasoconstrictors; PAI-1 is a procoagulant.

cross: DocT GT keys veno-pulmonary ECMO for massive PE with RV failure and shock. Truth: VA-ECMO is the guideline configuration (ESC 2019, ELSO) because it bypasses both the RV and the obstructed pulmonary bed; VP (oxy-RVAD) returns blood proximal to the clot. If VA is offered, pick VA; pick VP only if VA is absent.

lines: DocT GT: Abrupt hypoxaemia with post-membrane blood as dark as pre-membrane = no gas transfer at all: sweep gas disconnected or cylinder empty, classically after transport. Oxygenator thrombosis is gradual (rising ΔP, post-oxygenator PO2 falling over days), and recirculation makes the DRAINAGE line bright red.

cross: DocT GT keys anidulafungin for lower UTI by Candida auris. Truth: echinocandins reach very low urine levels (the card's rule); for azole-resistant species IDSA/CDC advise amphotericin B deoxycholate (0.3–0.6 mg/kg ± bladder irrigation) or flucytosine. Pick amphotericin if offered; DocT's key reflects CDC's echinocandin-first advice for invasive C. auris.

lines: DocT GT: Hypothermia's main haemostatic hit is on platelets: adhesion and activation fall (about a third less adhesion at 33 °C), with clotting-enzyme slowing mostly below ~33 °C. PT/aPTT are run at 37 °C, so they look normal while the patient oozes; rewarming, not more products, fixes it.

DocT GT: Choose IVIG over plasma exchange when the patient is haemodynamically unstable or septic: PLEX needs a large-bore line, shifts volume and removes albumin, clotting factors and immunoglobulin, so it can worsen hypotension and sepsis, while IVIG (0.4 g/kg/day × 5) is equally effective. PLEX is preferred when the patient is stable and speed matters.

Recall25: For 'commonest CLABSI organism' the exam answer is coagulase-negative staphylococci: skin flora that form biofilm on the catheter (NHSN data). The card's Indian series ranks Enterobacteriaceae (18%) just above CoNS (16%), so pick CoNS unless the stem asks about Indian ICU data.

DocT Recall25: In neutropenia, fever may be the ONLY sign of infection: without neutrophils there is no pus, little redness or swelling and often no infiltrate on CXR. So any fever in a neutropenic patient is an emergency needing empirical antibiotics within 1 hour.

DocT Recall25: Blood cultures come first in febrile neutropenia not to delay treatment (antibiotics still within 1 hour) but so the organism and susceptibilities can guide targeted therapy and de-escalation later.

Recall25: Levetiracetam has replaced phenytoin for early (7-day) post-traumatic seizure prophylaxis because of SAFETY, not efficacy: equal seizure prevention, but no CYP induction or interactions, no level monitoring, no hypotension/arrhythmia, no purple glove. Neither drug prevents late seizures.

DocT Recall25: Postpartum endometritis is a clinical diagnosis and FEVER is the key criterion (>=38 C after the first 24 h, typically with uterine tenderness); foul lochia and leucocytosis are supportive but non-specific, since leucocytosis is normal after delivery.

Recall25: SBP 90 with lactate 3 after trauma = early shock, not extremis: keep resuscitating and repeat the lactate (clearance shows adequacy). Damage-control surgery is for the physiologically exhausted (lethal triad: pH <7.2, core <35 °C, coagulopathy); early total care only once stable with lactate <2.5.

Recall25: ATLS (10th ed.) ties base deficit to shock class: I 0 to −2, II −2 to −6, III −6 to −10, IV −10 or worse mEq/L. The card's mild/moderate/severe bands are a different scheme, so answer class questions with the ATLS bands.

DocT Recall25: Penetrating chest wound + Beck's triad (hypotension, raised JVP, muffled sounds) + clear lungs = traumatic tamponade. Pericardiocentesis is the bedside life-saving step when offered; the definitive treatment in trauma is thoracotomy or sternotomy to repair the injury.

DocT Recall25: Sudden respiratory distress, hypoxaemia and high airway pressures just after inflating a Sengstaken–Blakemore tube = gastric balloon in (or migrated into) the airway: cut and deflate the balloons at once. Hence intubate first and confirm the gastric balloon below the diaphragm on X-ray before full inflation.

cross: Recall25 keys emergency cricothyrotomy after a Cormack–Lehane 4 view and two failed intubations with DIFFICULT (not impossible) mask ventilation. Truth: DAS/OAA Plan B is a second-generation SGA to oxygenate; front-of-neck access only for CICO (SGA and final face mask fail, SpO2 falling). If the stem says ventilation is impossible pick cricothyrotomy; if difficult but possible, pick an SGA.

lines: DocT Recall25: NIV works where positive pressure reverses the problem: COPD hypercapnia, cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, high-risk post-extubation. It fails in ILD/IPF exacerbation (stiff, non-recruitable lungs; failure >70%) and delays intubation in severe hypoxaemia.

DocT Recall25: In neutropenic/immunocompromised respiratory failure, poor baseline performance status (ECOG ≥3) is the best pre-treatment predictor of NIV failure; others are severity score, shock, ARDS, need for RRT and an undetermined cause. With poor predictors use only a time-limited trial and intubate early.

DocT Recall25: Symptomatic bradycardia after ACS/stenting: atropine first, then pacing or dopamine/adrenaline infusion. Caveat: atropine rarely works in Mobitz II or complete block below the node (typical of anterior MI) or in a transplanted heart; go straight to pacing there.

DocT GT: NIV is a trial option only in mild ARDS without contraindications; with P/F below ~150, refractory hypoxaemia or shock it often fails and delays intubation (LUNG SAFE: NIV at P/F <150 had higher ICU mortality). DocT's 'mild ARDS, P/F 200' is technically moderate by Berlin (mild 201–300).

DocT GT: A mainly bilirubin/ALP (cholestatic) rise points to rifampicin; isoniazid and pyrazinamide give a hepatocellular ALT rise. Stop the drugs when bilirubin exceeds 2× normal (jaundice) as well as on the card's ALT rules; a fluoroquinolone stands in for rifampicin if it cannot be reintroduced.
cross: GT6 Q34 key: option D, garbled ('…should not be substituted by Q'), as the false statement. Truth: a fluoroquinolone is the standard substitute when rifampicin cannot be reintroduced, so D read as 'never substitute a quinolone' is false. If an option says a quinolone must never replace rifampicin, pick it as the false one.

lines: DocT GT: Surugadai (Tokyo) ECPR criteria exclude a presumed non-cardiac cause, ROSC within 10 min of arrival, core temperature <30 °C and pregnancy; a core temperature of 30–35 °C is NOT an exclusion (hypothermia is a favourable reversible cause).

DocT GT: AV block complicates 10–25% of acute MIs and is usually transient, mostly first-degree or Mobitz I. Inferior MI gives AV-nodal block with a narrow escape that usually resolves; anterior MI gives infranodal block with a wide escape that needs pacing.
cross: DocT GT keys 'Mobitz I, benign, will resolve' for a block after ANTERIOR MI, contradicting its own explanation. Truth: block after anterior MI is infranodal (LAD, His–Purkinje), does not respond to atropine and needs pacing. Pick the infranodal/pacing option.
DocT GT keys 'AV block develops transiently in acute MI', but 'inferior MI most commonly produces 1st and 2nd degree block' is also true. If both appear, pick the transient-block statement as keyed.

lines: DocT GT: TandemHeart is contraindicated in VSD (LA decompression reverses the shunt right-to-left → hypoxaemia), isolated RV failure (an LA-to-artery device cannot fill), severe peripheral vascular disease, LA thrombus and moderate–severe AR; LV failure/cardiogenic shock is its indication.

DocT GT: The commonest mechanism of β-lactam resistance in Gram-negatives is β-lactamase hydrolysis (ESBL, AmpC, carbapenemases); porin loss and efflux-pump up-regulation are add-ons. Altered PBPs are the Gram-positive mechanism, and MRSA's PBP2a has LOW, not increased, β-lactam affinity.

fix.t: Class C: AmpC cephalosporinases (not ESBLs; not inhibited by clavulanate/tazobactam).
fix.why: Says "Class C: AmpC beta-lactamases (ESBL)". AmpC is not an ESBL.

lines: DocT GT: Unstable Mobitz II (infranodal) → transcutaneous pacing at once as the bridge to transvenous pacing. Atropine acts on the AV node, rarely helps infranodal block (it can worsen the conduction ratio) and must not delay pacing; dobutamine is not the rescue.

DocT GT: Intubate GBS on the TREND, before CO2 rises: VC falling toward 20 mL/kg (20/30/40 rule: VC <20 mL/kg, MIP weaker than −30, MEP <40 cmH2O; DocT keys 22 mL/kg with rising work of breathing) or bulbar weakness. A normal PaCO2 is falsely reassuring, and BiPAP is avoided (bulbar weakness, aspiration, relentless progression).

DocT GT: Granulomatous hypercalcaemia (sarcoid, TB, lymphoma: low PTH, high 1,25-vitamin D from macrophage 1-alpha-hydroxylase) is treated with glucocorticoids (prednisolone 20-40 mg/day), which suppress that enzyme; fluids and a bisphosphonate are for severe levels, ketoconazole or hydroxychloroquine are steroid-sparing.

cross: DocT GT keys SBP <140 before the aneurysm is secured. Truth: AHA 2012 and NCS give <160 (the card); AHA 2023 gives no number, only control with short-acting agents; <140 comes from ICH-derived protocols. If only one is offered pick it; if both, DocT wants 140, guideline-based banks 160.

lines: DocT GT: ALF with abdominal pain, tender hepatomegaly and ascites in a myeloproliferative neoplasm (PV, ET; test JAK2) = Budd–Chiari syndrome from hepatic-vein or IVC thrombosis. Doppler ultrasound confirms it; anticoagulate, then angioplasty/TIPS, transplant if fulminant (ALF-32).

DocT GT: Short-course TXA (<72 h, before securing) does cut REBLEEDING in aSAH, which is why it is keyed for 'reduces rebleeding'; ULTRA showed no better functional outcome, so routine antifibrinolytics are not recommended (AHA 2023). Magnesium, fludrocortisone and an EVD do not prevent rebleeding (an EVD can provoke it).

cross: DocT GT keys raising MAP to >80 mmHg in a comatose post-arrest patient already at MAP 65. Truth: ERC-ESICM 2021 and AHA 2025 target MAP ≥65; BOX (2022) found no difference between MAP 63 and 77. If the stem is DocT's, pick >80; on any guideline-framed question, keep ≥65.

lines: Marrow: Start co-trimoxazole PCP prophylaxis in HIV when CD4 <200 cells/µL (or with oropharyngeal candidiasis); stop once CD4 stays >200 for 3 months on ART.

Marrow: In local-anaesthetic arrest run standard ACLS first, then 20% lipid emulsion (1.5 mL/kg bolus, 0.25 mL/kg/min, max ~12 mL/kg); use smaller adrenaline doses (≤1 µg/kg); propofol is no substitute for lipid, and waiting for ECMO must not delay either.

Marrow: A raised but NON-pulsatile JVP with a negative abdominojugular reflux = SVC obstruction (e.g. lung cancer): the jugular column no longer communicates with the right atrium, so it does not reflect RA pressure.

Marrow: At catheterisation, constriction shows equalised diastolic pressures in all four chambers (within ~5 mmHg), a dip-and-plateau ('square root') RV trace, Kussmaul's sign and DIScordant RV/LV systolic pressures with respiration (concordant in restriction).

DocT GT: AHA 2025: routine electrical pacing is NOT recommended in established cardiac arrest (asystole or PEA), whatever the timing, because it does not improve ROSC or survival. Pacing belongs to bradycardia WITH a pulse: transcutaneous, then transvenous if refractory.

DocT Recall25: Weaning order: FiO2 first, down to ≤0.4–0.5 (oxygen toxicity, absorption atelectasis) keeping SpO2 92–96%; then PEEP in 2 cmH2O steps to 5–8; then pressure support and rate; then screen (RSBI) and SBT.

DocT GT: Norepinephrine raises MAP but HR often falls slightly despite its β1 action: the rise in pressure fires the baroreflex, and vagal slowing of the SA node outweighs its modest β1 chronotropy. Adrenaline (β1 + β2 vasodilation) raises HR; pure α1 phenylephrine causes marked reflex bradycardia.

Marrow: Septate hyphae branching at acute (~45°) angles in lung and brain = Aspergillus; the host defect to name is profound neutropenia (ANC <500) or chronic granulomatous disease (failed phagocyte oxidative burst). HIV itself is only intermediate risk.

Marrow: Acinetobacter in VAP, even early-onset with no local MDR, is treated empirically with a carbapenem (meropenem); third-generation cephalosporins and fluoroquinolones are unreliable, and daptomycin is inactivated by surfactant, so it never treats pneumonia.
Marrow: Adult intussusception is different: a pathological lead point (often a tumour, frequently malignant in the colon) in ~90%, so treatment is operative resection, not enema reduction.

Marrow: Chronic hepatitis E (HEV RNA >3 months, genotype 3) occurs in solid-organ transplant recipients and can progress to cirrhosis: first reduce immunosuppression (clears ~30%), then ribavirin for 3 months. Diagnose by HEV RNA PCR, because antibodies are unreliable under immunosuppression.

DocT GT: Ascites is the commonest decompensating event (~50% of compensated cirrhotics within 10 years), and cirrhosis causes ~80–85% of all ascites. Its onset marks decompensation: about 15–20% die within 1 year and ~44% within 5 years.

DocT GT: CT predictors of poor TBI outcome: brainstem (pontine/midbrain) haemorrhage, worst with thalamic extension; compressed or absent basal cisterns, midline shift >5 mm, traumatic SAH and IVH (Marshall/Rotterdam); clinically fixed pupils, low motor score, age, hypoxia and hypotension (IMPACT).

Marrow: Exercise-associated hyponatraemia (marathon) with symptoms: 100 mL 3% saline over 10 min, repeat up to twice if no improvement; acute hyponatraemia tolerates rapid correction and fluid restriction is too slow.
Marrow: Prolonged high FiO2 generates reactive oxygen species → diffuse alveolar damage (oxygen toxicity), so titrate FiO2 to the SpO2 target rather than leaving patients on 100%.
cross: Marrow keys oxygen toxicity for day-4 bilateral opacities in a rib-fracture patient on 100% O2. Truth: pneumonia or ARDS from contusion is at least as likely. Pick oxygen toxicity only if the stem stresses days of FiO2 1.0.

lines: DocT GT (×2): Bedside clues that favour ICH over infarct: headache, vomiting, early fall in consciousness, very high BP and progression over minutes–hours (haematoma expansion, raised ICP). Hemiparesis, sudden onset and field defects occur in both, so only CT separates them.

Recall25: Vasopressor choice in pregnancy depends on the setting: spinal hypotension at caesarean → phenylephrine (less fetal acidosis than ephedrine; norepinephrine boluses if bradycardic); shock (septic, or haemorrhagic after volume) → norepinephrine first, as outside pregnancy (the card's 'as in any patient').
cross: Recall25 keys phenylephrine as 'the vasopressor of choice in pregnancy' with no setting given. Truth: phenylephrine is right for spinal hypotension at caesarean (2018 international consensus); norepinephrine is first line for shock in a pregnant ICU patient. Answer phenylephrine to the bare question; pick norepinephrine if the stem describes septic shock.

lines: Recall25: Cold storage uses University of Wisconsin solution: 'intracellular' electrolytes (high K+ ~125, low Na+ ~30 mmol/L) to stop Na/K-pump losses; lactobionate and raffinose as impermeants against cell swelling, hydroxyethyl starch as colloid; PHOSPHATE is the buffer (not bicarbonate); glutathione, adenosine and allopurinol against oxidant injury and for ATP regeneration.

fix.t: bacterial meningitis dexamethasone (0.15 mg/kg 6-hourly for 4 days)
fix.why: WATCH note repeats the 5-day dexamethasone error from CNS-26.

fix.t: TB meningitis continuation phase given as "HRZ for 10 months"; WHO/NTEP continue HRE (pyrazinamide stops after the intensive phase). Dexamethasone taper is usually 6–8 weeks, not 8–12.

fix.why: Calls GCS 13–14 "mild", leaving GCS 15 without a band (mild is 13–15).

ABG01.topic: The capnogram: phases and abnormal patterns
ABG01.q: Name the phases of the normal time capnogram and the pattern each abnormality gives.
a: Phase I: inspiratory baseline and the first dead-space gas, CO2 near zero (on a volumetric capnogram its volume is the anatomical dead space).
Phase II: steep expiratory upstroke as dead-space gas mixes with alveolar gas.
Phase III: alveolar plateau, near flat, uniform alveolar gas - EtCO2 is read at its END (normally 3-5 mmHg below PaCO2).
Phase 0 or IV: inspiratory downstroke as fresh gas enters.

Patterns: up-sloping shark-fin phase III = bronchospasm, COPD or airway obstruction (EtCO2 does not fall); gradual fall in EtCO2 = less CO2 delivered (low cardiac output, haemorrhage, PE) or gas lost or diluted (cuff or circuit leak, hyperventilation); raised baseline = rebreathing; cleft = patient effort; sudden zero = disconnection, oesophageal tube or arrest.

ABG01.topic: Oxygenation index: formula, worked example, cut-offs
ABG01.q: Mean airway pressure 18, FiO2 0.6, PaO2 45 - what is the oxygenation index and what does it mean?
a: OI = (mean airway pressure x FiO2 x 100) / PaO2.
Higher is worse, because it charges for the pressure and oxygen used to achieve the PaO2 - unlike P/F, which ignores both.
Neonates: OI above 25 prompts inhaled nitric oxide, above 40 ECMO.
PARDS severity by OI: 4-8 mild, 8-16 moderate, 16 or more severe.

ABG01.q: Mainstream vs sidestream capnograph - what does each gain and lose?
a: Mainstream: the infrared sensor sits on the airway adapter - NO transit delay (a true real-time trace) and no sampling line to block.
Its cost: added dead space and weight at the tube, and a fragile, expensive sensor.
Sidestream: pumps ~50-200 mL/min down a fine line to a remote analyser - a few seconds' delay, the line blocks with water or secretions, and it under-reads EtCO2 at very small tidal volumes.
Its gain: light, no added dead space, and usable on non-intubated patients through a nasal cannula.
Exam trap: 'adds no airway dead space' describes SIDESTREAM, not mainstream.

ABG02.q: Three acid–base approaches — Boston, Copenhagen, Stewart?
a: Boston (physiological): HCO3 and PaCO2 via Henderson–Hasselbalch, with compensation rules and the anion gap.
Copenhagen: standard base excess quantifies the metabolic component independent of PaCO2.
Stewart (physicochemical): pH set by PaCO2, strong ion difference (~40) and total weak acids (albumin, phosphate); HCO3 is dependent; electroneutrality and mass conservation.
They agree in most patients; Stewart explains saline acidosis (low SID) and hypoalbuminaemic alkalosis.

ABG02.q: IV sodium bicarbonate — dose, harms, and when to stop?
a: Dose ≈ 0.3 × weight (kg) × base deficit (mEq); give half, then reassess.
Harms: hypernatraemia and HYPERosmolality (not hypo-osmolar hyponatraemia), volume load, CO2 generation (intracellular/CSF acidosis if ventilation is fixed), hypokalaemia, low ionised calcium.
Stop once pH >7.2; SSC uses it only for pH ≤7.2 with AKI.

ABG02.q: In the Stewart approach, how does a raised PaCO2 cause acidaemia?
a: pH is set by three independent variables: PaCO2, the strong ion difference (strong cations minus strong anions, normally about 40) and Atot (albumin and phosphate).
CO2 is not a strong ion, so it does not change the SID; more CO2 drives water dissociation, so hydrogen ion concentration rises and pH falls.
Bicarbonate rises only as a DEPENDENT variable - it is an effect, not a cause.
Metabolic disorders are SID or Atot changes: low SID from hyperchloraemia or lactate (acidosis), low albumin (alkalosis).
The exam trap is the option saying CO2 lowers the SID.

ABG02.q: Which conditions LOWER the anion gap?
a: Hypoalbuminaemia - the commonest, since albumin is the main unmeasured anion (add 2.5 to the gap per 1 g/dL below 4).
Unmeasured CATIONS: lithium, and severe hypercalcaemia or hypermagnesaemia.
Halide overload: bromide and iodide, which are read as chloride by the analyser.
IgG myeloma (cationic paraprotein); also laboratory error with a very high triglyceride.
Iron does NOT lower it - iron poisoning raises the gap through lactic acidosis.

BS01A.q: Descriptive vs inferential statistics: what does each do?
a: Descriptive: summarise the data you HAVE (mean/median, SD/IQR, proportions, tables, graphs); no conclusions beyond the sample.
Inferential: draw conclusions about the POPULATION (p-values, CIs, hypothesis tests, regression).
A p-value or CI is never descriptive: it is an inference about people you did not measure.

BS01A.q: Why report an effect size alongside the p-value?
a: Effect size = HOW BIG the effect is (mean difference, RR/OR, ARR/NNT, Cohen's d): clinical importance.
The p-value only says whether chance is unlikely and shrinks with sample size: a huge trial makes a trivial effect 'significant'.
Report effect size + 95% CI (CONSORT).

BS01B.q: Survival analysis: what does it handle, and what are its tools?
a: Analyses TIME-TO-EVENT data and handles CENSORING (lost to follow-up or event-free at study end).
Kaplan-Meier: survival probability over time (step curve; median survival where it crosses 0.5).
Log-rank test: compares two or more KM curves.
Cox proportional hazards regression: adjusts for covariates; output = HAZARD RATIO.

BS01B.q: Heteroscedasticity = non-constant ____ of residuals across a predictor's range.
a: Variance: the scatter 'fans out' (variability rises with the value); opposite = homoscedasticity.
Constant variance is an assumption of linear regression, t-test and ANOVA.
It makes SEs and p-values unreliable; fix with log transform, robust SEs or weighted regression.

CCM02.q: CAUTI: what counts, what is essential in treatment, and what NOT to do?
a: CAUTI (IDSA) = symptoms/signs with no other source + ≥10^3 CFU/mL of ≥1 organism in catheter urine; the 10^5 cut-off is for non-catheterised patients and asymptomatic bacteriuria (not treated).
Catheter in >2 weeks → replace (or remove) BEFORE antibiotics and culture from the new catheter: antibiotics cannot sterilise the biofilm; never culture from the bag.
Duration: 7 days if prompt response, 10–14 days if delayed.
Prevent: insert only when indicated, aseptic insertion, closed drainage, bag below bladder, daily review, early removal.
Don't: routine fixed-interval catheter change (e.g. every 72 h), bladder irrigation, antimicrobial prophylaxis, screening for bacteriuria.

CCM02.q: Pseudomonas vs Enterococcus faecalis endocarditis: regimen and duration?
a: Pseudomonas (IVDU): two active classes even if susceptible: high-dose anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam (cefepime 2 g 8-hourly) + aminoglycoside (tobramycin 8 mg/kg/day), ≥6 weeks.
Why: high inoculum, slow killing, resistance on monotherapy; left-sided → early surgery, tricuspid often medical.
E. faecalis: ampicillin + gentamicin 4 weeks native, 6 weeks prosthetic or symptoms >3 months.
Ampicillin + ceftriaxone 6 weeks preferred if HLAR or renal risk (ESC 2023); vancomycin + gentamicin only for beta-lactam allergy.

CCM02.q: When is an indwelling urinary catheter appropriate in ICU?
a: Acute retention/outlet obstruction; accurate hourly output in the critically ill; selected surgery (perioperative, epidural).
Healing sacral/perineal wounds in incontinence; prolonged immobilisation (unstable spine, pelvic fracture); end-of-life comfort.
NOT for incontinence alone, nursing convenience or a urine sample.
CAUTI risk rises ~3–7% per catheter-day: review daily, remove early.

CCM02.q: Deep sternal wound infection (mediastinitis) after cardiac surgery: organisms, risk and treatment?
a: Staphylococci dominate: S. aureus (MSSA and MRSA) and coagulase-negative staphylococci; Gram-negatives less often.
Risk: diabetes, obesity, bilateral IMA grafts, COPD, re-exploration, prolonged ventilation.
CT: retrosternal fluid/gas; treat with surgical debridement ± negative-pressure dressing + vancomycin-based cover until cultures return.

CCM02.topic: Central vein stenosis after central lines
CCM02.q: Dialysis patient: whole-arm and face swelling, pulsatile aneurysmal fistula, previous ipsilateral central line?
a: Central vein stenosis (subclavian/brachiocephalic) from the earlier catheter.
High fistula flow cannot drain: venous hypertension, collaterals, oedema, prolonged bleeding after needling.
Fistulogram/venography → angioplasty ± stent.
Prevent: avoid subclavian lines in CKD (internal jugular preferred).

CCM03.q: ICU infection by source: primary endogenous vs secondary endogenous vs exogenous, and what drives colonisation?
a: Primary endogenous: organism carried on admission (community or hospital flora) → infection usually within ~4 days

Secondary endogenous: NOT carried on admission; acquired in the ICU, colonises throat/gut first (surveillance swab turns positive), then infects, typically after day 4–5; the commonest late ICU infection
Exogenous: organism introduced straight from the environment or a device without prior colonisation
Systemic broad-spectrum antibiotics are the strongest driver of oropharyngeal colonisation with AGNB/S. aureus (they kill protective commensal flora)
SDD targets primary and secondary endogenous; hand hygiene and isolation target secondary endogenous and exogenous
VAC: ≥2 days stable or improving, then ≥2 days of worsening oxygenation (PEEP up ≥3 cmH2O or FiO2 up ≥0.20).
IVAC: VAC + temperature >38 or <36 °C or WBC ≥12,000/≤4,000, AND a new antimicrobial continued ≥4 days.
PVAP: IVAC + purulent secretions and/or positive respiratory microbiology.
No chest X-ray in VAE (unlike CPIS): objective surveillance, not a bedside diagnosis.

CCM06.q: Vancomycin-resistant enterococcus: VanA vs VanB vs VanC, and the drug for VRE bacteraemia?
a: VanA: high-level vancomycin (MIC ≥64) AND teicoplanin resistance; transferable; mostly E. faecium
VanB: variable vancomycin resistance, teicoplanin SUSCEPTIBLE, transferable; VanC: intrinsic low-level (E. gallinarum/casseliflavus)
VRE faecium bacteraemia: high-dose daptomycin 8–12 mg/kg/day (bactericidal) ± ampicillin or ceftaroline; weekly CK (myopathy), and useless in pneumonia (surfactant inactivates it)
Linezolid 600 mg BD alternative (bacteriostatic; thrombocytopenia after ~2 weeks, serotonin syndrome)
Tigecycline: low serum levels, not for bacteraemia; ampicillin works for E. faecalis, not usually E. faecium

CCM06.q: Vancomycin flushing vs levofloxacin hypotension: what each is and how to prevent it?
a: Vancomycin infusion reaction ('red man'): direct, non-IgE mast-cell histamine release (MRGPRX2), rate-related, with flushing and itch of face/neck/trunk ± hypotension
Vancomycin: stop the infusion, give an antihistamine, restart slower (≥60 min per 1 g, ≤10 mg/min); not an allergy
Levofloxacin IV: infuse over 60–90 min to avoid hypotension
Fluoroquinolones also: QT prolongation, tendon rupture, myasthenia flare, dysglycaemia

CCM08.q: Cryptococcal meningitis (HIV or transplant): induction, consolidation, maintenance and the pressure rule?
a: Induction: liposomal AmB 3–4 mg/kg/day + flucytosine 25 mg/kg QID for ≥2 weeks (WHO 2022: single L-AmB 10 mg/kg + 14 days flucytosine + fluconazole)
Why combination: faster CSF sterilisation and lower mortality; fluconazole or AmB alone fails in induction
Consolidation fluconazole 400–800 mg/day for 8 weeks; maintenance 200 mg/day for ≥1 year
Opening pressure ≥25 cmH2O → daily therapeutic LP; no acetazolamide, mannitol or steroids
HIV: delay ART 4–6 weeks (COAT: early ART raised mortality); transplant: reduce immunosuppression stepwise

CCM08.q: ADEM vs anti-NMDAR encephalitis: who, clue, test, treatment?
a: ADEM: children, 1–4 weeks after infection or vaccine; monophasic multifocal demyelination with encephalopathy; large bilateral T2 white-matter ± thalamic lesions; sterile CSF
ADEM: high-dose IV methylprednisolone → IVIG or plasma exchange only if refractory (vs MS: no encephalopathy, oligoclonal bands, relapsing)
Anti-NMDAR: young women; psychiatric prodrome → seizures, orofacial dyskinesia, autonomic instability, hypoventilation; lymphocytic CSF, MRI often normal; CSF antibody diagnostic
Anti-NMDAR next step: look for ovarian teratoma (pelvic US/MRI) → resection + steroids with IVIG or PLEX, then rituximab/cyclophosphamide
Haloperidol is a trap in anti-NMDAR: these patients are prone to NMS

CCM08.q: Fever, encephalitis and asymmetric flaccid paralysis with lymphocytic CSF after mosquito bites: diagnosis and treatment?
a: West Nile virus: flavivirus, Culex mosquito vector, birds the reservoir
Neuroinvasive disease: meningoencephalitis + polio-like acute flaccid paralysis (anterior horn cells)
Diagnose with IgM in CSF/serum; confirm by plaque-reduction neutralisation test, because IgM cross-reacts with other flaviviruses (dengue, JE)
Treatment is supportive only; IVIG and interferon are unproven
vs GBS: asymmetric, purely motor and axonal (low CMAPs, normal sensory studies); CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis vs GBS albuminocytological dissociation

CCM08.q: Meningococcal disease: the adrenal/coagulation complications and who gets chemoprophylaxis?
a: Waterhouse–Friderichsen: adrenal haemorrhage in meningococcaemia → shock with hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia → hydrocortisone
DIC with purpura fulminans (skin necrosis, limb ischaemia) is the associated coagulopathy
Chemoprophylaxis for close contacts within 24 h: household, roommates, kissing/oral-secretion exposure, staff who intubated or suctioned without a mask
Ciprofloxacin 500 mg once, rifampicin 600 mg BD × 2 days, or ceftriaxone 250 mg IM once (pregnancy: ceftriaxone; rifampicin avoided)

CCM08.topic: Ring-enhancing lesions: toxoplasma vs CNS lymphoma
CCM08.q: Multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions in an immunosuppressed patient: toxoplasma vs primary CNS lymphoma (vs Nocardia)?
a: Toxoplasma: multiple basal-ganglia/corticomedullary lesions, CD4 <100 or long-term high-dose steroids, toxoplasma IgG positive
Treat: pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + leucovorin (protects the marrow) for 6 weeks; TMP-SMX alternative
PCNSL: often single, periventricular; EBV DNA in CSF; thallium SPECT/PET 'hot'
Nocardia: brain abscess + lung lesion in steroid users → TMP-SMX
No improvement after 10–14 days of anti-toxoplasma therapy → biopsy

CCM08.q: WHO criteria for SEVERE falciparum malaria in adults (any one)?
a: Clinical: impaired consciousness/coma, prostration, ≥2 convulsions in 24 h, shock (SBP <80 with poor perfusion), pulmonary oedema/ARDS, significant bleeding, jaundice
Lab: glucose <40 mg/dL (2.2 mmol/L), acidosis (HCO3 <15 or lactate ≥5), Hb ≤7 g/dL, creatinine >3 mg/dL
Lab: bilirubin >3 mg/dL with parasitaemia >100,000/µL; parasitaemia >10%
Any one → IV artesunate 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12, 24 h, then daily
Thrombocytopenia and fever are NOT criteria

CCM08.topic: Orbital cellulitis vs septic cavernous sinus thrombosis
CCM08.q: Orbital cellulitis vs septic cavernous sinus thrombosis: clue, organism, treatment?
a: Orbital (post-septal) cellulitis: proptosis, painful/limited eye movement ± reduced vision, from ethmoid/frontal sinusitis
Orbital: S. aureus (incl. MRSA), streptococci → vancomycin + ceftriaxone (+ metronidazole if intracranial or dental spread); CT orbit, drain any abscess
Cavernous sinus thrombosis: facial 'danger triangle' furuncle or sinusitis → ptosis, proptosis, CN III, IV, VI, V1/V2 palsies, spreading to the other eye
Cavernous sinus: S. aureus ~70% → vancomycin + ceftriaxone + metronidazole ± anticoagulation; contrast CT/MR venography
Preseptal cellulitis: normal eye movements, no proptosis

CCM08.q: Fulminant 'bacterial-looking' meningitis days after swimming in warm fresh water: organism, test and treatment?
a: Naegleria fowleri: enters through the cribriform plate along the olfactory nerve
CSF looks bacterial (neutrophils, high protein, low glucose) but the Gram stain is negative
Fresh, warm (never refrigerated) CSF wet mount shows motile trophozoites, easily mistaken for leucocytes; PCR confirms
Miltefosine + amphotericin B (± azole, rifampicin, azithromycin) with aggressive ICP control; mortality >95%

CCM08.topic: Malaria species on the blood film
CCM08.q: P. falciparum vs P. vivax/ovale on the blood film and clinically?
a: Falciparum: rings predominate, multiply infected normal-sized RBCs, double chromatin dots, banana-shaped gametocytes, often high parasitaemia → severe malaria
Vivax/ovale: enlarged RBCs with Schüffner dots (ovale: oval, fimbriated), all stages seen, low parasitaemia
Vivax/ovale: 48-h (tertian) cycle and liver hypnozoites → relapse, so add primaquine after a G6PD check; chloroquine-sensitive (vivax resistance in parts of Asia/Oceania)
Thick film detects, thin film speciates (CNS-36)

CCM09.q: Painless black eschar with marked oedema after livestock, hides or soil exposure: diagnosis and treatment?
a: Cutaneous anthrax (Bacillus anthracis): ulcer → black eschar, disproportionate non-pitting oedema, vesicles, no pus
Localised: oral ciprofloxacin or doxycycline 7–10 days (60 days if aerosol exposure)
Systemic/extensive: IV ciprofloxacin + clindamycin or linezolid (stops toxin), + meropenem if meningitis possible, + antitoxin
Do not incise; ecthyma gangrenosum = Pseudomonas in neutropenia

CCM09.q: Vesiculopustular rash with systemic toxicity: smallpox vs varicella vs mpox?
a: Smallpox: centrifugal (face, limbs, palms/soles), all lesions at the SAME stage, deep firm pustules
Smallpox → airborne + contact isolation, notify, tecovirimat, ring vaccination within 3–4 days; vaccinia immune globulin treats vaccine complications, not smallpox
Varicella: centripetal (trunk), crops at DIFFERENT stages → IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg 8-hourly for pneumonitis
Mpox: lymphadenopathy, genital/perianal lesions → supportive; tecovirimat if severe

CCM09.q: Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) in an HIV-positive patient: diagnosis and treatment?
a: Fever, weight loss, massive splenomegaly, pancytopenia; LD bodies on splenic (most sensitive) or marrow aspirate; rK39 less sensitive in HIV
HIV co-infection (WHO 2022, South Asia): L-AmB 5 mg/kg on days 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 + miltefosine 100 mg/day × 14 days
Immunocompetent Indian VL: single-dose L-AmB 10 mg/kg
Antimonials: toxic, >60% resistance in Bihar, avoided in HIV; give ART and secondary prophylaxis (relapse is common)

CCM10.q: Returned traveller with fever, bleeding and shock (Ebola, Lassa, CCHF, yellow fever): priorities and the specific clues?
a: Strict isolation and PPE first: spread by blood and body fluids

Aggressive supportive care: Ebola is mainly a GI illness (diarrhoea and vomiting 5–10 L/day), so crystalloid, K+ correction, vasopressors, RRT and blood products cut mortality; exclude and treat malaria in parallel
Ebola Zaire → monoclonal antibodies (PALM: mortality ~34% vs ~50%); encephalopathy, high viral load, AKI and shock predict death (bleeding is late and uncommon); Lassa/CCHF → ribavirin
Yellow fever (Africa/S. America): Faget sign (fever with relative bradycardia) + jaundice + bleeding; supportive only, no antiviral
Interferon and convalescent plasma do not work

CVS03.q: Chronic HF by LVEF — which drugs improve prognosis, and which only relieve symptoms?
a: Classes: HFrEF ≤40% · HFmrEF 41–49% · HFpEF ≥50% (plus structural/diastolic abnormality or raised natriuretic peptides).

HFrEF: four pillars started together, before discharge once stable after a decompensation — ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan beat enalapril in PARADIGM-HF) or ACEi/ARB, β-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor; each cuts death and HF admission.
HFpEF/HFmrEF: SGLT2 inhibitor is the class I outcome drug (EMPEROR-Preserved, DELIVER); treat BP, AF and comorbidities.
Loop diuretics relieve congestion in every class but do not change survival.
No mortality benefit: digoxin (fewer admissions only), nitrates; IV inotropes (milrinone) raise mortality.
Slide — move across the skin; sweep — slide a long distance (track a vessel).
ROCK (heel–toe) — tilt along the long axis with the contact point fixed.
Fan/tilt — angle across the short axis, contact fixed.
Rotate — turn on the spot (PLAX → PSAX); compress — press (vein compressibility).

Probe choice: linear 5–15 MHz for superficial work (pleura, vascular access, ONSD, airway); curvilinear 2–5 MHz for abdomen, FAST and lung bases; phased array 1–5 MHz between ribs (heart, TCD). Higher frequency = better resolution, less depth.

CVS05B.q: Shock on POCUS (RUSH: pump, tank, pipes) — which type?
a: Pump: poor LV contraction with dilated chambers → cardiogenic; hyperdynamic LV → hypovolaemic or distributive.
Tank: small IVC (<1.5 cm) collapsing >50% with 'kissing' papillary muscles → hypovolaemic (VTI rise >10–15% on PLR confirms responsiveness).
Plethoric IVC + a cause → obstructive: effusion with RA/RV diastolic collapse (tamponade), RV > LV with D-shaped septum (PE), absent sliding (tension pneumothorax).
Plethoric IVC + poor LV + bilateral B-lines → cardiogenic; normal/small IVC + hyperdynamic LV → early sepsis.
Pipes: aortic aneurysm/dissection flap and leg-vein compression complete the scan.

CVS05B.q: When is TEE the right tool — and when is it not?
a: TEE: prosthetic and native valve detail, LA/LAA thrombus before cardioversion, aortic dissection, endocarditis (vegetation, abscess), guiding valvuloplasty, LAA occlusion and ASD/PFO closure, intra-operative monitoring.
Pericardiocentesis is guided by TTE (subcostal/apical) — TEE sees the anterior pericardial space poorly.
TEE is semi-invasive (sedation, oesophageal injury); TTE comes first in most ICU questions.

In shock, the transgastric mid-papillary short-axis view gives LV size, systolic function and wall motion in all three coronary territories in one look; mid-oesophageal views give valves and chambers, upper-oesophageal views the great vessels.

CVS05B.q: AR severity cut-offs and normal prosthetic-valve Doppler?
a: AR vena contracta <0.3 mild / 0.3–0.6 moderate / >0.6 cm severe.
AR regurgitant volume <30 / 30–59 / ≥60 mL; pressure half-time >500 / 200–500 / <200 ms.
Normal prosthetic aortic valve: peak velocity ≤3 m/s, mean gradient ≤20 mmHg.
Normal prosthetic mitral valve: peak velocity <1.9 m/s, mean gradient ≤5 mmHg.

CVS06A.q: Determinants of myocardial O2 demand — and why does dobutamine cause ischaemia in CAD?
a: Heart rate (most important: more beats AND a shorter diastole for coronary filling), contractility and wall tension.
Laplace: wall stress = P × r / 2h — rises with pressure and radius, falls with wall thickness (the logic of compensatory hypertrophy).
Dobutamine raises HR and contractility → demand outruns a fixed supply → ST depression.
Reducing preload/radius lowers demand; anaemia lowers supply, not demand.

CVS07A.q: Pittsburgh Cardiac Arrest Category (PCAC) after ROSC — the four levels?
a: I: awake, follows commands.
II: comatose, mild cardiopulmonary dysfunction.
III: comatose with moderate–severe cardiopulmonary failure (SOFA cardiovascular + respiratory ≥4).
IV: comatose with loss of brainstem reflexes.
Survival falls step-wise (~80% → 60% → 40% → <10%), so it stratifies outcome at ICU entry.

CVS08B.q: Irregular pulse; ECG shows early, wide (>120 ms), bizarre QRS with no preceding P wave — diagnosis and ICU approach?
a: Ventricular premature beats: premature wide QRS, T wave opposite the QRS, full compensatory pause.
PACs differ: premature abnormal P wave, narrow QRS, incomplete pause.
ICU causes: low K/Mg, ischaemia, hypoxia, catheter/wire irritation, inotropes — treat the cause, not the beats; couplets or R-on-T in ischaemia warn of VT/VF.

CVS08B.q: Elderly patient on no drugs: sinus bradycardia with pauses — cause, what to exclude, and fix?
a: Sick sinus syndrome: idiopathic degenerative fibrosis of the SA node is the commonest cause in the elderly; may coexist with AV-nodal disease and AF (tachy–brady).
Exclude reversible causes first: β-blocker, CCB, digoxin, hypothyroidism, hyperkalaemia, hypothermia, raised ICP.
Symptomatic → permanent pacemaker; atropine or transcutaneous pacing only as a bridge if unstable.
Unipolar: tip electrode is the cathode and the can is the anode, so the circuit spans the chest wall → large spike, more myopotential/EMI oversensing and pocket muscle stimulation.
Bipolar: tip + ring electrode ~10 mm proximal → small local circuit, less oversensing; the standard today (so 'unipolar is better' is false).
One lead per paced chamber; RA lead usually in or near the appendage.

CVS08C.topic: Echo at the CPR pulse check
CVS08C.q: Focused echo at a CPR pulse check — what does each finding mean, and true vs pseudo-PEA?
a: Effusion with RV diastolic collapse = tamponade → pericardiocentesis during CPR.
Dilated RV with a D-shaped LV = massive PE → lysis; small hyperdynamic 'kissing' ventricles = hypovolaemia → volume or blood.
No cardiac motion = true PEA (CPR + adrenaline; poor prognosis); coordinated motion without a pulse = pseudo-PEA — profound shock where fluids/vasopressor may restore a pulse, better survival.

AHA 2025: POCUS may be used by experienced operators to find a reversible cause only if it does not lengthen pauses (subxiphoid or TEE views, <10 s); not routine, not a replacement for pulse checks and not a sole reason to stop. CTPA, MRI or CXR mean leaving the resuscitation.

CVS08C.q: Drowning — the insult, the first resuscitation step, and why observe the 'well' patient?
a: The insult is hypoxia: 5 rescue breaths, then CPR (ERC); no Heimlich; fresh vs salt water does not change management.
Post-hypoxic cerebral oedema builds over hours and peaks at 24–72 h, so an alert patient can deteriorate later.
Observe at least 6–8 h; ARDS can also appear late.
Pulseless after long submersion: start CPR if submerged <60 min (cold water protects the brain); hypothermic → continue CPR with active rewarming (ECLS if available) — 'not dead until warm and dead'.

CVS08C.q: How do you confirm a perioperative reaction was anaphylaxis?
a: Serum mast-cell tryptase 15 min–3 h after onset (peak 1–2 h), plus a baseline >24 h later.
A rise above 1.2 × baseline + 2 ng/mL confirms mast-cell activation; a normal value does not exclude anaphylaxis (asthma does not raise it).
Refer for skin testing at 4–6 weeks (NMBAs, cefazolin, chlorhexidine, latex).

CVS08C.q: Anaphylaxis — first drug, dose, route and site?
a: IM adrenaline 0.5 mg (0.5 mL of 1 mg/mL; child 0.01 mg/kg) into the anterolateral thigh (vastus lateralis): faster, higher peak than deltoid or SC; repeat every 5 min.
Refractory after 2 IM doses → IV adrenaline infusion; on β-blockers add glucagon.
Antihistamine and steroid are adjuncts that never replace adrenaline; confirm with tryptase at 1–2 h.

CVS09.q: Minimum anticoagulant stop times before neuraxial or spinal-drain placement (ASRA 2018)?
a: Aspirin alone: no hold; clopidogrel 5–7 days.
Enoxaparin prophylactic 12 h, therapeutic 24 h; IV UFH 4–6 h with a normal aPTT.
Apixaban, rivaroxaban: 72 h.
Dabigatran: 120 h (5 days) by default (72 h only if CrCl >80 and no other risk) — the longest hold.

CVS10A.q: Chest pain relieved by nitroglycerin, normal ECG, negative troponin — what does the nitrate response tell you?
a: Nothing diagnostic: nitrates relax smooth muscle, so they relieve both myocardial ischaemia and oesophageal spasm (NTG response does not predict ACS in ED studies).
One normal ECG + one negative troponin excludes MI, not unstable angina → repeat hs-troponin at 1–3 h and risk-stratify (HEART score).
Oesophageal spasm clues: dysphagia, relation to swallowing or hot/cold liquids; confirm by manometry.

CVS10B.q: Wellens vs de Winter — two STEMI-equivalent patterns of the proximal LAD?
a: Wellens: deep symmetric or biphasic T waves in V2–V3 with isoelectric or <1 mm ST, preserved R waves and no Q waves, usually recorded pain-free → critical proximal LAD stenosis: angiography, avoid stress testing.
de Winter: 1–3 mm UPsloping ST depression at the J point in V1–V6 with tall symmetric T waves and ~1 mm ST elevation in aVR → acute proximal LAD occlusion = STEMI equivalent → primary PCI.
ST elevation in aVR is not a Wellens feature.

CVS10E.q: Hypotension with back/flank pain hours after femoral-access PCI, no visible groin haematoma?
a: Retroperitoneal haematoma: high puncture above the inguinal ligament; women, obesity, anticoagulation.
Diagnose with CT abdomen/pelvis; resuscitate, stop/reverse anticoagulation.
Covered stent or embolisation (or surgery) if ongoing bleeding.
Pneumonitis (Mendelson): sterile acidic gastric contents, witnessed event in reduced consciousness (seizure, overdose, induction)
Pneumonitis: hypoxaemia and infiltrates within hours, often resolves in 24–48 h; no antibiotics unless it fails to resolve

Pneumonia: colonised oropharyngeal secretions in elderly/dysphagic patients (stroke, dementia, nursing home) → antibiotics; supine aspiration hits the posterior upper-lobe and superior (apical) lower-lobe segments, upright aspiration the basal segments, right more than left
High BAL amylase marks aspirated oropharyngeal secretions (early pneumonia within 48–72 h of intubation)

ACE inhibitors REDUCE aspiration pneumonia (more substance P and bradykinin → stronger cough and swallow reflexes, notably after stroke); procalcitonin helps separate bacterial pneumonia from chemical pneumonitis
Upper-lobe lobar consolidation with a BULGING fissure (voluminous exudate).
Early cavitation and abscess formation; empyema common.
Typical host: alcoholic or diabetic; 'currant-jelly' sputum.

D04A.q: Sore throat or recent mononucleosis, then sepsis, a tender 'cord' in the neck and septic lung emboli: diagnosis and work-up?
a: Lemierre syndrome: Fusobacterium necrophorum septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein
Septic emboli → multiple cavitating lung nodules, empyema, septic arthritis
Contrast CT neck + chest is the test of choice (ultrasound misses fresh thrombus; MRV more sensitive)
Treat: β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor or carbapenem (or metronidazole + ceftriaxone) for 3–6 weeks, drain collections; anticoagulation is debated

D04B.q: First-line anti-TB drugs: which are bactericidal, which bacteriostatic, and which is most potent?
a: Isoniazid: greatest early bactericidal activity (kills rapidly dividing bacilli); pyridoxine prevents neuropathy
Rifampicin: bactericidal and the key sterilising drug (semi-dormant bacilli), which is why 6-month regimens work
Pyrazinamide: bactericidal in acid intracellular/caseous sites (first 2 months); streptomycin and amikacin are bactericidal
Ethambutol: bacteriostatic at therapeutic doses (bactericidal only at doses that cause optic neuritis); added to prevent resistance

D04B.topic: TB respiratory failure in the ICU
D04B.q: TB causing acute respiratory failure in the ICU: forms and prognostic markers?
a: Forms: miliary TB, extensive TB pneumonia (consolidation), TB-ARDS
Poor prognosis: dense bilateral non-cavitary consolidation (diagnosis delayed), ARDS/MV, multi-organ failure, low albumin, lymphopenia, delayed ATT
Mortality on mechanical ventilation ~50–70%
Send sputum/BAL GeneXpert and start ATT early; do not wait for cultures

D04B.q: Receptor and protease for SARS-CoV-2 cell entry, and why it matters?
a: Spike protein binds ACE-2 on type II pneumocytes, endothelium, gut and kidney; host TMPRSS2 primes the spike
Endothelial ACE-2 infection explains COVID endotheliitis and microthrombosis
DPP-4 is the MERS-CoV receptor; CD4 is HIV's

D05A.q: Transplant recipient on tacrolimus with confusion, tremor, AKI, hyperkalaemia and a normal-anion-gap acidosis: diagnosis and checks?
a: Calcineurin-inhibitor toxicity: neurotoxicity (tremor, confusion, seizures, PRES) + afferent-arteriole nephrotoxicity
Type 4 RTA picture: hyperkalaemia + hyperchloraemic acidosis; also hypertension, hypomagnesaemia, new-onset diabetes (tacrolimus), TMA
CYP3A4: diltiazem, azoles, macrolides, grapefruit raise levels; rifampicin, phenytoin lower them

Check the trough, hold or reduce the dose, exclude PRES and infection; persistent nephrotoxicity → switch to or add an mTOR inhibitor (sirolimus/everolimus) to minimise the CNI (tacrolimus is also a CNI)
They do NOT cause adrenal insufficiency (that is steroid withdrawal)

D05A.q: Transplant rejection: hyperacute vs acute cellular vs antibody-mediated vs chronic?
a: Hyperacute: minutes–hours; preformed anti-donor antibody + complement → graft thrombosis (cyanotic, mottled, anuric kidney); no rescue, remove graft
Acute cellular: T cells, weeks–months (most in the first year); lung = dyspnoea, fever, falling FEV1, GGO, perivascular infiltrates
Acute cellular treatment: pulse IV methylprednisolone 10–15 mg/kg (0.5–1 g) × 3 days → oral taper; exclude infection on BAL first
Antibody-mediated: donor-specific antibodies, C4d+ → plasma exchange, IVIG, rituximab
Chronic: months–years, fibrosis/vasculopathy (lung: CLAD/bronchiolitis obliterans)

D05A.q: HIV patient worsens 2–12 weeks after starting ART with a known infection (e.g. TB) flaring: name it and manage it.
a: IRIS: the recovering CD4 response attacks pathogen antigens (paradoxical = treated infection flares; unmasking = hidden infection appears)
Risk: CD4 <50–100 at start, high viral load, ART started soon after OI treatment
Manage: continue ART and anti-infectives; moderate–severe TB-IRIS → prednisone 1.5 mg/kg/day × 2 weeks then 0.75 mg/kg × 2 weeks
Timing: ART within 2 weeks of TB therapy if CD4 <50, otherwise by 8 weeks; delay 4–6 weeks in cryptococcal/TB meningitis

D05A.q: Branching, beaded, weakly acid-fast Gram-positive rod in a steroid, transplant or CGD patient: organism and treatment?
a: Nocardia: lung nodules or cavities, brain abscess (image the brain in every pulmonary case), skin
CGD = catalase-positive organisms (S. aureus, Nocardia, B. cepacia, Serratia, Aspergillus)
TMP-SMX (15 mg/kg/day TMP); add imipenem ± amikacin if severe or CNS
Duration 6 months, ≥12 months if immunosuppressed or CNS
Actinomyces differs: anaerobic, not acid-fast, penicillin

D05A.topic: Primary graft dysfunction after lung transplant
D05A.q: Hypoxaemia with bilateral infiltrates within 72 h of lung transplant: diagnosis, risks and treatment?
a: Primary graft dysfunction: ischaemia–reperfusion injury graded by P/F + infiltrates at 0–72 h (grade 3: P/F <200); main cause of early death
Exclude hyperacute rejection, infection, pulmonary venous anastomotic obstruction, volume overload
Risks: recipient pulmonary hypertension (strongest), IPF/sarcoid, BMI >25–30; donor smoking/aspiration; bypass, long ischaemic time, big transfusion
Treat: lung-protective ventilation, restrictive fluids, inhaled NO; ECMO for refractory grade 3

D05A.q: Lung transplant complications by time after surgery?
a: First 72 h: PGD, hyperacute rejection, PULMONARY VEIN anastomotic stenosis/thrombosis (unilateral oedema)
Pulmonary vein problem → TOE: vein diameter <0.5 cm or flow velocity >1 m/s
Weeks–months: acute cellular rejection, opportunistic infection (CMV, fungi, PJP), BRONCHIAL anastomotic stenosis or dehiscence
After 6–12 months: chronic rejection (CLAD/bronchiolitis obliterans); so a decline at 3 months is least likely pulmonary vein stenosis
Up to 90% excreted unchanged in urine, so AKI causes accumulation
High-dose MTX: hydrate and alkalinise the urine; glucarpidase if levels stay high with AKI
Leucovorin (folinic acid) rescues marrow and mucosa if started within 24–36 h; it does not prevent hypersensitivity pneumonitis
Also hepatotoxicity (to cirrhosis), mucositis, myelosuppression, erythematous rash in ~15%
Eye: cataract, glaucoma; gut: ulcers, synergistic with NSAIDs; immunosuppression is dose-dependent
Psychiatric effects in ~6%, dose the main risk; steroid psychosis → reduce the dose promptly (not a slow taper) ± antipsychotic
HPA suppression unlikely <5 mg/day prednisolone; likely >20 mg/day for ≥3 weeks
Also hyperglycaemia, myopathy, poor wound healing, osteoporosis

D05A.q: Patient on oral ART must stay nil by mouth with no enteral route: what happens to the ART?
a: Stop ALL antiretrovirals together and restart them together once enteral access allows
Why: dolutegravir, tenofovir and emtricitabine have no IV form, and partial continuation breeds resistance
Any enteral route (NG/NJ) → crushed or liquid forms instead of stopping
NNRTI regimens (efavirenz, nevirapine) have a long tail → staggered stop under boosted-PI cover
Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis by CD4 (<200) is not a substitute for ART

D05B.q: Mucormycosis in the ICU: who gets it, how it looks, and the three-part treatment?
a: Hosts: DKA/uncontrolled diabetes (acidosis frees iron), neutropenia, steroids, transplant, deferoxamine, breakthrough on voriconazole
Clues: black palatal/nasal eschar, proptosis, cavernous-sinus spread; pulmonary or cutaneous forms; broad aseptate ribbon-like hyphae with right-angle branching; angioinvasion → necrosis
Treat (1): urgent radical debridement, repeated as needed
Treat (2): liposomal AmB 5–10 mg/kg/day; isavuconazole or posaconazole as alternative or step-down. Treat (3): reverse the host defect (correct DKA, cut steroids)
Voriconazole, fluconazole and echinocandins have no activity; galactomannan and β-D-glucan are negative

D05B.q: Candida >10^5 CFU/mL in the urine of a catheterised ICU patient without symptoms: what to do?
a: Usually colonisation: no antifungal; remove or replace the catheter (clears ~40%)
Treat asymptomatic candiduria only if neutropenic, a very-low-birth-weight infant, or before urological manipulation
Candiduria with sepsis → blood cultures; treat as invasive candidiasis if candidaemic
Symptomatic C. glabrata cystitis: often fluconazole-resistant → AmB deoxycholate or flucytosine; echinocandins barely reach urine

Fungus ball in the renal pelvis = significant infection at any colony count: remove/replace the catheter, relieve obstruction and remove the ball (nephrostomy/endoscopic) + fluconazole ± amphotericin irrigation via nephrostomy

D05C.q: Neutropenic patient with fever, RLQ pain and caecal/colonic wall thickening ± pneumatosis on CT: diagnosis and management?
a: Neutropenic enterocolitis: mucosal injury + neutropenia lets gut flora (Gram-negatives incl. Pseudomonas, anaerobes such as C. septicum, Candida) invade the wall
Bowel rest, NG decompression, G-CSF; send C. difficile testing early (it mimics typhlitis)
Antipseudomonal β-lactam with anaerobic cover: piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem (penicillin allergy: cefepime or aztreonam + metronidazole)
Add antifungal if fever persists; vancomycin only for standard FN indications (IC-57)
Surgery only for perforation, uncontrolled bleeding or deterioration; wall >10 mm = higher mortality

D05C.q: CMV after solid-organ transplant: prophylaxis vs pre-emptive therapy vs treating disease?
a: Prophylaxis: valganciclovir 900 mg/day for 3–6 months in high-risk D+/R− (letermovir an alternative in kidney D+/R−)
Pre-emptive: weekly CMV PCR for ~12 weeks; treat when viraemia crosses the local threshold, before symptoms
Established disease (fever, cytopenias, hepatitis + high viral load): IV ganciclovir 5 mg/kg BD (valganciclovir 900 mg BD if mild), reduce immunosuppression
Treat ≥2 weeks and until PCR is negative

D05C.q: CD4 <50, painless visual loss and floaters; fundus shows haemorrhage over white necrotic retina ('pizza pie'). Diagnosis and treatment?
a: CMV retinitis: commonest HIV retinitis; brushfire necrosis along vessels with haemorrhage, minimal vitritis
PORN (VZV): rapid, multifocal outer retina, little haemorrhage; Toxoplasma: focal 'headlight in fog' with dense vitritis
Valganciclovir 900 mg BD × 21 days (or IV ganciclovir) ± intravitreal ganciclovir if sight-threatening
Maintain until CD4 >100 for 3–6 months on ART

ECMO01.q: Why was ECMO developed, and from what?
a: It grew out of cardiopulmonary bypass (Gibbon, 1953), which was safe only for short intra-operative runs.
Membrane oxygenators (1960s) cut blood trauma and allowed days of support; first successful prolonged ECMO: Hill, 1972.
Aim: prolonged extracorporeal gas exchange beyond what CPB allows — not renal perfusion.

ELEC01A.topic: Renal salt-water hormones: angiotensin II vs ANP, and the three triggers of renin
ELEC01A.q: What does angiotensin II do to the kidney that ANP and BNP undo - and what actually releases renin?
a: Renin release has three triggers: low afferent arteriolar pressure (baroreceptor), LOW NaCl delivery to the macula densa (not low oxygen), and beta-1 sympathetic stimulation.
Renin cleaves angiotensinogen to angiotensin I; ACE in the lung endothelium (not renin) makes angiotensin II.
Angiotensin II: constricts efferent more than afferent so GFR is preserved while medullary flow falls; raises proximal NHE3 exchange, aldosterone, thirst and ADH - sodium and water retained.
ANP and BNP: natriuresis and diuresis, afferent dilation (GFR up), suppression of renin, aldosterone and ADH - circulating sodium and water fall.
Aldosterone: distal sodium reabsorption in exchange for potassium and hydrogen ions.

ELEC01A.topic: Intrarenal dopamine: the local natriuretic system
ELEC01A.q: A salt load increases sodium excretion with unchanged renal perfusion - which local mechanism?
a: Intrarenal dopamine, made in the proximal tubule from filtered L-DOPA and increased by a salt load.
It inhibits Na-K-ATPase and NHE3 in the proximal tubule and collecting duct, giving natriuresis without a change in perfusion.
It does NOT raise aldosterone (that would retain sodium).
PGE2 inhibits, not stimulates, NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb.
Endothelin opposes ADH-driven water reabsorption.

ELEC02.topic: Hypothermia and potassium: shift in, rebound out
ELEC02.q: Why does potassium fall during cooling (CPB, TTM), and what is the trap on rewarming?
a: Cold drives K into cells (Na/K-ATPase, catecholamines, alkalosis), and cold diuresis adds urinary loss - hypokalaemia with U waves during cooling.
On rewarming K shifts back out, giving rebound hyperkalaemia.
So replace cautiously during cooling (target ~3.5-4 mmol/L) and stop replacement before or at rewarming.
Check K hourly through the transition.

ELEC03A.topic: Cinacalcet in secondary and tertiary hyperparathyroidism
ELEC03A.q: What is the main adverse effect of a calcimimetic in a dialysis patient?
a: Cinacalcet is a calcimimetic: it sensitises the parathyroid calcium-sensing receptor, so PTH and calcium both fall.
The main adverse effect is HYPOCALCAEMIA, which prolongs the QT and can cause arrhythmia - check calcium before and during treatment.
Also nausea, vomiting and anorexia (dose-limiting), and hypophosphataemia.

Used for secondary hyperparathyroidism on dialysis and for parathyroid carcinoma or tertiary disease when surgery is not possible. Parathyroidectomy is for disease refractory to medical therapy, persistent hypercalcaemia or HYPERphosphataemia, calciphylaxis, or tertiary disease after transplant - hypophosphataemia is not an indication.
Contrast with a vitamin D analogue, which raises calcium and phosphate.

ELEC04.topic: Which electrolyte disorders cause encephalopathy - and the one that does not
ELEC04.q: Which electrolyte derangement is least likely to cause encephalopathy?
a: They do: hyponatraemia and hypernatraemia, hypercalcaemia (lethargy to coma), hypocalcaemia and hypomagnesaemia (tetany, seizures), severe hypophosphataemia (<1 mg/dL), hypoglycaemia and hyperglycaemia.
It does not: HYPERKALAEMIA - peaked T waves, weakness and ascending paralysis with a CLEAR sensorium.
Why: the blood-brain barrier and astrocyte potassium uptake buffer the brain against plasma potassium.
Hyponatraemia is the commonest electrolyte cause of encephalopathy in hospital.

ENDO01A.topic: Non-thyroidal illness (sick euthyroid): mechanism, pattern, what to do
ENDO01A.q: A septic or post-operative patient has a low T3 with a normal or low TSH - what is happening, and what do you do?
a: Cytokines, cortisol and fasting cut type 1 and 2 deiodinase (less T4 to T3) and raise type 3 (more reverse T3), so T3 falls first.
Hypothalamic TRH falls, so TSH is normal or low: an acquired, transient CENTRAL hypothyroidism (dopamine and steroids suppress TSH further).
Low T3 alone = mild illness; low T4 with low TSH = severe (total T4 <4 microgram/dL carries about 50% mortality).
In recovery TSH can overshoot to 10-20 mIU/L - this is not primary hypothyroidism.
Do not screen TFTs or give thyroxine: treat the illness, feed the patient, recheck 4-6 weeks after recovery; treat only clear primary disease (TSH >20 with low free T4).

ENDO01A.q: Autoimmune thyroiditis with subacute confusion, seizures and stroke-like episodes - what is it, and how is it treated?
a: Steroid-responsive encephalopathy with autoimmune thyroiditis: high anti-TPO, usually EUTHYROID.
Subacute confusion, seizures, myoclonus, stroke-like episodes, headache or visual change.
CSF protein high, EEG diffusely slow, MRI often non-specific; a diagnosis of exclusion.
High-dose steroids (methylprednisolone 1 g/day for 3-5 days, then taper) - the response is the confirmation.
IVIG or plasma exchange if refractory.

ENDO01B.topic: Phaeochromocytoma: clue, confirmation, and the blockade order
ENDO01B.q: Paroxysmal headache, palpitations and sweating with surging blood pressure - how do you confirm it and prepare the patient?
a: Paroxysmal headache, palpitations and sweating with episodic severe hypertension; crises are triggered by surgery, tumour handling, steroids, metoclopramide, beta-blockers and contrast. In pregnancy the episodic pattern with normal labs separates it from pre-eclampsia.
Confirm with plasma free (fractionated) metanephrines, sensitivity 96-100% - COMT converts catecholamines continuously, so they stay high between bursts; 24-h urine metanephrines are the alternative.

Image only after biochemistry (>3-4x upper limit is near-diagnostic); MRI in pregnancy (no MIBG or CT). Untreated in pregnancy, maternal and fetal mortality approaches 40-50% (crises at labour or anaesthesia), so remove the tumour laparoscopically in the second trimester or at caesarean section.
Alpha-blockade FIRST: phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin for 10-14 days with liberal salt and fluid; IV phentolamine 1-5 mg (or nitroprusside, nicardipine, clevidipine) for a crisis.
Beta-blocker only AFTER alpha-blockade, and never labetalol first (beta:alpha about 7:1 leaves alpha unopposed). After removal expect hypotension and hypoglycaemia.

ENDO01B.topic: The adrenal gland: what each zone makes, and how cortisol acts
ENDO01B.q: Which zone makes what, and by what mechanism does cortisol act?
a: Zona glomerulosa: aldosterone, driven by angiotensin II and potassium - which is why it is SPARED in secondary adrenal insufficiency.
Zona fasciculata: cortisol (ACTH-driven). Zona reticularis: androgens. GFR = salt, sugar, sex.
Medulla: adrenaline and noradrenaline (chromaffin cells, sympathetic ganglion origin).
Cortisol binds a cytoplasmic receptor; the complex enters the nucleus and alters gene transcription - hence the delay of hours.
About 90% is bound to CBG and albumin; only free cortisol is active.

ENDO01B.topic: The cortisol axis in critical illness: what rises and what falls
ENDO01B.q: In prolonged critical illness, why is cortisol high while ACTH is low?
a: Early: CRH, ACTH and cortisol all rise.
After a few days ACTH falls while cortisol stays high - the ACTH-cortisol dissociation.
Drivers: paracrine and cytokine (IL-6) stimulation of the adrenal cortex, plus slower cortisol breakdown as hepatic and renal enzymes are suppressed.
CBG FALLS (cleaved by neutrophil elastase, synthesis reduced), so free cortisol rises further and a total cortisol underestimates activity.
Consequence: a single total cortisol cannot diagnose CIRCI in the ICU.

ENDO01B.q: Young patient with resistant hypertension, hypokalaemia, HIGH renin AND high aldosterone, normal metanephrines and a renal mass?
a: Reninoma (juxtaglomerular cell tumour) causing secondary hyperaldosteronism.
Pattern rule: primary aldosteronism = high aldosterone with LOW renin; renovascular disease or reninoma = BOTH high.
Hypokalaemia comes with metabolic ALKALOSIS, not acidosis.
Diagnose with CT (small hypovascular cortical mass), not ultrasound.
Blood pressure is very hard to control until resection; ACE inhibitors or ARBs help most. Alpha-before-beta is a phaeochromocytoma rule, not a reninoma rule.

ENDO01B.q: When does carcinoid syndrome occur without liver metastases, and how is a crisis treated?
a: Mediators (serotonin, histamine, bradykinin, prostaglandins) must reach the systemic circulation - usually only after liver metastases, because the liver inactivates gut-derived amines.
