Exception: bronchial, ovarian and retroperitoneal primaries drain outside the portal system, so they cause the syndrome WITHOUT metastases.
Features: flushing, diarrhoea, bronchospasm, right-sided valve fibrosis (tricuspid regurgitation, pulmonary stenosis).
Crisis (anaesthesia, tumour handling): octreotide 50-100 microgram IV bolus, then 50-100 microgram/h.
Avoid catecholamines and histamine releasers; use vasopressin or phenylephrine for hypotension.

ENDO02A.topic: Hypoglycaemia in a non-diabetic: insulin, C-peptide and the sulfonylurea screen
ENDO02A.q: Glucose 42 with no diabetes - how do insulin, C-peptide and a sulfonylurea screen separate the causes?
a: Exogenous insulin: insulin HIGH, C-peptide LOW or undetectable, sulfonylurea screen negative.
Sulfonylurea: insulin HIGH, C-peptide HIGH, screen POSITIVE.
Insulinoma: insulin HIGH, C-peptide HIGH, screen negative.
Non-islet tumour hypoglycaemia: large mesenchymal tumours secrete big pro-IGF2, so insulin, C-peptide, proinsulin and beta-hydroxybutyrate are all SUPPRESSED, with an IGF2:IGF1 ratio >10.

Draw the critical sample DURING the low (glucose <55): insulin, C-peptide, proinsulin, beta-hydroxybutyrate and a sulfonylurea screen, then treat. It works because C-peptide is cleaved 1:1 from endogenous proinsulin, while injected insulin carries none.

ENDO02A.topic: Oral diabetes drugs: the ICU-relevant facts
ENDO02A.q: Which oral diabetes drugs matter in the ICU, and at what thresholds?
a: Metformin: full dose at eGFR 45 or above, reduce at 30-44, stop below 30 (the old eGFR <60 cut-off is outdated). Hold it in shock, hypoxia or sepsis because of lactic acidosis, and around contrast if eGFR <30 or AKI.
SGLT2 inhibitors: volume depletion, AKI and euglycaemic DKA - stop about 3 days before surgery.
Sulfonylureas: prolonged, recurrent hypoglycaemia; octreotide treats the overdose. They cut microvascular complications, with weak macrovascular benefit (a late UKPDS legacy effect).
GLP-1 agonists and DPP-4 inhibitors: reported pancreatitis; GLP-1 agonists also delay gastric emptying, which matters for aspiration risk.
In the ICU all are stopped and replaced by an IV insulin protocol.

ENDO02B.topic: Intubating severe DKA: why, and the ventilator trap
ENDO02B.q: Severe DKA (pH 7.08) tiring despite maximal breathing - why intubate, and what is the trap?
a: The indication is impending respiratory-muscle fatigue: the huge compensatory minute ventilation is what keeps the pH survivable.
Ventilation does not correct the metabolic acidosis itself.
Trap: a 'normal' ventilator rate lets PaCO2 rise and the pH crash - set a high minute ventilation (RR 25-30+) matching the pre-intubation PaCO2.
Keep apnoea at induction as short as possible; even a minute can drop the pH sharply and precipitate arrest.

EPI01A.q: Propensity score matching: what is it, and what can it not fix?
a: Each patient's PROBABILITY of receiving treatment is modelled from measured baseline variables (logistic regression).
Treated and untreated patients with similar scores are matched, mimicking randomisation and reducing confounding.
Limit: balances only MEASURED confounders; unmeasured confounding remains (only randomisation removes it).

EPI01C.q: ICU teamwork failures: which culture trait or tool is missing?
a: Psychological safety: staff believe they can speak up (e.g. to a senior skipping hand hygiene) without humiliation; without it silence lets latent errors cause harm; strongest predictor of team learning.
Shared mental model: common grasp of goal, patient state, roles and next steps, built by a pre-procedure briefing (plan aloud, roles, what-ifs); a hierarchy or checklist alone does not create it.
Shared team identity: one goal across professions with clear roles and every discipline in planning (daily goals sheet, interprofessional rounds, closed-loop talk).
Alert fatigue: frequent low-value alerts (e.g. AI sepsis warnings) desensitise staff → tune thresholds to the local population, filter, alert only when action is possible.
I-PASS handoff: Illness severity, Patient summary, Action list, Situation awareness/contingency, Synthesis by receiver; cut preventable adverse events ~30%.

EPI01C.q: Reliability vs validity of a measuring tool, and the types of validity?
a: Reliability = CONSISTENCY on repetition (test-retest, kappa, Cronbach's alpha); validity = ACCURACY (measures what it claims).
Reliable but invalid is possible (scale always 2 kg heavy); valid without reliable is not.
Face = looks right; CONTENT = experts confirm all domains covered (e.g. QoL questionnaire).
Construct = behaves as theory predicts; criterion = agrees with a gold standard now (concurrent) or later (predictive).

EPI01C.q: De-identification = removing or masking ____ so participants cannot readily be identified.
a: Direct identifiers (name, address, ID/MRN, phone, exact dates), with indirect ones coded or encrypted.
Pseudonymised/coded data can be re-linked with a separately held key; fully anonymised data cannot be re-linked by anyone.
Renaming variables is not de-identification.

EPI01C.q: The largest source of preventable harm in the ICU is ____.
a: Medication errors: ~78% of serious ICU errors, mostly at prescribing and administration.
Exposure is huge (>140 interventions/patient/day) with high-alert drugs: insulin, opioids, anticoagulants, KCl, vasopressors.
Fixes: pharmacist on rounds, CPOE with decision support, smart pumps, standard concentrations, barcode administration.

EPI01C.q: Hub-and-spoke tele-ICU for a low-intensity ICU: what outcome does the evidence support?
a: High-intensity tele-ICU (remote intensivist allowed to intervene) is linked to lower ICU mortality and shorter ICU/hospital stay.
Benefit is largest where baseline staffing was low-intensity (no night intensivist).
It supports, not replaces, bedside nurses and doctors.
Organised: defined target population invited, set intervals, recall, quality control and assured follow-up = the effective model.
Opportunistic: offered when the patient happens to attend; no invitation or recall, coverage low and unequal = NOT effective (DocT's false statement).
Screening targets apparently healthy people; a positive screen only triggers diagnostic testing.

GI02A.q: Cutaneous haemorrhage signs in acute pancreatitis: names, sites and what they tell you?
a: Grey Turner: flank; Cullen: periumbilical; Fox: upper thigh below the inguinal ligament; Bryant: scrotum
Retroperitoneal blood tracking from haemorrhagic necrotising pancreatitis
Seen in <5% of severe AP: very low sensitivity and NPV, so their absence excludes nothing; their presence signals high mortality
Cullen also occurs in ruptured ectopic pregnancy and other haemoperitoneum

GI02B.q: Fluctuating confusion, agitation and myoclonus on day 5 of severe necrotising pancreatitis: what is it, and what must be excluded?
a: Pancreatic encephalopathy: ~10–20% of severe acute pancreatitis, usually in the first 2 weeks
Mechanism: circulating phospholipase A2/lipase demyelinate, plus cytokines and microcirculatory injury
Exclude Wernicke's (usually later, >2 weeks; alcohol, vomiting, TPN), withdrawal, low Ca/glucose/Na, sepsis, drugs
Treat the pancreatitis and give empirical thiamine

GI03.q: Stable patient, small CONTAINED mid-oesophageal perforation after endoscopy, minimal mediastinal soiling. Initial therapy?
a: Non-operative: covered oesophageal stent (or endoscopic clip), nil by mouth, PPI
Broad-spectrum antibiotics + antifungal, nutrition (jejunal/parenteral), drain any collection
Surgery (primary repair + drainage; diversion or oesophagectomy if non-viable) for uncontained leaks, sepsis or instability
Boerhaave (barogenic, full-thickness, usually distal) is more often surgical
Any full-thickness oesophageal perforation (caustic, instrumental, Boerhaave) → acute POSTERIOR mediastinitis: chest pain, fever, sepsis, mediastinal air; anterior mediastinitis follows sternotomy

GI03.topic: Board-like abdomen: perforated ulcer vs bile peritonitis
GI03.q: Board-like rigid abdomen: perforated peptic ulcer vs bile peritonitis — clue, first test, treatment?
a: Perforated ulcer: sudden severe epigastric pain, shoulder-tip pain (diaphragm, C3–5), ulcer/NSAID history, shock
Erect CXR after 10 min upright shows free gas in ~75–85% (CT if negative) → resuscitate, NG, IV PPI, antibiotics, urgent omental-patch repair
Bile peritonitis: days after cholecystectomy, liver biopsy or trauma; generalised pain, ascites, ileus, rising bilirubin
Confirm by US/CT collection, HIDA leak or bile on aspiration → percutaneous drainage + ERCP stent/sphincterotomy; surgery if generalised peritonitis

GI03.topic: Clostridial gas gangrene of the abdomen
GI03.q: Diabetic with peritonitis, shock, abdominal-wall crepitus and gas in bowel wall, mesentery and soft tissue: organism?
a: Clostridium perfringens: anaerobic, spore-forming Gram-positive rod
Alpha-toxin (lecithinase) → myonecrosis, haemolysis and shock
Immediate radical debridement + penicillin with clindamycin (stops toxin synthesis) ± hyperbaric O2
Gas without myonecrosis in diabetics (emphysematous pyelonephritis/cholecystitis) is usually E. coli/Klebsiella

GI03.q: Where is visceral abdominal pain felt, by embryological gut?
a: Foregut (stomach, duodenum, biliary tree, pancreas) → epigastrium
Midgut (small bowel, appendix, colon to mid-transverse) → periumbilical
Hindgut (distal colon, rectum) → hypogastrium
Visceral pain is dull and midline (bilateral autonomic afferents); parietal pain is sharp and localised, so appendicitis moves from umbilicus to RIF

GI03.q: How does the diaphragm clear peritoneal fluid and bacteria?
a: Expiration: the diaphragm relaxes, stomata on its peritoneal surface open, and fluid and bacteria enter lymphatic lacunae
Inspiration: it contracts and pushes lymph on to the thoracic duct
So peritoneal infection reaches the blood fast, and splinting (IAH, ventilation) slows clearance

GI03.q: Which perforation gives the worst faecal peritonitis, and why?
a: Bacterial load rises down the gut: stomach <10^3/mL (acid), jejunum ~10^4, ileum ~10^7–8, colon ~10^11–12
Colon flora is anaerobe-dominant (Bacteroides ~1000:1 over aerobes)
So distal colonic perforation = heaviest polymicrobial contamination → source control + cover for Gram-negatives and anaerobes
Gastroduodenal perforation is initially chemical peritonitis with a low bacterial load

GI03.q: Two weeks after a Whipple: abdominal pain, hypotension responding to transfusion, free fluid. Next step?
a: Delayed post-pancreatectomy haemorrhage (>24 h): usually a gastroduodenal-artery stump pseudoaneurysm eroded by a pancreatic leak
Often heralded by a 'sentinel bleed' (blood in drain or NG)
Responds to resuscitation → urgent CT angiography and interventional radiology (embolisation or covered stent)
Unstable or IR fails → laparotomy; early (<24 h) haemorrhage goes back to theatre

GI06.topic: Severe alcoholic hepatitis vs Zieve syndrome
GI06.q: Jaundiced alcoholic: severe alcoholic hepatitis vs Zieve syndrome — how to tell, and what to do?
a: Severe alcoholic hepatitis: Maddrey DF ≥32 (or MELD >20) → admit, prednisolone 40 mg/day × 28 days if no infection or GI bleed
Lille score at day 7 >0.45 = non-response → stop steroids; 30-day mortality 30–50%; not for outpatient care
Zieve syndrome: after a binge on fatty liver/hepatitis; Coombs-negative haemolysis (spherocytes, high LDH) + jaundice + marked hypertriglyceridaemia
Zieve treatment is supportive (abstinence, transfusion); settles in 4–6 weeks; no steroids
Acute decompensation (AD): rapid ascites, HE, variceal bleed or infection needing HOSPITAL admission
Non-acute decompensation (NAD): slowly progressive ascites or mild HE NOT needing admission
ACLF: AD plus organ failure(s), high 28-day mortality
Stable decompensated: previous decompensation, now controlled; hospitalisation is the dividing line between AD and NAD

GI06.q: Agitated, tachycardic alcoholic with cirrhosis: initial treatment and drug choice?
a: Alcohol withdrawal → symptom-triggered benzodiazepine (CIWA-Ar)
With liver disease prefer lorazepam (or oxazepam): glucuronidation only, no active metabolites
Diazepam/chlordiazepoxide accumulate (oxidative metabolism, active metabolites) and can precipitate HE
Thiamine before glucose; phenobarbital or dexmedetomidine adjunct for refractory withdrawal

GI07B.q: Cirrhotic with chronic HE; MRI shows bilateral T1-HYPERintense globus pallidus. What is it?
a: Manganese deposition: manganese is cleared in bile, and portosystemic shunting (cirrhosis, TIPS) lets it reach the pallidum
Linked to parkinsonism (acquired hepatocerebral degeneration); regresses after transplant
Wilson disease differs: T2-hyperintense putamen/thalami ('face of the giant panda')

HAEM01.topic: Why a red-cell transfusion may not raise tissue oxygen consumption
HAEM01.q: You transfuse for lactic acidosis at Hb 7 and VO2 does not rise - why?
a: Stored red cells lose 2,3-DPG (near zero by about 2 weeks), so the curve is left-shifted and oxygen is not unloaded until DPG regenerates over 24-72 h.
Other storage lesions: stiffer, less deformable cells and nitric oxide scavenging by free haemoglobin, both impairing microcirculatory flow.
So DO2 rises while VO2 may not change.
Fresher blood did not help (ABLE, RECESS, TRANSFUSE), so there is no case for selecting fresh units.
Transfuse on the threshold (Hb <7 g/dL), not on the lactate.

HAEM01.q: Which findings tell intravascular from extravascular haemolysis?
a: Both: high LDH, high unconjugated bilirubin, high reticulocytes, low haptoglobin.
Intravascular: haemoglobinaemia and HAEMOGLOBINURIA (dipstick positive for blood with no red cells), later haemosiderinuria; schistocytes when it is a MAHA.
Intravascular causes: MAHA (TTP, HUS, DIC, mechanical valves), ABO mismatch, G6PD crisis, PNH, malaria.
Extravascular: spherocytes, splenomegaly, NO haemoglobinuria (warm AIHA, hereditary spherocytosis).

A positive Coombs test means immune, not necessarily extravascular: drug immune-complex haemolysis (ceftriaxone, piperacillin) is DAT-positive and abruptly INTRAVASCULAR - stop the drug, never re-challenge. DAT-negative spherocytes with family history and splenomegaly = hereditary spherocytosis (confirm with EMA binding).

HAEM01.topic: Anaemia of critical illness: what actually reduces transfusion
HAEM01.q: Nearly every ICU patient is anaemic by day 8 - what prevents it, and what does not?
a: Causes: phlebotomy 40-70 mL/day, bleeding, and inflammation (hepcidin traps iron, the EPO response is blunted).
On CRRT add circuit loss: each clotted filter loses about 100-200 mL, which explains an Hb fall over days with no bleeding and a negative haemolysis screen.
What works: fewer and smaller samples (paediatric tubes, point-of-care tests, closed arterial-line conservation systems), returning circuit blood at filter change, better citrate anticoagulation.
Restrictive transfusion at Hb 7 g/dL (TRICC, TRISS); a target above 9 gives no benefit in sepsis.
What does not: EPO (marginal reduction, more thrombosis) and routine IV iron. Marrow suppression and EPO deficiency take weeks, not days.

HAEM01.topic: Malignant SVC syndrome: urgency, collaterals, treatment
HAEM01.q: Lung cancer with facial swelling, dyspnoea and distended neck veins - how urgent, why so severe, and what treatment?
a: Rarely an immediate emergency: emergent only with stridor, laryngeal or cerebral oedema, or haemodynamic compromise.

Severity depends on the azygos: obstruction ABOVE its entry blocks the main collateral, forcing return through small chest-wall and epidural collaterals; rapid onset (SCLC, lymphoma) gives collaterals no time to form.
Get a tissue diagnosis BEFORE chemotherapy or radiotherapy when malignancy is unproven - lymphoma and SCLC respond to chemotherapy.
Endovascular stenting gives the fastest relief (24-72 h) and comes first for severe symptoms; then treat the tumour.
Steroids and diuretics are of unproven benefit (steroids for lymphoma or airway oedema); anticoagulate only if there is thrombus.

HAEM01.topic: Cold antibody haemolysis: PCH vs cold agglutinin disease
HAEM01.q: Cold-triggered haemolysis - paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria or cold agglutinin disease?
a: PCH: IgG Donath-Landsteiner antibody against the P antigen; binds in the cold, fixes complement and lyses on rewarming - INTRAVASCULAR haemolysis with haemoglobinuria.
PCH patient: usually a child after a viral illness; self-limiting.
Cold agglutinin disease: IgM (often anti-I), DAT C3d-positive and IgG-negative, mainly EXTRAVASCULAR (liver) haemolysis with acrocyanosis of fingers and ears in the cold.
CAD patient: older adult with a lymphoproliferative disorder, or after Mycoplasma or EBV.
CAD treatment: keep the patient and all fluids warm, rituximab; steroids do not help.

HAEM02.topic: Antiphospholipid syndrome: diagnosis, mechanism, treatment by scenario
HAEM02.q: How is APS diagnosed, and what anticoagulation does each scenario need?
a: Diagnose: thrombosis or pregnancy morbidity PLUS lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin or anti-beta2-glycoprotein I (IgG/IgM) positive twice at least 12 weeks apart. Anti-dsDNA is SLE, not APS.

Mechanism: antibodies bind beta2-GPI on membranes, activating endothelium, platelets, monocytes and complement - venous, arterial and placental thrombosis, while the lupus anticoagulant prolongs the aPTT in the tube.
Thrombosis: heparin now, then lifelong warfarin INR 2-3 (INR 3-4 adds bleeding, not protection); avoid DOACs if triple-positive or arterial (TRAPS 12% vs 3%).
Recurrence on INR 2-3: check adherence, then switch to therapeutic LMWH, raise the INR to 3-4, or add aspirin - all acceptable.

Pregnancy with recurrent loss: low-dose aspirin plus prophylactic LMWH to 6 weeks postpartum (warfarin is teratogenic). Catastrophic APS (3 or more organs within a week): anticoagulation plus high-dose steroids plus plasma exchange or IVIG.

HAEM02.topic: von Willebrand disease: the type decides DDAVP
HAEM02.q: Mucocutaneous bleeding with suspected von Willebrand disease - which type, which product, which target?
a: Commonest inherited bleeding disorder: lifelong epistaxis, menorrhagia and post-dental or surgical bleeding with a family history.
Type 1 (partial deficiency, ~75%): desmopressin 0.3 microgram/kg releases stored vWF and FVIII - first line.
Type 2B (gain of function - vWF binds platelets spontaneously): DDAVP releases more abnormal vWF and worsens thrombocytopenia - relatively contraindicated.

Type 3 (vWF virtually absent) and DDAVP failures: vWF-containing FVIII concentrate (Humate-P, Wilate) or recombinant vWF (which has no FVIII - add FVIII with the first dose if low); cryoprecipitate if nothing else.
Target vWF:RCo and FVIII:C above 50% for major bleeding; tranexamic acid helps mucosal bleeding in every type.
Acquired vWS in essential thrombocythaemia (platelets >1,000-1,500 x 10^9/L adsorb large multimers): lower the count - urgent platelet apheresis, then hydroxyurea; aspirin worsens it.

HAEM02.topic: Haemophilia, inhibitors and rare factor deficiencies
HAEM02.q: Isolated long aPTT with bleeding - how do mixing studies and the factor level guide treatment?
a: Long aPTT that CORRECTS on mixing in a young man with haemarthrosis = haemophilia A (FVIII) or B (FIX): give the specific concentrate, not FFP.
Targets: joint or muscle bleed 30-40% in older texts (DocT key), 40-60% peak in WFH 2020; life-threatening bleed or major surgery 80-100%. 1 IU/kg FVIII raises the level ~2%, FIX ~1%.

Long aPTT that does NOT correct, with spontaneous muscle haematomas in an older adult (postpartum, autoimmune, cancer) = acquired haemophilia A (anti-FVIII IgG); lupus anticoagulant also fails to correct but clots rather than bleeds.
Inhibitor bleeding: bypassing agents (rFVIIa, aPCC/FEIBA) or recombinant porcine FVIII; eradicate with steroids +/- cyclophosphamide or rituximab.
Factor V deficiency: FFP to FV 20-30% (no concentrate exists); with an FV inhibitor add PLATELETS, whose alpha granules carry ~20% of FV protected from the antibody.
Prothrombin (FII) deficiency with ICH: PCC to FII ~20-40% (DocT: 30%); FFP if PCC is unavailable.

HAEM02.topic: VTE when anticoagulation is not enough, or not possible
HAEM02.q: Iliofemoral DVT with a threatened limb, caval thrombus on treatment, or a DVT with absolute contraindication - what next?
a: Start therapeutic heparin immediately in every case where it is not absolutely contraindicated - it is never the wrong first step.
Phlegmasia cerulea dolens (pale or ecchymotic limb, sensory loss): limb-threatening - catheter-directed thrombolysis or thrombectomy, after screening lysis contraindications.
Acute IVC thrombus despite anticoagulation: catheter-directed lysis or thrombectomy (about 85% early success) to prevent lethal PE.
DVT with an absolute contraindication (recent ICH, active GI bleed): no anticoagulation - weigh risks with the specialists and consider a retrievable IVC filter.
Filters cut recurrent PE at the cost of more DVT, so they are not routine and should be retrieved.

HAEM02.topic: Uraemic platelet dysfunction: test and treatment
HAEM02.q: Uraemic patient with mucosal bleeding and a normal platelet count - what test, and what corrects it?
a: Mechanism: a vWF-GPIb adhesion defect from uraemic toxins (guanidinosuccinic acid), NO excess and anaemia; PT, aPTT and fibrinogen are normal.
Test: prolonged PFA-100 closure time (or bleeding time).
Desmopressin 0.3-0.4 microgram/kg IV releases vWF and factor VIII: acts in ~1 h, lasts 4-8 h, tachyphylaxis after 2-3 doses; watch the sodium.
Dialysis, and correct anaemia to Hct ~30% (red cells push platelets to the vessel wall).
Cryoprecipitate for quick vWF; conjugated oestrogens act slowly but last ~2 weeks; tranexamic acid as adjunct.
Avoid heparin, especially LMWH, which accumulates in renal failure.

HAEM02.topic: Newly diagnosed ITP: treatment by bleeding, and in pregnancy
HAEM02.q: Platelets 12,000 in new ITP - what do you give, and what changes in pregnancy?
a: Platelets <30,000 or minor bleeding: a corticosteroid - ORAL dexamethasone 40 mg/day for 4 days or prednisone 1 mg/kg (ASH 2019).
Need a rapid rise (significant bleeding, before surgery): add IVIG 1 g/kg for 1-2 days.
Life-threatening bleeding: IVIG plus IV methylprednisolone 1 g/day plus platelet transfusion, with a TPO agonist if needed.
Transfused platelets alone are destroyed quickly, and marrow biopsy is not needed in typical ITP.
Pregnancy: steroids or IVIG first; if refractory, rituximab (or splenectomy in the second trimester). Mycophenolate is contraindicated.
It is chronic venous hypertension - pain, swelling, pigmentation, ulceration - months to years after a DVT, in up to a third of patients.
The only prevention is preventing the DVT: thromboprophylaxis for every at-risk hospitalisation and prompt, adequate anticoagulation of a DVT.
Graduated compression stockings, pentoxifylline and venous intervention TREAT established symptoms; they do not prevent it.
Risk is highest after proximal iliofemoral DVT and recurrent ipsilateral DVT.

HAEM02.topic: Irradiated vs leucodepleted vs CMV-negative blood
HAEM02.q: Irradiated, leucodepleted or CMV-negative blood - what does each prevent, and who needs it?
a: Irradiated (gamma, ~25 Gy): inactivates donor lymphocytes, preventing transfusion-associated GVHD, which is almost always fatal.
Irradiate for: Hodgkin lymphoma, HSCT recipients, purine analogues (fludarabine), congenital T-cell immunodeficiency, directed donations from relatives, HLA-matched platelets.
Leucodepleted: fewer febrile non-haemolytic reactions, less HLA alloimmunisation (platelet refractoriness) and less CMV transmission - it does NOT prevent TA-GVHD.
CMV-negative: largely replaced by leucodepletion, kept for pregnancy and intrauterine transfusion.

HAEM02.q: Life-threatening bleed on chronic anticoagulation with a normal PT and aPTT - which drug can hide like that?
a: Factor Xa inhibitors: apixaban barely prolongs the PT, rivaroxaban and edoxaban only variably, and the aPTT is usually normal - use a drug-calibrated anti-Xa level.
Dabigatran prolongs the aPTT and especially the thrombin time; a normal TT excludes dabigatran.
Warfarin: PT/INR. Argatroban: aPTT, and it falsely raises the INR.
LMWH: anti-Xa; the aPTT barely moves.

HAEM02.q: Name the three phases of the cell-based model and where each happens.
a: Initiation, on tissue-factor-bearing cells: TF-VIIa makes small amounts of Xa and thrombin.
Amplification: that thrombin activates platelets and factors V, VIII and XI.
Propagation, on the activated platelet: tenase (VIIIa/IXa) and prothrombinase (Xa/Va) produce the thrombin burst and fibrin.
Haemorrhagic-shock coagulopathy despite adequate fibrinogen and platelets, and haemophilia (VIII/IX), fail at PROPAGATION - which is why the initiation-based PT stays normal in haemophilia.

HEMO04.q: Mean systemic filling pressure (Pms) and venous return?
a: Pms = the pressure everywhere in the circulation when the heart stops and flow ceases (~7–15 mmHg); it drives venous return.
Venous return = (Pms − RAP) ÷ resistance to venous return — flow TO the right heart, not from the LV.
Pms rises with volume or venoconstriction (unstressed volume recruited to stressed); falls with vasodilation and sedation.
A rising RAP (PEEP, tamponade, RV failure) shrinks the gradient and venous return.

Opioid or anaesthetic hypotension with preserved contractility = venodilation: unstressed volume rises, Pms and venous return fall → treat with fluid or a venoconstrictor (low-dose noradrenaline, phenylephrine); contractility and stroke volume act on the cardiac-function curve, not venous return.

HEMO05A.topic: Why transfusion may not raise VO2
HEMO05A.q: Septic patient, Hb 7, lactic acidosis — why may a red-cell transfusion not raise tissue O2 consumption?
a: Stored red cells lose 2,3-DPG → left-shifted curve (higher affinity) → less O2 unloading; it recovers over 24–72 h.
Stored cells are less deformable and release free Hb that scavenges NO → microcirculatory plugging.
VO2 rises only if the patient is supply-dependent; in sepsis the defect is often extraction (mitochondrial), not delivery.

HEMO05A.q: Vascular occlusion test (VOT): how is it done and what do the slopes mean?
a: NIRS StO2 on the thenar eminence (not pulse oximetry).
Cuff 30 mmHg above SBP for ~3 min or until StO2 <40%.
Desaturation slope = local O2 consumption; reoxygenation slope after release = microvascular reserve (blunted in sepsis).

HY2.q: Hypertensive emergency: define it, how fast to lower, with what, and the exceptions?
a: BP ≥180/120 + acute organ damage (encephalopathy, ICH/stroke, ACS, pulmonary oedema, dissection, AKI/TMA, eclampsia) = emergency → ICU + IV titratable drug; no organ damage = urgency → oral drugs over 24–48 h.
Lower MAP by ≤25% in the 1st hour → 160/100–110 over the next 2–6 h → normal over 24–48 h (autoregulation is reset upward; fast drops cause watershed ischaemia).

Drugs by organ: encephalopathy/stroke → labetalol, nicardipine or clevidipine; acute pulmonary oedema → IV nitroglycerin + loop diuretic + NIV (avoid labetalol/β-blockers in decompensated HF); renal failure → fenoldopam, nicardipine or clevidipine (no prolonged nitroprusside: cyanide/thiocyanate); avoid nitroprusside with raised ICP; oral drugs are too slow.

Go faster: dissection SBP <120 and HR <60 within 20 min (β-blocker first); severe pre-eclampsia SBP <160 within 1 h; phaeochromocytoma α before β. Ischaemic stroke: treat only if >185/110 (before lysis) or >220/120.
Clonidine withdrawal: restart clonidine; if organ damage, phentolamine or labetalol — never an unopposed pure β-blocker.

Why it spirals: an abrupt BP rise injures the endothelium (lost NO, fibrinoid necrosis) and activates RAAS → more vasoconstriction; malignant hypertension's pressure natriuresis and RAAS surge cause volume depletion, hypokalaemia, polyuria and weight loss.

HY2.q: Infective endocarditis in the ICU: organism by setting, first steps, complications, and when to call the surgeon?
a: Organism: acute (days, sepsis, new severe regurgitation) = S. aureus — commonest overall, incl. IVDU right-sided and damaged/rheumatic valves; subacute native = viridans strep; early prosthetic (<1 y) = CoNS/S. aureus; after GU/GI procedures = enterococci; culture-negative = HACEK, Coxiella, Bartonella.
First: 3 sets of blood cultures from separate sites before antibiotics, then TTE (TEE if negative/non-diagnostic, prosthetic valve, or complication suspected); empirical cover including MRSA.

Diagnosis (Duke-ISCVID 2023): definite = 2 major, 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor; major = typical organism in 2 sets (non-typical, e.g. E. coli, needs ≥3) or vegetation/abscess on echo/PET-CT; minor = predisposition (RHD, prosthesis, IVDU), fever, embolic or immune signs (septic lung emboli, stroke, splenic infarct, red-cell-cast GN).

Urgent surgery: new AV block (= perivalvular/aortic-root abscess), HF from valve destruction, uncontrolled infection, large vegetation with emboli (splenic or cerebral embolus → cardiothoracic opinion).

Antibiotics: viridans strep MIC ≤0.12 → penicillin or ceftriaxone 4 wk; MIC >0.12–<0.5 → add gentamicin 2 wk, or ceftriaxone ALONE if gentamicin is unsafe (CKD, elderly); vancomycin only for β-lactam allergy. Culture-negative early prosthetic IE → vancomycin + gentamicin + cefepime + rifampicin; fungal prosthetic IE → liposomal amphotericin ± flucytosine plus early surgery.

HY2.topic: First rhythm in sudden cardiac arrest
HY2.q: First recorded rhythm in sudden cardiac arrest — which is commonest?
a: Overall out-of-hospital arrest: asystole/PEA now outnumber VF (VF ~20–25% and falling).
Witnessed collapse in the young or athletes: VF/VT is classic (HCM, channelopathy, commotio cordis) — the earlier the rhythm is recorded, the likelier VF.
Late sudden death weeks after MI: asystole ~50%, PEA ~20% as first rhythm (Tintinalli).

HY2.q: Hypertensive emergency (end-organ damage), no stroke or dissection: fundus grades and how fast to lower?
a: Keith-Wagener-Barker: I narrowing; II AV nipping; III haemorrhages, exudates, cotton-wool; IV = III + papilloedema (malignant).
Lower MAP 10–20% (≤25%) in the first hour, then to 160/100 over 2–6 h, normal over 24–48 h.
Exceptions: aortic dissection (SBP <120 in 20 min), pre-eclampsia (<160/110, aim 140–150/90–100), ischaemic stroke and ICH have their own targets.

HY3.q: Accidental hypothermia: stage, signs and rewarming?
a: 1. Core by lower-third oesophageal probe (epitympanic thermistor if not intubated); rectal lags, IR ear under-reads.
2. Mild 32–35 °C: shivering, tachycardia, cold diuresis, confusion → passive external rewarming.
3. Moderate 28–32 °C: shivering stops, bradycardia, AF, Osborn J waves, long PR/QRS/QT → forced-air + warmed IV fluid 38–42 °C.
4. Severe <28 °C or unstable (SBP <90, VA): VF with rough handling or a central wire → VA-ECMO/CPB (VV gives no circulation); lavage if no ECLS.

5. Traps: hypoglycaemia (alcohol; elderly, HF, PVD shiver less); rewarming shock (vasodilation after cold diuresis → hypotension: warmed fluid ± vasopressor); afterdrop (cold peripheral blood returns to the core). Post-arrest TTM 32–36 °C = mild range.

HY3.topic: Heat exhaustion vs classic vs exertional heat stroke
HY3.q: Heat exhaustion vs classic vs exertional heat stroke?
a: Heat exhaustion: core <40 °C, normal mentation, sweating → shade, rest, oral electrolyte fluid.
Heat stroke: core >40 °C + CNS dysfunction; CT may show diffuse cerebral oedema (loss of grey–white, effaced sulci: direct thermal BBB injury + endotoxaemia), later cerebellar Purkinje loss.
Classic: elderly/chronically ill in heat waves, dry skin; weak heart cannot raise skin blood flow to dump heat.
Exertional: young and fit; lactic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis (high CK), hyperkalaemia, AKI, DIC.
Early circulation hyperdynamic (high CO, low SVR); AST/ALT in the thousands = poor prognosis.
1. Hypoxia causes the arrest → 5 rescue breaths first, then CPR (ABC, not CAB).

2. No abdominal thrusts or draining water. Fresh vs salt water: both wash out/denature surfactant → collapse, shunt, ARDS-like hypoxaemia; managed the same (aspirated volume too small to shift electrolytes).
3. O2 to SpO2 >94%; awake and protecting airway → CPAP/NIV; falling GCS, exhaustion or NIV failure → intubate, lung-protective with PEEP.
4. Brief submersion, now normal SpO2, chest and CXR → observe 6–8 h, then discharge ('secondary drowning' is not an entity); no prophylactic antibiotics, steroids or routine bronchoscopy.
5. Prognosis: submersion time is the only validated predictor (<5 min good, >10 min poor); cold water and the diving reflex (apnoea, bradycardia, vasoconstriction; strongest in children) can protect.

HY3.topic: Necrotising soft-tissue infection and toxic shock
HY3.q: Necrotising soft-tissue infection or toxic shock: the path from suspicion to source control?
a: Suspect: pain out of proportion, bullae, crepitus, anaesthetic skin, putrid discharge, rapid spread (diabetic, any site incl. neck)
Urgent surgical exploration and debridement; do not delay for CT or culture; relook at 24–48 h
Broad cover (e.g. meropenem or pip-tazo + vancomycin/linezolid) PLUS clindamycin: it suppresses toxin synthesis (protein-synthesis inhibitor) even in resistant strains
Toxic shock (S. aureus/GAS): remove the source (nasal packing, tampon), fluids, β-lactam + clindamycin, ICU; IVIG for streptococcal TSS
Hyperbaric O2 only as an adjunct that never delays surgery (twice daily where used; EF <35% is a relative, not absolute, contraindication)

HY3.topic: Heat loss and fever vs hyperthermia
HY3.q: How does the body lose heat, and how do fever and hyperthermia differ?
a: At rest: radiation ~60%, evaporation ~20–25%, convection ~15% (moving air/water), conduction ~3%.
Sweat cools only by evaporation; when ambient exceeds skin temperature it is the only route, and it fails in high humidity.
Thresholds: vasoconstriction ~36.5 °C, shivering ~35.5 °C, shivering fails below ~32 °C.
Fever: cytokines → hypothalamic PGE2 raise the set point; antipyretics work.
Hyperthermia: normal set point, heat gain exceeds loss; antipyretics useless, cool physically.

HY3.topic: Necrotising soft-tissue infection: LRINEC, types and gas gangrene
HY3.q: Necrotising soft-tissue infection: LRINEC, the polymicrobial type, and gas gangrene with HBO?
a: LRINEC: CRP ≥150 mg/L (4) · WBC 15–25 (1), >25 (2) · Hb 11–13.5 (1), <11 (2) · Na <135 (2) · creatinine >1.6 mg/dL (2) · glucose >180 mg/dL (1); ≥6 suspicious, ≥8 high risk. No procalcitonin, lactate or CK.
Low sensitivity: a low score never excludes NSTI; suspicion → surgical exploration.
Synergistic (type I) gangrene: coliforms, staphylococci, Bacteroides, anaerobic streptococci; AEROBES destroy living tissue first, lowering redox potential so anaerobes thrive.
Gas gangrene (C. perfringens): crepitus, bronze skin, shock → radical debridement + penicillin + clindamycin (switches off toxin synthesis).
HBO2 is an adjunct after surgery: high tissue PO2 halts alpha-toxin production and is bacteriostatic; it must never delay theatre.

HY3.q: Unanticipated difficult intubation in an adult (DAS): the plan?
a: 1. Oxygenation beats intubation: preoxygenate and keep apnoeic oxygenation running (nasal O2 15 L/min or HFNO) to prolong safe apnoea time.
2. Plan A: at most 3 laryngoscopy attempts + 1 by the most experienced operator (bougie, videolaryngoscope), then declare failure.
3. Plan B: second-generation SGA, at most 3 attempts; if it oxygenates, stop and think: wake, proceed via SGA, or fibreoptic intubation through it.
4. Plan C: final face-mask attempt (two-person, adjuncts) with full neuromuscular block.
5. Plan D (CICO): scalpel–bougie–tube front-of-neck access.

HY3.q: Frostbite with clear blisters on intact fingers: thawing management?
a: Rapid rewarming in 37–39 °C water for 15–30 min until soft and red/purple; not if refreezing is possible.
Ibuprofen ~12 mg/kg/day in 2 doses (≈400 mg twice daily): analgesia + anti-thromboxane.
Drain clear blisters; leave haemorrhagic blisters intact.
Deep injury: iloprost or tPA within 24–48 h.

HY3.q: Lightning strike: unconscious, fixed dilated pupils, cold pale pulseless legs with weakness, normal CT. Explanation and triage?
a: Keraunoparalysis: transient lower > upper limb paralysis with pallor and absent pulses from catecholamine-mediated vasospasm; resolves over hours.
Fixed dilated pupils can be autonomic: never use them to stop resuscitation.
Reverse triage: resuscitate the 'apparently dead' first (asystole/respiratory arrest recovers if ventilated).
Also: Lichtenberg figures, tympanic rupture, later cataracts.

HY3.q: Epistaxis in an elderly hypertensive/IHD patient: where is it, and how do you stop it?
a: Elderly with IHD/HTN: posterior (sphenopalatine) source is more likely; anterior (Little's area) is the young.
Anterior: pressure, vasoconstrictor, chemical or electrical cautery.
Posterior: posterior pack or 12–14 Fr Foley balloon + anterior pack; refractory → sphenopalatine ligation or embolisation.
Cautery cannot reach a posterior source, so it is not the treatment of choice.

HY4.q: Lethargy to coma, and coma vs vegetative vs minimally conscious vs locked-in vs psychogenic: the separating feature?
a: Delirium = acute fluctuating inattention and disorganised thinking. Lethargy (rousable to voice) → obtundation (repeated stimulation) → stupor (only vigorous/painful, lapses back) → coma (unrousable, eyes closed).
Vegetative (unresponsive wakefulness): eyes open, sleep–wake cycles, reflexes only; minimally conscious: inconsistent but reproducible awareness (tracking, commands), better prognosis.
Locked-in (ventral pons: basilar thrombosis, pontine bleed): aware, quadriplegic, mute, vertical eye movement/blink; EEG normal. Brain death: no brainstem reflexes, apnoea, known irreversible cause.
Akinetic mutism (medial frontal): awake-appearing, no movement or speech from abulia.

Psychogenic: resists eyelid opening, gaze deviates to the ground whichever side is down, dropped hand avoids the face, cold calorics give nystagmus (needs an intact cortex; true coma = tonic deviation without nystagmus), normal reactive EEG.

HY4.q: Suspected anterior-circulation ischaemic stroke: the imaging-to-reperfusion path?
a: 1. NCCT first to exclude bleed; early ischaemia = loss of grey–white, insular ribbon, obscured lentiform, sulcal effacement (ASPECTS); hyperdense MCA = clot, not tissue.
2. <4.5 h and no bleed → IV lysis (wake-up: DWI–FLAIR mismatch).
3. LVO (ICA/M1), NIHSS ≥6, ASPECTS ≥6, <6 h → thrombectomy (± lysis).
4. 6–24 h or in-hospital/wake-up → CTA + CTP/MRI: DAWN clinical–core mismatch or DEFUSE-3 (core <70 mL, ratio ≥1.8) → thrombectomy; large core (ASPECTS 3–5) also benefits.
5. PROACT II (1999, IA prourokinase ≤6 h): recanalisation 66% vs 18%, mRS 0–2 40% vs 25%, sICH 10% vs 2%, benefit similar across risk strata = first proof of IA reperfusion.
6. After lysis: new headache, vomiting or decline → stop infusion, urgent NCCT (bleed/oedema). Glucose 140–180 mg/dL: SHINE (2019) intensive 80–130 gave no benefit and more hypoglycaemia.

HY4.topic: Deterioration in the days after ischaemic stroke
HY4.q: Worse in the first days after ischaemic stroke or thrombectomy: what is it and what do you do?
a: Haemorrhagic transformation: large infarct, high NIHSS, cardioembolic, hyperglycaemia, lysis; reperfusion into vessels damaged by ischaemia (MMP-9, BBB breakdown).
Petechial HT (GRE blooming, no mass effect) → supportive, BP control, hold anticoagulant; parenchymal haematoma with mass effect → manage as ICH.
New deficit in another territory right after thrombectomy = distal embolisation (~5–10%); new hyperdensity = contrast staining vs bleed (dual-energy CT; contrast clears by 24 h).
Fever + respiratory distress day 3–4 = aspiration pneumonia (dysphagia in up to 50%): NBM until swallow screen, head-up 30°.
Enhancement in an infarct at day 3–5 is usually luxury perfusion; abscess is rare.

HY4.q: Cerebral venous (sinus) thrombosis: recognise, image, treat?
a: 1. Suspect: thunderclap or progressive headache, seizures, papilloedema; young woman (OCP, pregnancy, puerperium), dehydration, infection.

2. Clue on CT: bilateral/parasagittal lobar bleed (superior sagittal); temporal haemorrhagic infarct = transverse sinus/vein of Labbé; chemosis + ptosis + CN VI palsy after face/ear infection = cavernous sinus.

3. Confirm: MRI with MR venography (absent flow void, clot in a sinus or cortical vein, haemorrhagic venous infarcts) = test of choice, also for isolated cortical vein thrombosis; CT venography if no MRI. CSF and skull X-ray do not diagnose it.
4. Treat: immediate UFH/LMWH even with haemorrhagic infarct; antiplatelets have no role; antibiotics for septic thrombosis.
5. Raised ICP: osmotherapy (mannitol, osm <320); worsening despite anticoagulation → endovascular thrombectomy; herniation → decompressive surgery.

HY4.q: When to start long-term antiseizure drugs in the ICU, which drug in liver failure, and how to find NCSE?
a: Seizure within 7 days of stroke = acute symptomatic (~10–30% recurrence): treat the episode, no long-term or primary prophylaxis.
Late seizure (>7 days) = epileptogenic scar (~70% recurrence) → long-term levetiracetam or lamotrigine.
LPDs without clinical or EEG seizure: supportive care + continuous EEG; treat if >2.5 Hz, evolving, 'plus' features or clinical correlate.
Liver failure: levetiracetam (renal, no interactions; lower dose + post-dialysis dose in ESRD); avoid valproate, phenytoin, carbamazepine.

NCSE: 10–30% of ICU patients with unexplained coma (after convulsive SE, TBI, stroke, CNS infection, sepsis, cefepime); commonest sign = altered mental status, twitching or gaze deviation only sometimes. Continuous EEG ≥24 h (48 h if comatose): a 30-min routine EEG misses many seizures.

HY4.q: Stroke and seizure mimics: what gives each away?
a: Hypoglycaemia: focal deficit reversing within minutes of dextrose; check glucose before lysis.
Todd's paresis: post-ictal deficit lasting hours (up to ~36–48 h); TIA by definition resolves <24 h; transient cortical DWI change reverses.
Syncope: trigger, pallor, <15 s stiffening or a few jerks, rapid full recovery, no post-ictal state.
Seizure: lateral tongue bite, head/eye deviation, tonic-clonic >30 s, post-ictal confusion; incontinence does not discriminate.
Lysing a mimic risks ICH for no gain.

HY4.q: Seizures, headache, visual loss, bilateral parieto-occipital vasogenic oedema: diagnosis, causes, treatment?
a: PRES: symmetrical posterior white-matter T2/FLAIR oedema WITHOUT diffusion restriction.
Two arms: raised capillary pressure beyond autoregulation (hypertensive encephalopathy, eclampsia, post-CEA) vs endothelial dysfunction (calcineurin inhibitors, chemotherapy, HELLP, HUS, sepsis).
Posterior predominance: sparse sympathetic innervation of the vertebrobasilar bed.
Tacrolimus toxicity: CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitors (diltiazem, azoles, macrolides, grapefruit) raise levels → check trough, reduce or switch to mTOR inhibitor.
Treat: lower MAP ≤25% in first hour, control seizures, remove trigger; usually reverses in days–weeks.

HY4.q: Back pain with new leg weakness, saddle anaesthesia or retention: the path?
a: 1. Emergency MRI whole spine with gadolinium (contrast CT/CT myelogram if no MRI).
2. Cauda equina (commonest: disc): saddle anaesthesia, retention, lax anal tone → decompression ASAP, not bed rest.
3. Fever + back pain after skin infection/IVDU = spinal epidural abscess → vancomycin + 3rd-gen cephalosporin + urgent neurosurgery.
4. After LP or neuraxial block in coagulopathy (DIC, petechiae, anticoagulant) = spinal epidural haematoma → reverse + urgent decompression (best within 8–12 h).

HY4.q: Vertigo, dysarthria, ipsilateral ataxia and Horner, crossed pain/temperature loss: syndrome, artery and scan?
a: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome: intracranial vertebral artery most often, PICA = classic exam answer.
Crossed sensory loss (face same side, body opposite) without limb weakness: pyramids are medial.
Scan: MRI DWI + MRA/CTA; CT misses most posterior-fossa infarcts.
ICU risk: dysphagia/hoarseness (nucleus ambiguus) → aspiration; can extend to basilar occlusion (→ thrombectomy).

HY4.q: TIA/minor stroke from 70–99% intracranial stenosis: best treatment?
a: Aggressive medical therapy: aspirin + clopidogrel 90 days, high-intensity statin, SBP <140 (SAMMPRIS).
Stenting was worse: 30-day stroke/death 14.7% vs 5.8%.
IV heparin: no benefit, more bleeding.
Minor stroke (NIHSS ≤3) or high-risk TIA of any cause: DAPT for 21 days (CHANCE/POINT).

Amaurosis fugax = retinal TIA: painless monocular 'curtain', usually 1–5 min, mostly spontaneous (not positional); emboli from carotid, arch or heart → urgent TIA work-up (carotid imaging, endarterectomy if ≥70% symptomatic, echo, ECG); exclude giant-cell arteritis if >50.

HY4.q: Malignant MCA infarction with falling GCS and shift: what saves life, and in whom?
a: Decompressive hemicraniectomy (flap ≥12 cm + duraplasty), ideally within 48 h.
Age ≤60 (DECIMAL/DESTINY/HAMLET pooled): 1-year mortality ~71% → 22% (NNT 2).
Age >60 (DESTINY II): mortality halves but most survivors mRS 4–5; decide with family.
Oedema peaks day 2–5; osmotherapy, hyperventilation, hypothermia only buy time; steroids do not help.

HY4.topic: Stroke in the young and moyamoya
HY4.q: Ischaemic stroke under 50: commonest causes, and how is moyamoya treated?
a: Cardioembolism (AF, PFO with paradoxical embolus, endocarditis, cardiomyopathy) — AF on ECG settles it.
Cervical artery dissection (neck pain, minor trauma, Horner): commonest under 45 with a normal ECG.
Antiphospholipid syndrome; cocaine/amphetamine.
Moyamoya (terminal ICA occlusion + 'puff of smoke' collaterals): revascularisation (direct/indirect bypass); efficacy judged by cerebrovascular reactivity (acetazolamide or CO2 challenge).

HY4.q: Young patient, stroke-like episodes crossing vascular territories, seizures, lactic acidosis, maternal history: diagnosis and ICU rules?
a: MELAS: mtDNA m.3243A>G, maternal inheritance; deafness, short stature, diabetes.
Lesions cortical/subcortical, often parieto-occipital, not in an arterial territory; raised blood/CSF lactate.
Confirm: muscle biopsy ragged-red fibres + genetic testing.
Acute: IV L-arginine; NO tPA (metabolic, not vascular).
SE: avoid valproate (blocks beta-oxidation, carnitine depletion, liver failure) and prolonged propofol; use levetiracetam, benzodiazepines, lacosamide.

HY4.q: NORSE: definition, commonest cause and treatment?
a: New-onset refractory SE without prior epilepsy or an acute structural, toxic or metabolic cause found within 72 h.
About half cryptogenic; commonest identified cause = autoimmune/paraneoplastic encephalitis (anti-NMDAR, LGI1, GAD65); MRI and CSF often bland.
Work-up: serum + CSF autoimmune panels, tumour screen (ovarian teratoma).
Treat: immunotherapy within 72 h (methylprednisolone 1 g × 5, IVIG or PLEX) → rituximab/cyclophosphamide; ketogenic diet; anakinra in FIRES (see SC-E-17).

HY6.q: Overt or occult GI bleeding with a normal OGD and colonoscopy: the pathway?
a: Treat as suspected small-bowel bleeding (~5–10% of GI bleeds); repeat a scope only if the first was inadequate
Stable → capsule endoscopy first (highest yield, non-invasive)
Capsule positive → device-assisted (balloon) enteroscopy to treat the lesion
Brisk bleeding or unstable → CT angiography, then catheter embolisation
Stable, slow intermittent bleed (0.1–0.5 mL/min) with negative scopes → Tc-99m red-cell scintigraphy: most sensitive and images for up to 24 h, but localises poorly

Commonest lesion in the elderly: angiodysplasia (right colon/small bowel; CKD, vWD, aortic stenosis = Heyde); recurrent bleeding despite endotherapy and unfit for surgery → octreotide (or thalidomide)

HY6.q: Bleeding peptic ulcer at endoscopy: Forrest class → rebleed risk → what to do?
a: Ia spurting / Ib oozing: active bleeding → endoscopic therapy (dual: adrenaline + clip or thermal)
IIa visible vessel: rebleed ~40–50% → endoscopic therapy
IIb adherent clot: ~20–30% → remove clot and treat the base if possible (high-dose PPI alone is acceptable)
IIc flat pigmented spot (~10%) and III clean base (<5%) → no endotherapy, oral PPI, early feeding
After endotherapy of Ia–IIb: high-dose PPI for 72 h (intermittent IV bolus is non-inferior to infusion)

HY6.q: GI bleed on aspirin + clopidogrel with a coronary stent placed 20 days ago: what happens to the antiplatelets?
a: Never stop aspirin: stopping DAPT in the first month after a stent carries a high risk of stent thrombosis (often fatal MI)
DocT keys: continue DAPT
ESGE 2021 / ACG-CAG 2022: if bleeding is life-threatening with high-risk stigmata, interrupt the P2Y12 inhibitor briefly and resume within ≤5 days, with cardiology input
Control the bleed: urgent endoscopic haemostasis + high-dose IV PPI; platelet transfusion does not help
Primary-prevention aspirin can be stopped; secondary-prevention aspirin restarts as soon as haemostasis is secure

HY7.q: Rapid sequence intubation — the sequence and the drugs?
a: Preoxygenate 3 min or 8 vital-capacity breaths (HFNC/NIV if hypoxaemic).
Induction agent then the neuromuscular blocker in immediate succession, without waiting for loss of consciousness or testing mask ventilation.
Gentle mask ventilation is now allowed if hypoxaemic (PREVENT).
Induction: ketamine 1–2 mg/kg or etomidate 0.3 mg/kg (haemodynamically safer); propofol if stable.
Paralysis: rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg (sugammadex reversal) or suxamethonium 1.5 mg/kg (avoid in hyperkalaemia, burns >24 h, denervation).

MISC05A.q: Diver, rapid ascent: within minutes chest pain, confusion, hemiparesis. Next step?
a: Arterial gas embolism → 100% O2, lie flat (not head-down), urgent hyperbaric oxygen.
Why: pressure shrinks bubbles (Boyle's law) and O2 washes out nitrogen; same for iatrogenic air embolism.
Drain a pneumothorax before recompression; steroids and thrombolysis have no role.

MV01.q: HME vs heated humidifier — when must you switch?
a: HME = passive 'artificial nose': returns only the heat and water the patient exhales; adds dead space (~50–100 mL) and resistance.
Switch to a heated humidifier for thick, copious or bloody secretions (they clog the HME).
Also switch for hypothermia, a large leak (bronchopleural fistula), minute ventilation >10 L/min, very low VT, and nebulised drugs.

VAP: HMEs leave less circuit condensate (a contaminated reservoir), but meta-analyses show no clear VAP or mortality difference; never combine HME with a heated humidifier, do not change circuits routinely, and drain condensate away from the patient.
Pores of Kohn — alveolus to alveolus.
Canals of Lambert — bronchiole to alveolus; channels of Martin — bronchiole to bronchiole.
They let gas bypass an obstructed airway, delaying absorption atelectasis.

MV01.q: West zones of the lung — pressure order and meaning?
a: Zone 1: Palv > Pa > Pv — no flow (alveolar dead space); appears with low pulmonary pressure (hypovolaemia) or high alveolar pressure (PEEP).
Zone 2: Pa > Palv > Pv — flow set by the arterial–alveolar difference (waterfall).
Zone 3: Pa > Pv > Palv — continuous flow; a PA catheter tip must sit here for PAWP to reflect LA pressure.

MV01.q: How do lung volumes and mechanics change with ageing?
a: Lost elastic recoil + stiffer chest wall: closing capacity rises and exceeds FRC (supine ~44 y, sitting ~65 y) → airway closure, V/Q mismatch, falling PaO2.
RV and FRC rise slightly, vital capacity falls, TLC roughly unchanged.
FEV1 and FEV1/FVC fall; lung compliance rises, chest-wall compliance falls.

MV03.q: Patient suddenly fighting the ventilator after settling well — the sequence?
a: Disconnect and hand-bag with 100% O2 — separates patient problems from machine problems.
Easy bagging and the distress settles → ventilator/circuit problem (settings, leak, trigger).
Check the tube: pass a suction catheter (displacement, obstruction, plug, biting), check cuff and position.
Examine and image: pneumothorax, bronchospasm, plug/collapse, pulmonary oedema, auto-PEEP (CXR, ABG, lung US).
Then patient causes: pain, delirium, high drive — raise pressure support or add mandatory breaths if under-supported.
No sedation or paralysis until the cause is found.

MV04B.q: Tracheostomy complications — early (<7 days) vs late, and the sign of each?
a: Early: bleeding, displacement/false passage, surgical emphysema, pneumothorax, tube obstruction, stoma infection.
Early ooze (hours) → pack around the tube (iodophor gauze), check Hct, keep the tube in — this is not a tracheo-innominate fistula.
Late bleeding >48 h, especially a sentinel bleed from day 3 to 6 weeks = tracheo-innominate fistula until proven otherwise → hyperinflate the cuff, finger compression through the stoma, theatre.

Other late: hard-to-pass suction catheter/bleeding → granuloma; persistent cuff leak → tracheomalacia; stridor after decannulation → stenosis (cuff >30 cmH2O); feed in secretions → tracheo-oesophageal fistula.

MV04B.q: Complications of tracheal intubation — immediate, while intubated, late?
a: Immediate: failed or oesophageal intubation, dental/pharyngeal/laryngeal trauma, aspiration, hypoxia, hypotension, arrhythmia.
While intubated: tube blockage or displacement, VAP, sinusitis.
Late (weeks after extubation): laryngeal oedema or granuloma, vocal-cord palsy, tracheal stenosis, tracheomalacia — so 'early tracheal stenosis' is the odd one out.

MV04B.q: Percutaneous tracheostomy — contraindications and the pre-procedure check?
a: Contraindications: impalpable cricoid or unfavourable anatomy, midline neck mass/goitre, high-riding innominate artery (pulsatile swelling), uncorrected coagulopathy, children, PEEP ≥15 cmH2O.

Pre-procedure neck ultrasound maps vessels (innominate artery, anterior jugular veins, thyroid-isthmus vessels) to choose or abandon the site; bronchoscopy shows the lumen, not the vessels in front of it.
Higher-risk necks: obesity, short neck, goitre, previous neck surgery → open surgical tracheostomy if anatomy is unfavourable.

MV04B.q: Tracheostomy patient desaturating and a suction catheter won't pass — the NTSP sequence?
a: Call for help; high-flow O2 to the face AND the stoma.
Remove speaking valve/cap and the inner tube.
Try a suction catheter: if it passes, the tube is patent — suction, reassess, ventilate.
If it does not pass, deflate the cuff; if no improvement, REMOVE the tracheostomy tube.
Oxygenate from above (bag-mask, stoma covered) or via the stoma (small mask/LMA on the stoma).
Then secure the airway: oral intubation, or re-insert a tube through a mature stoma.
Percussion and vibration with postural drainage.
Positive expiratory pressure (PEP) devices — positive, never 'negative end-expiratory pressure' therapy.
Intrapulmonary percussive ventilation; high-frequency chest-wall oscillation (vest); active cycle of breathing.
Vasogenic: BBB breakdown, extracellular fluid, WHITE matter, finger-like, spares cortex; T2/FLAIR bright, NO diffusion restriction (high ADC).
Causes: tumour, abscess, PRES, contusion. Tumour oedema → dexamethasone (10 mg IV, then 4 mg 6-hourly): tightens the leaky BBB over hours–days; mannitol/hypertonic saline only bridge herniation.
Cytotoxic: failed Na/K-ATPase, cell swelling, grey + white matter; DWI bright, low ADC.
Causes: ischaemia, hypoxia, trauma, hyponatraemia, acute liver failure; steroids useless (and raise mortality in TBI, CRASH).

NEURO01.q: Basal skull fracture: signs and the ICU rules?
a: Haemotympanum, Battle's sign (mastoid bruising at 24–48 h), raccoon eyes, CSF rhinorrhoea/otorrhoea (halo test, beta-2 transferrin), VII/VIII palsy.
No nasal tubes (NG, nasotracheal): can pass intracranially; use orogastric.
Avoid nasal NIV/CPAP: forces air through the defect → pneumocephalus.
Post-traumatic meningitis is usually pneumococcal.

NEURO01.q: FOUR score: the four components, each 0–4 (max 16)?
a: E: 4 open, tracking/blinking to command · 3 open, not tracking · 2 closed, open to loud voice · 1 closed, open to pain · 0 closed with pain.
M: 4 thumbs-up/fist/peace sign · 3 localises pain · 2 flexion · 1 extension · 0 none or myoclonic status.
B: 4 pupil and corneal reflexes present · 3 one pupil wide and fixed · 2 pupil OR corneal reflexes absent · 1 both absent · 0 pupil, corneal and cough absent.
R: 4 not intubated, regular · 3 Cheyne–Stokes · 2 irregular · 1 breathes above ventilator rate · 0 at ventilator rate or apnoea.
Why: works in intubated patients and tests the brainstem, which GCS misses.

NEURO02.q: Why can brain temperature exceed core temperature after brain injury?
a: The brain loses heat only through blood flow.
Oedema, haemorrhage or hypoxia cut that flow, so injured brain runs ~0.5–2 °C above core.
A normal bladder temperature can hide a febrile injured brain: hence strict fever prevention after brain injury.

NEURO02.q: Blood biomarkers of brain injury: which cell does each come from?
a: GFAP: astrocytes (glial-specific), rises within 1 h, stays up days.
UCH-L1: neuronal cell body, early peak (~8 h); GFAP + UCH-L1 together FDA-cleared to rule out CT lesions in mild TBI (high NPV).
NSE: neurons + red cells (haemolysis confounds; post-arrest prognosis).
S100B: astrocytes but also extracranial (a normal value within 6 h rules out a CT lesion in mild TBI, Scandinavian guideline); MBP: myelin; tau and neurofilament light: axonal injury, prognosis.

NEURO04.topic: Age of blood on MRI and infarct on CT
NEURO04.q: Age the blood on MRI (T1/T2), and what marks an old infarct on CT?
a: Hyperacute (oxyHb): T1 iso, T2 hyper. Acute (deoxyHb): T1 iso, T2 HYPO.
Early subacute (intracellular metHb): T1 HYPER, T2 hypo. Late subacute (extracellular metHb): T1 HYPER, T2 HYPER.
Chronic (haemosiderin): T1 and T2 hypo rim. (Mnemonic: It Be, Iddy Biddy, BaBy, Doo Doo.)
Chronic infarct on CT: volume loss with ex vacuo dilatation of the adjacent ventricle/sulci and CSF-density encephalomalacia; acute = hyperdense vessel, lost grey–white, sulcal effacement.

NEURO04.q: ABCD2 score after TIA — items and risk bands?
a: Clinical: unilateral weakness 2, speech disturbance without weakness 1.
Duration ≥60 min 2, 10–59 min 1; Diabetes 1.
0–3 low, 4–5 moderate, 6–7 high 2-day stroke risk; CHA2DS2-VASc is the AF score, not this.

NEURO05.q: Multimodal monitoring: what do a high PRx and a high lactate:pyruvate ratio mean?
a: PRx = moving correlation of slow MAP and ICP waves: ≤0 intact autoregulation; >0.2–0.3 pressure-passive, worse outcome.
High PRx → target CPPopt (CPP where PRx is lowest) instead of a fixed 60–70.
Microdialysis LPR: normal <25, >40 = metabolic crisis.
High LPR + LOW pyruvate = ischaemia (raise CPP/O2); high LPR + normal/high pyruvate = mitochondrial dysfunction.
Low glucose = hypoglycaemia/hypermetabolism; high glutamate/glycerol = excitotoxicity/membrane breakdown.

NEURO05.q: Hydrocephalus and CSF disorders: first test and the classic facts?
a: CT is first line for suspected hydrocephalus (fast, shows ventricles); MRI defines the cause.
Communicating hydrocephalus: LP shows raised pressure and relieves it temporarily; contraindicated in obstructive.
IIH: raised CSF pressure with normal or small ventricles (young obese women; threat = visual loss).
NPH: reversible dementia + gait apraxia + urinary incontinence.

NEURO06B.q: Rib fractures or thoracotomy pain in ICU: why an epidural, and what if pain breaks through away from the tip?
a: Elderly with >3 rib fractures: thoracic epidural LA gives best analgesia, breathing and cough (better than IV PCA; mortality benefit unproven); ICU/HDU care.

Epidural contraindicated (antiplatelet/anticoagulant: neuraxial haematoma) → erector spinae, serratus anterior or paravertebral catheter; add paracetamol; avoid NSAIDs in CKD and opioid-only PCA (respiratory depression).
Breakthrough pain in dermatomes away from the tip: switch fentanyl to a hydrophilic opioid (hydromorphone/morphine), which spreads in CSF.
Then bolus/raise volume (spread follows volume) or re-site; double concentration at half rate = same dose, less spread.

NEURO06B.q: NPIAP pressure injury: full-thickness loss down to but not through fascia = stage ____; exposed bone, tendon or muscle = stage ____.
a: Stage 4 (no stage 5): fascia, muscle, tendon or bone exposed. Stage 1 intact non-blanchable erythema; 2 partial thickness, exposed dermis/blister; 3 full thickness into fat, down to but not through fascia (slough possible).
Unstageable = base hidden by slough/eschar; deep tissue injury = purple intact skin.

NEURO06B.q: Opioid withdrawal in the ICU: recognise, prevent, treat?
a: After >5–7 days of infusion: tachycardia, hypertension, sweating, yawning, mydriasis, diarrhoea, agitation.
Prevent: taper 10–20%/day.
Treat: enteral methadone conversion (Wanzuita 2012: faster weaning) ± clonidine/dexmedetomidine.
Opioid use disorder: continue/start buprenorphine (partial agonist, respiratory ceiling).
Never naloxone: precipitates withdrawal.

NEURO06B.q: After RSI with etomidate + rocuronium the patient is paralysed but unsedated — what next, and why?
a: Rocuronium (~45–60 min) outlasts etomidate (~5–10 min), so the patient can be awake and paralysed within minutes — start sedation as soon as the tube is confirmed.
PADIS is analgesia-first, but a chronic benzodiazepine user also needs a sedative to cover withdrawal: propofol (or a benzodiazepine) plus an opioid.
Watch for awareness: tachycardia, hypertension, lacrimation.

NEURO06B.q: AnaConDa = disposable ____ for inhaled ICU sedation.
a: Vaporiser + HME with a carbon filter that reflects ~90% of isoflurane/sevoflurane back to the patient.
Used for volatile sedation in ventilated ICU patients (scavenging needed).

NMD01.q: ICU neuromuscular blockers: organ-independent clearance, its catch, and causes of prolonged block?
a: Cisatracurium/atracurium: >75% Hofmann elimination (pH and temperature dependent) + ester hydrolysis = infusion of choice in multi-organ failure and ARDS.
Catch: metabolite laudanosine (renal/hepatic clearance, long t½) lowers seizure threshold.
Rocuronium/vecuronium: hepatic/biliary; pancuronium: renal.
Prolonged block: hypothermia, acidosis, hypokalaemia, hypermagnesaemia, hypocalcaemia, renal/hepatic failure, aminoglycosides.

NMD01.q: Tetanus after a puncture wound: recognise and first step?
a: Trismus (positive spatula test: bites the spatula), risus sardonicus, opisthotonus, rigid abdomen, spasms; autonomic storm later.
First: human tetanus immunoglobulin 500 IU IM/IV (as effective as higher doses) + wound debridement.
Metronidazole; benzodiazepines/magnesium for spasms; early airway and tracheostomy.
Tetanus toxoid too: disease does not confer immunity.

Week 2: autonomic storm (tetanospasmin also disinhibits sympathetic outflow): labile BP, tachy- then bradyarrhythmia, arrest = leading cause of death → magnesium infusion, deep sedation (benzodiazepine, morphine), cautious labetalol/esmolol; avoid unopposed β-blockade.

NMD01.q: Abdominal pain, hyponatraemia, confusion, hypertension or seizure after a trigger: acute porphyria crisis — what now?
a: 1. Suspect after triggers: thiopentone, etomidate, diclofenac, phenytoin, fasting, alcohol, OCP.
2. Urine porphobilinogen.
3. IV haem arginate/hemin (first-line) + IV glucose (carbohydrate loading).
4. Stop triggers; seizures → benzodiazepines/levetiracetam/gabapentin; avoid phenytoin and barbiturates.
5. Treat hyponatraemia, pain (opioids) and autonomic surges (beta-blocker); watch for GBS-like paralysis.

NMD01.q: Intrathecal baclofen pump, missed refill: picture and danger?
a: Rebound spasticity and rigidity, pruritus, hyperthermia, tachycardia, labile BP, delirium/hallucinations, seizures.
Can progress to rhabdomyolysis, DIC, multi-organ failure (mimics NMS, MH, serotonin syndrome, sepsis).
Treat: restore intrathecal baclofen urgently; oral baclofen and benzodiazepines as a bridge.

NMD02.q: Refractory generalised myasthenia: which biologics, and what do they target?
a: C5 complement inhibitors: eculizumab (REGAIN), ravulizumab, zilucoplan; block membrane-attack-complex damage at the end-plate; AChR-antibody-positive only; meningococcal vaccination first.
FcRn blockers (efgartigimod, rozanolixizumab): speed IgG breakdown, lowering pathogenic antibody.
Rituximab (anti-CD20): best in MuSK-positive disease.

OBS01.q: Asthma in pregnancy: what does poor control cost, and how is it treated by severity?
a: Poor control (maternal hypoxia) → pre-eclampsia (the most consistent risk), gestational hypertension, caesarean, fetal growth restriction, preterm birth; good control removes most of the risk.
Treat as outside pregnancy: MILD → inhaled SABA ± low-dose ICS (budesonide best studied); add LABA, then oral steroids for severe/uncontrolled disease; theophylline alone is inadequate.
Acute attack: O2 to SpO2 ≥95%, nebulised SABA + ipratropium, systemic steroids, IV magnesium; a 'normal' PaCO2 of ~40 signals failure (normal pregnant PaCO2 ~30).
Hypoxia harms the fetus more than any asthma drug.

OBS02A.q: CHIPS and HYPITAT: question and answer?
a: CHIPS (2015): non-severe hypertension, tight (DBP 85) vs less-tight (DBP 100).
No difference in pregnancy loss or neonatal high-level care; tight control cut severe hypertension (~28% vs 41%).
HYPITAT (2009): gestational hypertension/mild pre-eclampsia at 36–41 weeks, induction vs expectant.
Induction cut poor maternal outcome 44% → 31% without more caesareans.
Hence: treat to DBP 85; deliver mild disease at 37 weeks.

OBS02A.q: GDM on insulin, normal fasting glucose the day after caesarean: next step?
a: Stop insulin: placental anti-insulin hormones are gone.
Check glucose; 75 g OGTT at 6–12 weeks postpartum (lifelong type 2 risk).

OBS02B.topic: PPH risk and the shock index
OBS02B.q: Obstetric haemorrhage: admission risk (AWHONN) and the shock index?
a: Medium risk: prior caesarean/uterine surgery, multiple gestation, >4 vaginal births, chorioamnionitis, prior PPH, fibroids, EFW >4 kg, BMI >40, polyhydramnios.
High risk: praevia/low-lying, suspected accreta, Hct <30%, platelets <100,000, active bleeding, coagulopathy, OR ≥2 medium factors → crossmatch 2 units, plan MTP.
Shock index = HR/SBP: normal 0.5–0.7 (pregnancy 0.7–0.9).
≥0.9–1.1 = significant loss; >1.4–1.7 = urgent transfusion/MTP.

OBS02B.q: NYHA III–IV mothers are ~10% of pregnant cardiac patients but ~____% of cardiac deaths.
a: ~85%; NYHA I–II mortality <1%.
Pregnancy contraindicated in mWHO IV: PAH, EF <30%, severe MS or symptomatic AS, Marfan aorta >45 mm.
Peak danger: late 2nd/3rd trimester, labour, first days postpartum (autotransfusion).

RENAL01.topic: Contrast in two special situations: anuric ESRD and ACS
RENAL01.q: Does an anuric dialysis patient need urgent dialysis after contrast, and can contrast be delayed in ACS?
a: Anuric ESRD on haemodialysis: there is no residual function to lose, so there is no CI-AKI concern and no need for urgent post-contrast dialysis - keep the usual schedule.
An unscheduled urgent session only adds harmful fluid and electrolyte shifts.
In ACS never delay angiography or reperfusion because of contrast-nephropathy risk: the ischaemic cost outweighs it.
Mitigate instead: lowest diagnostic contrast dose, isotonic saline where tolerated, review nephrotoxins.
NAC and bicarbonate have no proven benefit (PRESERVE); holding an ACE inhibitor or ARB is supportive only.

RENAL01.q: What changed in CKD-EPI 2021, and why add cystatin C?
a: The 2021 equations removed the race coefficient, keeping age and sex terms.
eGFRcr-cys (creatinine plus cystatin C) is the most accurate, because cystatin C does not depend on muscle mass.
When cystatin C is high relative to creatinine (sarcopenia, critical illness), the combined eGFR comes out LOWER than the creatinine-only value.
Steroids, thyroid state and inflammation move cystatin C independently of GFR.
In AKI there is no steady state, so neither equation applies - use the creatinine trend and urine output.

RENAL02.q: New problems after a kidney transplant - what fits which interval?
a: Delayed graft function = need for dialysis within 7 days of transplant. Acute allograft dysfunction = creatinine rise >10% from baseline or an absolute rise of ~0.2 mg/dL (20 micromol/L) - either triggers Doppler, drug levels and biopsy.
Minutes: hyperacute rejection from preformed antibodies - now rare with crossmatching.

Hours to the first week: sudden anuria or graft pain with a patent catheter = vascular thrombosis. Renal VEIN thrombosis (commoner, peak day 3-7, haematuria, graft swelling) shows REVERSED diastolic arterial flow on Doppler; arterial thrombosis shows absent flow. Re-exploration rarely salvages the graft - nephrectomy is usual.

3 months to 2 years: new severe hypertension with rising creatinine, a bruit, and a biopsy showing no rejection means transplant renal artery stenosis - Doppler first (high peak systolic velocity), then angiography and stenting.
Keep the order: ultrasound and Doppler come before angiography in every one of these.

RENAL02.topic: Drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis: the management path
RENAL02.q: AKI three weeks after starting a PPI, with sterile pyuria and eosinophilia - what do you do?
a: Clue: a new drug (PPI, beta-lactam, NSAID, rifampicin - rifampicin AIN follows RE-exposure or intermittent dosing) plus AKI with sterile pyuria and WBC casts; the rash-fever-eosinophilia triad appears in under 10%. Non-drug causes: infection (Legionella, leptospira, CMV), SLE, Sjogren, sarcoid, TINU - hypertension causes nephrosclerosis, not AIN.
STOP the culprit drug at once - the first and most important step.
No creatinine recovery in 5-7 days: kidney biopsy if feasible, then prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day (maximum 60 mg) tapered over 4-6 weeks; earlier steroids mean less fibrosis.
Urine eosinophils are useless - poor sensitivity and specificity.
Dialysis only for the usual emergency indications.

RENAL02.q: Elderly vascular patient, livedo reticularis and blue toes with subacute AKI days to weeks after angiography?
a: Cholesterol atheroembolism (not contrast nephropathy, which starts within 48-72 h and recovers).
Clues: eosinophilia, eosinophiluria, low complement, Hollenhorst plaques on fundoscopy, and often a recent catheter procedure or new anticoagulation.

Course is subacute and stepwise over weeks after angiography, angioplasty, aortic surgery, anticoagulation or thrombolysis, often with stroke, gut or skin involvement - and creatinine often fails to recover, unlike contrast AKI.
Biopsy shows biconvex cholesterol clefts in arterioles.
Treatment is supportive with a statin; stop further catheter manipulation and avoid adding anticoagulation.

RENAL02.topic: Uraemic encephalopathy vs dialysis disequilibrium vs dialysis dementia
RENAL02.q: Confusion with asterixis and myoclonus in a dialysis patient - which of the three, and what do you do?
a: Uraemic (under-dialysis): guanidino compounds and urea inhibit GABA-A and activate NMDA - confusion, asterixis, multifocal myoclonus, seizures; the fix is more dialysis.
Before blaming uraemia, exclude drug accumulation (gabapentin, cefepime, opioids), hypoglycaemia and subdural haematoma.
Disequilibrium: during or just after a first or aggressive session - urea falls faster in blood than brain, giving cerebral oedema (headache, vomiting, seizures); stop dialysis, give mannitol.
Dialysis dementia: chronic aluminium (untreated dialysate, aluminium binders) - stuttering dysarthria to speech arrest, myoclonus, seizures, dementia; treat with desferrioxamine.
Aluminium is now rare with reverse-osmosis water, so under-dialysis is the commoner modern cause of asterixis with myoclonus.

RENAL02.q: Systemic sclerosis on high-dose steroids with BP 190/110, schistocytes and AKI - what now?
a: Scleroderma renal crisis: malignant hypertension plus microangiopathic haemolysis plus AKI.
An ACE INHIBITOR (captopril, short-acting, titrated to the maximum tolerated dose) is the treatment, even as creatinine rises.
High-dose corticosteroids precipitate it, so they are the clue in the stem and should be withdrawn where possible.
Anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies mark the at-risk patient; diffuse early disease is the usual setting.
This is not TTP: plasma exchange is not the answer, and ARBs and calcium-channel blockers do not substitute for the ACE inhibitor.

RENAL02.q: Rhabdomyolysis AKI followed by pulmonary oedema and cardiac decline - which cardiorenal type?
a: Type 1: acute heart to kidney (acute decompensated heart failure causing AKI).
Type 2: chronic heart to kidney (chronic heart failure causing CKD).
Type 3: acute KIDNEY to heart - AKI with volume and uraemic load causing pulmonary oedema and myocardial dysfunction (the rhabdomyolysis case).
Type 4: chronic kidney to heart (CKD driving cardiac disease).
Type 5: systemic disease hitting both (sepsis, amyloid).

RENAL02.q: Septic diabetic with flank pain and gas in or around the kidney - what is it and what do you do?
a: Gas in the renal parenchyma or collecting system in a septic diabetic = emphysematous pyelonephritis (E. coli, Klebsiella).
CT is the test of choice and classifies the extent.
Treat: resuscitation, antibiotics and relief of any obstruction (stent or nephrostomy) +/- percutaneous drainage; nephrectomy if extensive or failing.
Look-alikes: pyonephrosis (pus, no gas), xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis (staghorn calculus with a fat-laden mass).

RESP01A.topic: Goals in acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure
RESP01A.q: Therapeutic goals in acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure?
a: Least PEEP that gives SpO2 ≥90% on FiO2 <0.6.
Least VT/plateau pressure compatible with pH >7.2 (accept hypercapnia).
Least circulating volume/PAWP that keeps adequate O2 delivery and urine output.

RESP01B.topic: NIV: CPAP vs BiPAP and contraindications
RESP01B.q: NIV: CPAP vs BiPAP — what each pressure does, and who must not get NIV?
a: CPAP = one continuous pressure: recruits alveoli, raises FRC and oxygenation (cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, OSA).
BiPAP = IPAP + EPAP; pressure support (IPAP − EPAP) unloads breathing and clears CO2, EPAP recruits and oxygenates (and offsets auto-PEEP).
Contraindications: GCS <8 or cannot protect the airway, apnoea/arrest, vomiting or upper GI bleed, shock, agitation/non-cooperation, facial trauma, undrained pneumothorax.
Cardiogenic shock with confusion and hypoxaemic oedema → intubate, not NIV; overdose with GCS <8 and RR 6 → intubate.

RESP02A.q: Chest X-ray signs of emphysema / hyperinflation?
a: Flat hemidiaphragms (>6 anterior or >10 posterior ribs above them).
Wide retrosternal air space on the lateral film; long, narrow vertical heart.
Pruned peripheral vessels; bullae.
Why: lost elastic recoil raises FRC and RV, so the chest sits at high volume; acute asthma can hyperinflate too.

RESP02A.q: 'Asthma' that repeatedly needs intubation and settles once intubated — what is it, and how is it shown?
a: Suspect tracheomalacia or excessive dynamic airway collapse (EDAC): the tube stents the collapsing airway, so the 'bronchospasm' vanishes on intubation.
Diagnose by dynamic bronchoscopy after extubation (forced expiration/cough) or dynamic expiratory CT — an inspiratory CT can be normal.
Vocal-cord dysfunction is the other mimic (speech therapy); treat EDAC with CPAP, stenting or tracheobronchoplasty.

RESP02A.q: Pulmonary function pattern in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis?
a: Restrictive: TLC, FRC, RV, FEV1 and FVC all reduced; FEV1/FVC normal or raised (increased elastic recoil).
DLCO reduced early (thickened membrane); desaturation on exercise.
Volumes fall further as the lung stiffens.

RESP02B.q: MDI on a ventilated patient — how do you maximise delivery?
a: Spacer in the inspiratory limb ~15 cm from the Y-piece; actuate at the START of inspiration.
Low inspiratory flow, VT >500 mL, longer Ti with a pause; remove the HME (or place the device between HME and patient).
Wider ETT helps; deposition falls with high flow, small tubes and humidified gas; typical dose 4–8 puffs.

Nebuliser with the HME left in place: the filter traps the aerosol and almost no drug arrives — remove the HME during nebulisation; volume control with a square, low inspiratory flow carries aerosol more consistently than pressure control.
Vibrating-mesh nebuliser is electrically powered: no added driving gas, so VT, trigger and FiO2 are undisturbed and it refills without breaking the circuit; a jet nebuliser adds 6–8 L/min of gas.

RESP03.q: Respiratory failure types I–IV — mechanism and typical setting?
a: Type I (hypoxaemic): V/Q mismatch/shunt; PaO2 <60 with normal or low PaCO2 (pneumonia, ARDS, oedema).
Type II (hypercapnic): alveolar hypoventilation; PaCO2 >45–50 with acidosis (COPD, opioids, neuromuscular).
Type III (perioperative): atelectasis from low FRC, pain and splinting after upper abdominal surgery; mainly hypoxaemia, CO2 may rise.

Type IV (shock): normal lungs and pump, but respiratory-muscle hypoperfusion and high ventilatory demand (sepsis, cardiogenic shock) → fatigue; ventilate to unload the muscles until shock is reversed.

RESP03.q: Negative-pressure pulmonary oedema — mechanism and causes?
a: Forceful inspiration against an obstructed upper airway creates very negative intrathoracic pressure → raised transmural capillary pressure → non-cardiogenic oedema within minutes to hours.
Causes: post-extubation laryngospasm (commonest), upper-airway tumour or infection, vocal-cord palsy, strangulation/hanging, biting the ETT; cardiac failure is not a cause.
Treat: relieve the obstruction, O2/CPAP or reintubation; resolves in 12–48 h.

RESP03.q: Lymphoma with a large anterior mediastinal mass needs intubation — best predictor of collapse at induction, and the plan?
a: Symptoms when supine (orthopnoea, cough, stridor) predict compression; normal PFTs or auscultation do not reassure.
Induction, paralysis and positive pressure remove the muscle tone and negative intrathoracic pressure that hold the airway open, so the mass compresses trachea, bronchi or pulmonary artery.
Plan: CT first, keep spontaneous breathing (awake fibreoptic intubation, sitting up), rigid bronchoscope ready, ECMO standby if high risk; steroids or radiotherapy can shrink the mass first.

RESP03.q: Ventilated patient, sudden hypoxaemia not fixed by FiO2/PEEP/tube check; CXR: retrocardiac triangle with loss of the left hemidiaphragm — diagnosis and next step?
a: Left lower lobe collapse ('sail sign'), usually from a mucus plug.
Next: therapeutic bronchoscopy to clear the plug (plus suction, humidification, physiotherapy).
Not needle decompression (tension pneumothorax is hyperlucent with shift away); not advancing the tube (right mainstem intubation collapses the whole left lung).

RESP04.topic: Airway in neck infection or airway trauma
RESP04.q: Airway in neck infection or airway trauma — which technique?
a: Ludwig angina/deep neck infection with drooling or distress → secure the airway first by awake fibreoptic intubation (surgical airway ready); antibiotics and drainage after.
Suspected laryngeal injury (hanging, blunt neck) with stridor → flexible fibreoptic intubation: it sees tears and avoids a false passage.
Open tracheal wound after failed intubation → pass the tube through the wound; avoid cricothyrotomy when the larynx/cricoid is injured (the cricoid is the stent).
Tracheobronchial injury clues: surgical emphysema, pneumomediastinum, persistent air leak, elevated hyoid (cervical transection); up to 20% have a normal X-ray.

Critical subglottic stenosis after prolonged intubation with failed oral/nasal intubation → emergency tracheostomy BELOW the stenosis; a cricothyroidotomy enters at or above the narrowing, and NIV/HFNO cannot bypass a fixed obstruction.
Low: minor day-case surgery <30 min with early ambulation (e.g. inguinal hernia).
Moderate: major general, gynaecological, maxillofacial surgery or splenectomy without extra risk factors.
